en: The Scripture on the Ten Stages, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty.
1. The Stage of Joy (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*). First: The Stage of Joy.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was in the Maṇi-jewel palace of the king of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and had gathered there from various other realms.

These bodhisattvas have attained mastery over the entire range of wisdom-practice of all bodhisattvas; they have entered all points of entry into the wisdom of the Tathāgatas; they are skillfully able to teach and transform all worlds, universally manifesting supernatural powers and other such deeds according to the occasion.
In every moment of thought, they are able to accomplish and fulfill all the vows of bodhisattvas, constantly practicing all bodhisattva deeds in all worlds, throughout all eons, and in all lands.

They are fully endowed with all the merit and wisdom of all bodhisattvas, which is inexhaustible; they are able to bring benefit to all beings, reach the further shore of all bodhisattvas' wisdom and skillful means, and demonstrate to sentient beings the gates of birth-and-death and nirvana.

They do not cease any of the practices of bodhisattvas; they skillfully traverse all bodhisattva meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, supernormal powers, and clear wisdoms. They are well able to manifest all their activities and have fully attained all the effortless spiritual powers (*anabhisaṃskāra-ṛddhipāda*) of bodhisattvas. In a single thought-moment, they can reach the great assemblies of the Buddhas of the ten directions to exhort, inquire, and receive and uphold the Wheel of Dharma.
They constantly make offerings to all Buddhas with a vast mind, and are always able to cultivate the deeds and practices of all great Bodhisattvas.
Their bodies manifest universally throughout immeasurable worlds;
their voices are heard everywhere, reaching all places without exception.
Their minds are thoroughly penetrating, clearly seeing all bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
They have fully cultivated and perfected all their merits.
Thus, the merits of these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are immeasurable and boundless; even if one were to speak for incalculable eons, they could not be exhausted.
Their names were:
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, Ratnagarbha, Padmagarbha, Guṇagarbha, Padmaguṇagarbha, Sūryagarbha, and Candragarbha.
Bodhisattva Sāgaragarbha, Bodhisattva Vimalacandragarbha, Bodhisattva Sarvalokāvabhāsavyūhagarbha,
Bodhisattva Jñānāvabhāsagarbha, Bodhisattva Guṇakusumagarbha, Bodhisattva Candanaguṇagarbha,
Bodhisattva Puṣpaguṇagarbha, Bodhisattva Utpalaguṇagarbha, and Bodhisattva Devaguṇagarbha.
...the Bodhisattva Puṇyagarbha, the Bodhisattva Anāvaraṇaviśuddhajñānaguṇagarbha,

the Bodhisattva Guṇagarbha, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇaguṇagarbha, the Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha, the Bodhisattva Vigatamalaprabhāsagarbha, the Bodhisattva Citrakathāvyūhagarbha, and the Bodhisattva Mahāprabhājālagarbha.
...the Bodhisattva King-Treasury of Pure Radiant Majesty, the Bodhisattva King-Treasury of Majestic Radiance of the Great Golden Mountain,
the Bodhisattva Treasury of Pure Virtue Adorned with All Marks, the Bodhisattva Treasury of Adornment with the Marks of Vajra-Flame Virtue,
the Bodhisattva Treasury of Blazing Flames, the Bodhisattva Treasury of the Light-Illumination of the Constellation King, and the Bodhisattva Treasury of Space...
The Bodhisattva Unobstructed Treasury of Wondrous Sound, the Bodhisattva Treasury of Vows Sustaining All Worlds through the Merit of Dhāraṇīs,
the Bodhisattva Ocean Adornment Treasury, the Bodhisattva Sumeru Virtue Treasury, the Bodhisattva Treasury of Purified All Merits,
the Bodhisattva Tathāgatagarbha, the Bodhisattva Buddha Virtue Treasury, and the Bodhisattva Liberation...
The Bodhisattva Moon,
and other such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas— immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and inexpressible in number, with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Vajragarbha as their leader.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, entered the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom. Immediately, in each direction throughout the worlds—passing through as many worlds as there are atoms in ten billion buddha-fields—there was a Tathāgata named Vajragarbha.
Following this sequence, as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten billion buddha-fields all manifested their bodies, each named Vajragarbha;
it was likewise so throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
They raised their voices in unison and praised him, saying: “Excellent, excellent! Vajragarbha!”
Thus you are able to enter this Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom.
In this way, all the Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms of dust, who bear the same name, empower you with their majestic spiritual power;
furthermore, it is due to the power of the original vows of Vairocana Buddha and because you possess great wisdom.
Furthermore, they were granted the inconceivable light of the Dharma of all Bodhisattvas—namely, that which causes entry into the stage of wisdom;
which gathers all roots of goodness; which skillfully discriminates and selects all Buddha-dharmas;
which brings extensive knowledge of all phenomena; which definitively expounds all phenomena; and which is free from conceptual discrimination.
Because of his skillful discernment through wisdom; because he cannot be defiled by any worldly dharmas; because his supramundane roots of goodness are pure;
because he has attained the power of inconceivable wisdom; because he has attained the locus of the wisdom of the Omniscient One;
and furthermore, because he has attained the ten stages of the bodhisattva—he explains the distinctions among the ten bodhisattva stages according to reality.

Therefore, [it is taught] because it analytically explains the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) as being non-attached; because it is self-adorned by the excellent discernment of the light of great wisdom (*mahājñāna-āloka*);
because it causes entry into the gateway of perfected knowledge (*paripūrṇa-jñāna-mukha*); because it is explained according to the sequence of appropriate abidings;
because it attains the light of unhindered eloquence (*asaṅga-pratibhāna-āloka*); and because it possesses the ground of great unhindered knowledge (*asaṅga-jñāna-bhūmi*) without forgetfulness.
Because they do not lose the bodhisattva mind; because they bring to fulfillment the nature of all sentient beings through teaching and transformation;
and because they attain the definitive wisdom that reaches everywhere. Furthermore, Vajragarbha!

You should now explain the distinctions of this Dharma-gate, namely: because of the spiritual power of all Buddhas; because you are able to receive the spiritual power of the Tathāgata; because of the purity of your own roots of goodness; because of the nature of the pure *dharmatā*; because of the nature of benefiting sentient beings; because it causes sentient beings to attain the pure *dharmakāya* and *jñānakāya*; because one receives the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) from all Buddhas; because one attains the most exalted body among all worlds; because it transcends all worldly paths; and because of the purity of supramundane roots of goodness.

Immediately, the Buddhas of the ten directions revealed to Vajragarbha their true, unsurpassed Buddha-bodies, and bestowed upon him: unobstructed eloquence for joyful exposition; pure wisdom that skillfully discriminates; excellent mindfulness that never forgets; a well-determined mind; universal access to the sphere of all-knowledge; the indestructible power of the Buddhas; the fearlessness and lack of timidity of the Buddhas; the unimpeded wisdom of the Buddhas that discriminates all dharmas and skillfully opens the gates of Dharma; and the supreme, wondrous deeds of body, speech, and mind performed by all Buddhas.

Why is this? Because they have attained the dharma of the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of the Radiance of Great Wisdom; because of the power of their original vows; because their resolve is pure; because their wisdom is clear and bright; because they have well accumulated the dharmas that aid the path; because they have well cultivated their fundamental practices; because they are able to maintain immeasurable mindfulness; because they have faith and understanding in the pure and radiant dharma; because they have well attained the gate of dhāraṇī without discrimination; and because they have well sealed the nature of phenomena with the seal of wisdom.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions all extended their right hands and stroked the crown of the head of Vajragarbha Bodhisattva.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva immediately arose from samādhi; having arisen, he addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!..."

These bodhisattvas have previously all attained excellent self-determination; they are without fault and without discrimination, pure and lucid, as vast as the dharma-nature and ultimate as space, pervading all the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions and encompassing all sentient beings, for the sake of rescuing and delivering all the world, and protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas.
Why is this? Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter the ground of wisdom of the buddhas of the past, and likewise enter the ground of wisdom of the buddhas of the future and the present.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
What is the ground of wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas?
O Sons of the Buddha!"
There are ten stages of wisdom for Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
These have been taught by the Buddhas of the past, are being taught by those of the present, and will be taught by those of the future; it is for the sake of these stages that I speak thus.

What are these ten? First is named the Ground of Joy; second, the Ground of Purity; third, the Ground of Illumination; fourth, the Ground of Blazing; fifth, the Ground Difficult to Conquer; sixth, the Ground of Manifestation; seventh, the Ground of Profundity; eighth, the Ground of Immovability; ninth, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence; and tenth, the Ground of the Dharma Cloud.
O Sons of the Buddha!

These ten stages have been taught by all Buddhas of the three periods of time—those who have taught them in the past, those who teach them now, and those who will teach them in the future. I do not see any buddha-field where these ten stages of a bodhisattva are not taught.
Why is this? These ten stages are the most supreme and wondrous path of the bodhisattvas, the most supreme and luminously pure Dharma-gate, namely, the analysis of the matters of the ten abodes.
“O Sons of the Buddha!
This matter is inconceivable, namely, the wisdom of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas that accords with the various stages.

At that time, having finished expounding the names of the ten stages of the Bodhisattvas, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajragarbha remained silent, no longer further analyzing their meaning or significance.

At that time, when the entire assembly of bodhisattvas had heard the names of the ten bodhisattva stages being proclaimed, they were all filled with longing and desired to hear their explanation. Each of them thought to themselves:
"For what cause and for what reason has the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having spoken the names of the ten bodhisattva stages, remained silent and not further explained them?"

At that time, among the assembly of great bodhisattvas, there was a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Vimukticandra. Knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, he addressed the bodhisattva Vajragarbha in verse, saying:
"O person of pure wisdom, mindfulness, and insight!
Why, after having spoken the names of the bodhisattva stages, do you remain silent without explaining them?
Now all these great bodhisattvas harbor doubts in their hearts:
"For what reason have you spoken these names, yet do not expound their meaning?"
All these Bodhisattvas of great wisdom Desire to hear the meaning of these stages; I pray that you will explain them in detail.
This assembly of Bodhisattvas Is pure and free from all blemish.
Abiding in the firm and solid Dharma, endowed with wisdom and merit,
all gaze upon you, O Benevolent One, with hearts full of reverence;
they long to hear what you shall speak, as one parched with thirst longs for nectar.
When the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha heard this account,
desiring to bring joy to the great assembly, he immediately spoke these verses:
“The conduct of all bodhisattvas Is foremost among that which is inconceivable.”
The distinct differentiation of the various stages is the very foundation of all Buddhas.
Subtle and wondrous, it is exceedingly difficult to perceive; it is beyond the reach of the ordinary mind.
It emerges from the Buddha’s wisdom; were one to hear of it [without such wisdom], one would become lost and bewildered.
Maintain a mind like a vajra, with deep faith in the Buddha’s wisdom as the foremost excellence; let the mind be free from doubt and difficulty,
remaining far removed from the notion of a self and the sphere of mental activity.
Only such bodhisattvas as these are able to hear it.
The wisdom of cessation and the outflow-free is extremely difficult to explain in detail;
it is like painting in space, or like grasping the wind in the air.
"I contemplate the Buddha’s wisdom, which is foremost and inconceivable;
few sentient beings are able to believe it, and for this reason I remain silent.
When Bodhisattva Vimukticandra heard these words, he addressed Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:

“O Son of the Buddha! This assembly of great bodhisattvas possesses a profoundly pure mind; they have skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path, skillfully accumulated the factors conducive to enlightenment, and skillfully made offerings to and honored all Buddhas. Having planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas, they have accomplished immeasurable and profound merit. Free from delusion, doubt, and regret, they are without greed, attachment, or any fetters and obstructions. With deep-seated faith and understanding, they abide immovably, and within this Dharma, they do not follow the teachings of others.”
"Therefore, Son of the Buddha!
You should, by the power of the Buddha, expound this meaning, for these bodhisattvas are all able to realize and know this profound Dharma.
At that time, Vimukticandra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Please teach the Dharma of peace and security, the supreme conduct of the Bodhisattvas,
and the differentiation of the stages, so that wisdom may be purified.
When the various knowledges are pure and stainless, one dwells securely in profound faith and understanding.”
"Before all the immeasurable Buddhas, you have realized the meaning of the ten stages.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!"

Although this great assembly is entirely pure, free from delusion, doubt, and regret, and does not follow the teachings of others regarding this matter, there are others who delight in inferior dharmas; upon hearing these profound and inconceivable matters, they may give rise to doubt or regret. Such people will suffer various miseries and afflictions for a long night. Out of compassion for them, I remain silent.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning,
spoke these verses: "Though this assembly is pure, With profound wisdom free from doubt and regret,
Their minds are already resolved, No longer following the teachings of others."
Unshakable like Mount Sumeru, undisturbed like the great ocean; others,
who have not long practiced and whose wisdom is not yet clear,
follow consciousness rather than wisdom, and having heard this, give rise to doubt and regret.
"He would fall into the evil destinies; out of compassion, I did not speak.
Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!..."

I pray that, by the power of the Buddha, you may skillfully discern this inconceivable Dharma and the matters cherished by the Buddha’s protection, so that people may easily believe and understand them. Why is this?

Because you have well expounded the meaning of the ten stages, the Buddhas of the ten directions shall protect and mind you according to the Dharma; and because all Bodhisattvas shall protect this matter, you should practice with diligent vigor. Why is this?
This is the supreme practice of the Bodhisattva, for it leads to the attainment of all Buddha-dharmas.
It is like all scriptures, which are subsumed within their opening chapters; the opening chapter is the foundation, and there is not a single character that does not enter into it.
Thus it is, O Son of the Buddha!
These ten stages are the foundation of all Buddha-dharmas; when Bodhisattvas fully practice these ten stages, they are able to attain all-encompassing wisdom.
Therefore, Son of the Buddha!
We pray that you will explain this meaning.
May all Buddhas protect and mind us, and augment us with their spiritual power, so that people may believe and accept it, and it cannot be destroyed.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Excellent, O Son of Wisdom!
You are fully endowed with pure conduct."
I pray that you will explain the practices of the ten stages and the dharmas entered upon those ten stages,
so that one may be fully endowed with wisdom and thereby attain enlightenment.
All the Buddhas of the ten directions, the most supreme among the honored ones of humanity—
All together protect and keep you in mind as they explain the meaning of these ten stages.
The ten stages are the foundation; they are called the sphere of wise conduct and are also the ultimate path—the immeasurable mass of the Buddha’s teachings.
"Just as all written characters are contained within the initial chapter,
so too the merit and wisdom of all Buddhas have the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as their foundation.
At that time, all the bodhisattvas simultaneously addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha with a single voice in verse, saying:
"O person of supreme and wondrous wisdom!
You delight in immeasurable discourse; with virtues as weighty as the king of mountains, you compassionately explain the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
With purity of ethical discipline, mindfulness, and wisdom, you proclaim the meaning of these ten stages."
The root of the ten powers, the fundamental practice of unimpeded wisdom,
and the virtues of morality, concentration, and insight— all are gathered within the heart of the Benevolent One.
Arrogance and all false views have been utterly extinguished.
This assembly is free from doubt; we only wish to hear your excellent teaching,
as one who thirsts longs for water, as the hungry longs for delicious food,
as the sick longs for a skilled physician, and as bees long to taste honey.
We, likewise, have heard the flavor of the nectar-like Dharma.
Therefore, with a vast and noble mind, we pray that you open the gate of the first bhūmi,
and so on up to the tenth bhūmi, explaining them to us in their proper sequence.

At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows the radiant flame of the Bodhisattva’s Power-Illumination, with hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya rays as its retinue.

Having emitted this light, it universally illuminated the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions without exception; the sufferings of the three evil realms were all brought to rest, and it fully illumined the assemblies of all Buddhas in the great dharma-preaching congregations throughout the ten directions, manifesting the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata.

After this light had universally illuminated the bodies of the bodhisattvas in the great assemblies of the Buddhas of the ten directions, it formed a great cloud-palace of radiant light in the space above.

The Buddhas of the ten directions likewise did so; from the white tuft of hair between their eyebrows, they simultaneously emitted the flaming radiance of the power of bodhisattvas, with hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya rays as their retinue. They universally manifested the inconceivable power of the Tathāgatas, illuminating all the great assemblies of the Buddhas and the world of Sahā, Śākyamuni Buddha, and his great assembly, as well as Vajragarbha Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and his lion throne.
Having shone forth, they formed a great cloud-pavilion of light in the space above.
Then, from within those great cloud-pavilions of light, through the spiritual power of all Buddhas, a verse was spoken:
"The peerless Buddhas, whose merit is like space,"
Possessing the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth, the most honored Lord of the World manifested this supernatural power before Śākyamuni Buddha;
through the Buddha’s power, he revealed the Lion’s Treasury of the Dharma King.
I shall explain the practices of the stages and the distinctions in the meanings of those stages;
speaking by the power of all Buddhas, there is none who can refute me.
If a person hears this jewel of the Dharma, they will be protected by all the Buddhas.
Gradually perfecting all the stages, one attains the path to Buddhahood.
If there are those capable of hearing this, even if they are within the great ocean or amidst the fires at the end of an eon, they will surely hear this sutra.
If a person is deluded, doubtful, or regretful, they will ultimately be unable to hear it.
Therefore, the sons of the Buddha now explain the path of wisdom of the various stages and the method of contemplation on the power of entry; one should practice these in successive order.
"May they reach the other stages, each attaining their respective benefit.
To benefit all the world, we pray that you will speak so that [the teaching] is not interrupted.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha surveyed the ten directions and, wishing to increase the faith and reverence of the great assembly, spoke these verses:
“The path of the Buddhas, the Holy Lords, is subtle and exceedingly difficult to understand;
it cannot be attained through discursive thought, but is the domain of practice for the wise alone.
Its nature from the very beginning is tranquil, without arising or ceasing.”
Empty from the very beginning, it extinguishes all suffering and affliction;
far removed from the various realms of existence, it is identical to the mark of nirvana.
Without middle and without end, it cannot be expressed by words.
Transcending the three periods of time, its characteristic is like empty space.
The sphere of action of all Buddhas is pure, profound, and quiescent,
difficult to reach through verbal expression.
The practice of the stages is likewise; it is difficult even to describe, let alone to show it to others.
The wisdom of all Buddhas transcends the path of mental factors;
it is inconceivable and possesses no aggregates, elements, or sense bases.
It can only be known through wisdom; it is not within the reach of consciousness.
Like a track in the sky, which is difficult to describe, how can its characteristics be shown?
Such is the meaning of the Ten Stages: it cannot be known by a mind that is not boundless.
Although this matter is difficult, by generating the aspiration and practicing compassion, one gradually fulfills the various stages (*bhūmi*); this is beyond the reach of the ordinary mind.
Such practices of the stages are subtle and extremely difficult to perceive.
This cannot be known by the mind; it must be spoken through the power of the Buddha.
You all should be reverent and listen together with a single mind to the practices of the mutual entry of the stages and the dharma-gates for cultivation and transcendence.
Even in immeasurable billions of eons, it could not be fully explained;
now I shall briefly explain it according to reality, its meaning being complete without remainder.
Wait with single-minded reverence, for I now speak by the power of the Buddha.
The Great Sound proclaims through causes and metaphors; The meaning and the names do not contradict one another.
The Buddha’s spiritual power is immeasurable; Now it all resides within my own body.
That which I have spoken Is but a single drop from the great ocean.
After the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha had spoken these verses, he addressed the great assembly:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
If sentient beings have thickly accumulated roots of goodness, cultivated various virtuous deeds, well-gathered the factors conducive to the path, and made offerings..."
Those beings who have nurtured all Buddhas, accumulated all pure and white dharmas, been protected by spiritual friends, entered the profound and vast mind,
possessed a mind that delights in the Great Dharma, were largely inclined toward compassion, and loved to seek the wisdom of a Buddha—
only such beings are able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in order to attain it.
For the sake of attaining all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), for the sake of attaining the ten powers (*daśabala*), for the sake of attaining the great fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*),
for the sake of attaining the fulfillment of the Buddha-dharmas, for the sake of rescuing all worlds, for the sake of purifying the mind of great compassion (*mahāmaitrīkaruṇā*),
for the sake of proceeding toward the non-remainder and unobstructed wisdom of the ten directions, and for the sake of purifying all Buddha-fields...
Because there is nothing remaining, in order to know the events of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment,
and in order to freely turn the great wheel of Dharma and extensively manifest the spiritual powers of a Buddha, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to such a mind.

"O Sons of the Buddha! This mind takes great compassion as its foremost quality, is preeminent in wisdom, and is protected by skillful means. It is characterized by a straightforward mind and a profound mind of ultimate sincerity. Its measure is equal to the power of the Buddhas; it skillfully evaluates the power of sentient beings and the power of the Buddhas. It tends toward unimpeded knowledge and accords with spontaneous knowledge (*svayambhū-jñāna*). It is able to receive all Buddha-dharmas and, through the teaching of wisdom, is as vast as the *dharmatā* and as ultimate as space, extending to the end of time."
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva gives rise to such a mind, they immediately transcend the stage of ordinary beings, enter the rank of bodhisattvas, and are born into the family of the Buddhas. Their lineage becomes beyond reproach; they transcend all worldly paths and enter the supramundane path. They abide within the bodhisattva-dharma, become equal in number to the assembly of all bodhisattvas, and enter the lineage of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, becoming certain to attain ultimate *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
When a bodhisattva dwells in such dharmas, it is called dwelling in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because of the quality of immovability.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this Stage of Joy, they possess much joy, much faith, much purity, much exultation, much pliancy, and much receptivity; they do not delight in strife, do not delight in harassing sentient beings, and do not delight in anger or resentment."

"O Sons of the Buddha! When Bodhisattvas dwell in this Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting all Buddhas; they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting the teachings of all Buddhas; they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting the practices performed by all Bodhisattvas; they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting the pure characteristics of all *pāramitās*; they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting the peerless excellence of all Bodhisattvas; they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting the indestructible powers of all Bodhisattvas; they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting the methods of instruction of all Tathāgatas; they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting their ability to bring benefit to sentient beings; and they give rise to a heart of joy by recollecting the gates of wisdom and skillful means entered by all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas."
"O Sons of the Buddha! The Bodhisattva further reflects thus: 'I give rise to a heart of joy because I am turning away from all worldly realms;

I give rise to a heart of joy because I enter into the equality of all Buddhas; I give rise to a heart of joy because I distance myself from the stage of ordinary beings; I give rise to a heart of joy because I draw near to the stage of wisdom; I give rise to a heart of joy because I sever all evil paths; I give rise to a heart of joy because I act as a refuge for all sentient beings; I give rise to a heart of joy because I draw near to seeing all Buddhas; I give rise to a heart of joy because I am born into the realm of all Buddhas; I give rise to a heart of joy because I enter the ranks of all Bodhisattvas; I give rise to a heart of joy because I am free from all terrors such as the bristling of body hair.'"

Why is this? Because when these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), all fears are immediately and completely distanced from them—namely, the fear of not making a living, the fear of ill repute, the fear of death, the fear of falling into evil destinies, and the fear of the majesty of great assemblies—and they are thus freed from all such fears.
Why is this? Because these bodhisattvas have abandoned the mark of self, they do not even crave their own bodies, let alone the things they use.
Therefore, they have no fear of being unable to sustain themselves.

The mind does not harbor expectations for offerings or respect—thinking, "I should make offerings to sentient beings and provide them with their necessities"—and for this reason, there is no fear of ill repute.
Because they are free from the view of self and devoid of the mark of a self, they have no fear of death.
Furthermore, they think:
"Even after my death, I shall certainly not be separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
"Therefore, there is no fear of falling into the evil realms.
'The aspirations and delights I hold are without equal; how much less could there be anyone superior?
Therefore, there is no fear regarding the majesty and virtue of the great assembly."
O Sons of the Buddha!
In this way, Bodhisattvas are free from all such things as fear and the bristling of body hair.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This bodhisattva, taking great compassion as the foremost, possesses a profound and vast mind that is firm and steadfast; he further diligently cultivates all roots of goodness, namely:
through the excellence of faith, he frequently practices the pure mind, and through the purity of the mind of understanding, he frequently practices with faith.
Giving rise to a mind of compassion and accomplishing great loving-kindness, their minds never grow weary; adorned with a sense of shame and remorse, they accomplish patience and gentleness.
They respectfully accord with the Buddha’s teachings, honoring them with faith and reverence; day and night they constantly cultivate roots of goodness without satiety;
they draw near to spiritual friends, always delighting in the Dharma, seeking out extensive learning without weariness.

One correctly contemplates the phenomena as they are observed; the mind does not become greedily attached, nor does one seek profit, gain, fame, or honor. Regarding all necessities of life, the mind is free from stinginess, and one constantly gives rise to a sincere heart without ever feeling satiated.

They take delight in the ground of omniscience, constantly desiring to attain the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of all Buddhas; they seek assistance through the dharmas of the various pāramitās and remain free from all deceit and crookedness.

Acting in accordance with what they have taught, they always speak truthful words; they do not defile the family of the Buddhas, do not abandon the training precepts of a bodhisattva, and give rise to omniscience (*sarvajñā*).

Their minds are as immovable as the king of great mountains; they take no pleasure in any worldly affairs, accomplish supramundane roots of goodness, and amass the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) without ever becoming weary, constantly seeking the most excellent path among all superior paths.
O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish such dharmas for purifying the stages, they are said to be "dwelling securely in the Bodhisattva Stage of Joy.
When Bodhisattvas thus dwell securely in the Stage of Joy, they give rise to great vows and produce a mind of such certainty, namely:

I shall make offerings to all Buddhas without exception; with all requisites for offering, I shall offer according to my will, with a mind of pure liberation, and give rise to such a great vow—vast as the Dharma-nature and ultimate as space—to continue until the end of the future, making offerings to all Buddhas throughout all kalpas, with great offerings without ceasing.

Furthermore, they receive and uphold all the sutras and teachings spoken by all Buddhas, because they encompass the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas; they accord with all the methods of teaching employed by all Buddhas and are able to protect all the teachings of all Buddhas. They give rise to such great vows—vast as the *dharmatā* and ultimate like space—to protect all Buddha-dharmas throughout all kalpas until the end of the future, without ever ceasing.

"Furthermore, in all worlds, whenever all Buddhas descend from Tuṣita Heaven to enter the womb, while remaining in the womb, at the time of their initial birth, at the time of their renunciation, and at the time of their attainment of the Buddha-way, one shall always exhort them to turn the great wheel of Dharma and to manifest entry into Great Nirvāṇa."

At that time, I went to make offerings to them all, with the gathering of the Dharma as my primary concern, because I turned the wheel [of the Dharma] during the three periods of the day. Thus I made this great vow: vast as the *dharmatā* and ultimate as space, to welcome and make offerings to all Buddhas throughout the entirety of the future and across all kalpas, without ever ceasing.

"Furthermore, all the practices of the Bodhisattvas are vast, lofty, immeasurable, indestructible, and non-conceptual; they are encompassed by the various *pāramitās* and purified by the various stages (*bhūmis*). They give rise to all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), whether with signs (*sanimitta*) or signless (*animitta*), and involve the formation and dissolution of the Path.

All the practices of the Bodhisattvas, the paths, the stages, and the fundamental conduct of the *pāramitās* are taught for the purpose of leading others to practice them, so that their minds may increase and grow. They conceive such great vows—vast as the *dharmadhātu* and ultimate as space—to carry out the practices of all Bodhisattvas throughout the future and across all kalpas, maturing sentient beings through the teaching of the Dharma without ever ceasing."

Furthermore, for all sentient beings—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception, neither with nor without perception; whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; bound within the three realms and entering the six destinies, encompassed by name-and-form in every place of birth—they resolve to teach and mature all sentient beings, sever all worldly paths, cause them to abide in the Buddha-dharma, and gather all wisdom without remainder. They give rise to such great vows, as vast as the dharma-nature and ultimate as space, continuing until the end of the future and through all kalpas, teaching and transforming all sentient beings without rest.

"Furthermore, regarding all worlds—whether vast or narrow, extremely high, immeasurable, and beyond differentiation; immovable, and indescribable as coarse or subtle; upright, inverted, with heads and feet facing one another, or level, circular, and square—he enters such worlds according to their nature.
His wisdom is like Indra’s net, passing through the distinctions of illusory phenomena; thus, the distinctions of the worlds in the ten directions all appear before his knowledge."

They have made such great vows—vast as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and ultimate as space—which continue without ceasing throughout all future ages and all kalpas, clearly perceiving every such world as it manifests before them.

Furthermore, they cause all buddha-fields to enter into a single buddha-field, and a single buddha-field to enter into all buddha-fields; each and every buddha-field is adorned with immeasurable light, free from all defilement, and fully endowed with the path of purity. Within them dwell immeasurable sentient beings of wisdom who completely fill their midst. There, the great supernormal powers of the Buddhas are constantly manifested in accordance with the minds of sentient beings. They make such great vows—vast as the *dharmatā* and ultimate like space—to purify such lands throughout the entirety of future time and all kalpas, without ever ceasing.

"Furthermore, all bodhisattvas are of one mind and study together; they collectively accumulate all virtues without resentment or envy. Focusing on a single object, their minds are harmonious and unified, and they are never parted from one another."
They can manifest the body of a Buddha at will; within their own minds, they fully understand and comprehend the spiritual powers and wisdom-powers of all Buddhas.

They constantly attain supernatural powers according to their wishes, enabling them to travel through all lands and manifest their physical forms in every assembly of Buddhas. They are born universally among all places of birth, possessing such inconceivable great wisdom and being fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva.
They have made such great vows—vast as the dharma-nature and ultimate as space—to practice such a path of great wisdom throughout all future ages and all kalpas, without ever ceasing.

"Furthermore, riding upon the wheel of non-retrogression, one traverses all bodhisattva paths; the actions performed through body, speech, and mind are never in vain. Sentient beings who see me become fixed in the Buddha-dharma; those who hear my voice immediately attain the path of true wisdom; and those who behold me find joy in their hearts and are freed from all afflictions, like the king of great medicinal trees."

In order to attain such a mind, they practice all the bodhisattva paths and make such great vows—vast as the *dharmatā* and ultimate as space—that throughout the future world and for the duration of all kalpas, they practice the non-retrogressive path, ensuring that their deeds are never in vain and never cease.

Furthermore, in all worlds, they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and within the space of a single hair-tip, they manifest entering the womb, leaving home, sitting at the site of enlightenment, attaining the Buddha-way, turning the wheel of Dharma, delivering sentient beings, and manifesting Great Nirvāṇa.

They manifest the great power of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas; according to those among all sentient beings who are ready to be delivered, they attain the Buddha-way, deliver sentient beings, and extinguish suffering and affliction in every thought-moment, knowing that all phenomena are like the state of nirvāṇa.

With a single voice, they cause all sentient beings to rejoice; they manifest great nirvana while not severing the practices of bodhisattvas; they reveal to sentient beings the ground of great wisdom, enabling them to know that all phenomena are merely provisional and false.

Because they possess great wisdom and the sovereign mastery of great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they have made such a great vow: as vast as the *dharmatā* and ultimate as space, to accomplish the work of attaining the Buddha-way throughout the limits of the future and across all kalpas, seeking great wisdom, great supernormal powers, and so forth, without ever ceasing.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas dwell on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they produce as many as ten million asaṃkhyeya great vows, headed by these ten vows."
One generates this vow by means of ten inexhaustible dharmas, and practices with diligent vigor in order to fulfill this vow.

What are these ten? First, the inexhaustibility of sentient beings; second, the inexhaustibility of the world; third, the inexhaustibility of space; fourth, the inexhaustibility of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); fifth, the inexhaustibility of *nirvāṇa*; sixth, the inexhaustibility of the appearance of Buddhas in the world; seventh, the inexhaustibility of the wisdom of all Buddhas; eighth, the inexhaustibility of the objects of mental focus; ninth, the inexhaustibility of the arising of wisdom; and tenth, the inexhaustibility of the paths of the world, the paths of phenomena, and the paths of wisdom.
As long as sentient beings are not exhausted, my vow shall not be exhausted;

as long as the world is not exhausted, as long as space is not exhausted, as long as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not exhausted, as long as *nirvāṇa* is not exhausted, as long as the appearance of Buddhas in the world is not exhausted, as long as the wisdom of all Buddhas is not exhausted, as long as the objects of the mind are not exhausted, as long as the arising of wisdom is not exhausted, and as long as the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*) are not exhausted, my vow shall not be exhausted.

Yet sentient beings are truly inexhaustible; likewise, the world, space, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), nirvāṇa, the appearance of Buddhas in the world, the wisdom of all Buddhas, the objects of the mind, the arising of knowledge, and the types of the path are truly inexhaustible; thus, my vows and the merit thereof are also inexhaustible.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas resolutely give rise to these great vows, they then attain a mind of benefit and peace, a pliant mind, a well-disciplined mind, a virtuous mind, a mind of quiescence, a harmonious and moist mind, a straightforward mind, an undisturbed mind, an untroubled mind, and an unclouded mind.”
In this way, one becomes a person of faith, whose mind delights in the characteristics of faith and who discerns its merits.

One has faith in the path originally practiced by all Buddhas; faith that by practicing the various *pāramitās*, they attain growth and increase; faith in the entry into the various stages (*bhūmis*) and the attainment of supreme merit; faith in the attainment of the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Buddha; faith in the fulfillment of the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); faith in the indestructible unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*); faith in the inconceivable nature of all Buddha-dharmas; faith in the power of all Buddhas being neither middle nor boundless; faith in the immeasurable gateways of practice of all Tathāgatas; and faith that the fruit of retribution is accomplished through causes and conditions.
To state the essentials: one has faith in the universal practice of all bodhisattvas regarding the merit, wisdom, and majestic spiritual power of all buddhas.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
A bodhisattva forms this thought:"

“The True Dharma of all Buddhas is thus profound, thus devoid of marks, thus quiescent, thus empty, thus signless, thus wishless, thus unstained, thus immeasurable, thus vast, and thus indestructible.”

Yet the minds of all ordinary beings fall into false views; their eye of wisdom is shrouded by the darkness of ignorance and delusion; they constantly raise the banner of arrogance; they are ensnared in the net of craving; they follow along with flattery and crookedness; and they harbor stinginess and jealousy, thereby creating the causes and conditions for future births.

Having accumulated much greed, hatred, and delusion, they give rise to various grave karmas; the fierce winds of resentment blow upon the fire of their sinful minds, constantly causing it to blaze intensely, so that whatever actions they perform are all associated with perversion.

The continuity of the flow of desire, the flow of existence, the flow of ignorance, and the flow of views gives rise to the seeds of mind, intellect, and consciousness, producing the sprouts of suffering and affliction within the realms of the three worlds—namely:
the union of name-and-form leads to the growth of the six sense bases;
and through the mutual encounter of the sense bases with external objects, contact arises.
With contact as a condition, the various sensations arise;
because of a deep attachment to sensation, craving arises;
because craving increases, grasping arises.
Because of the increase of grasping (*upādāna*), there arises renewed existence (*punarbhava*);
because of the conditions of existence (*bhava*), there arise birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.

Thus, through the accumulation of these causal conditions, the mass of suffering gathers, and sentient beings undergo various sufferings and afflictions. Within this, there is no self (*ātman*) and nothing belonging to a self (*ātmīya*); there is no agent, no experiencer, and no knower. It is like grass, wood, tiles, or stones, and it is also like a shadow.
“Ordinary beings are pitiable; unaware and unawakened, they undergo suffering and affliction.
When the Bodhisattva sees that all these sentient beings cannot escape various sufferings, he gives rise to the wisdom of great compassion, thinking:
“We should rescue all these sentient beings.”
Furthermore, desiring to cause them to abide in the bliss of the ultimate Buddha-way, he immediately gives rise to great compassion and wisdom.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in accordance with such a dharma of great compassion, dwells in the First Stage (Prathamā Bhūmi) with a profound and wondrous mind, having no greed or attachment toward any thing.
Out of respect for the great and wondrous wisdom of all Buddhas, they practice great relinquishment; immediately, they are able to give away all things that can be given, namely:

Grain and wheat, storehouses, gold and silver, *maṇi* jewels, *musāragalva*, *aśmagarbha*, *vaidūrya*, coral, amber, conch shells, necklaces, ornaments for the body, and all manner of rare treasures; as well as elephants, horses, carriages, palanquins, people, slaves, retinues, kingdoms, cities, towns, villages, dwellings, gardens, groves, and pleasure parks; wives, children, sons, daughters, and everything beloved—all these he completely relinquishes. Even his head, eyes, ears, nose, limbs, hands, feet, and his entire body he gives away. Because he deeply cherishes the wisdom of the Buddha, he feels no greed or attachment. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) is able to practice great renunciation (*mahatyāga*).

"Because this bodhisattva rescues all sentient beings with a mind of great compassion and a mind of great equanimity, they apply themselves even more diligently to seek the supreme matters of worldly and world-transcending benefit, their minds never wearying or slackening; therefore, the bodhisattva gives rise to the merit of tirelessness."
One is able to understand various scriptures and treatises through self-illumination; therefore, one gives rise to the merit of knowing the scriptures.

Having attained such wisdom that knows the scriptures, one is well able to deliberate upon what should and should not be done, acting appropriately according to whether sentient beings are superior, middling, or inferior. One benefits those who come to rely on and approach them according to their capacity. For this reason, the bodhisattva gives rise to the merit of worldly knowledge (*lokajñāna*).

Having attained the merit of worldly wisdom, one knows the proper time and the proper measure; adorned with shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*), one cultivates the path that benefits both oneself and others, and thus the merit of shame and remorse arises.
Thus, by diligently practicing within these meritorious deeds with a mind that does not slacken or retreat, one attains the merit of non-retrogressive diligence;
having attained this power of endurance, one zealously performs offerings to the Buddhas and, following what the Buddhas have taught, acts exactly as they have instructed.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
These Bodhisattvas fully know how to give rise to such dharmas of the pure stages, namely:

faith, loving-kindness, compassion, equanimity, tirelessness, knowledge of all scriptures, skillful understanding of worldly dharmas, shame and remorse, the power of endurance, making offerings to all Buddhas, and practicing according to what has been taught."

Furthermore, when this bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Joy, by virtue of having made vows, they extensively behold hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of nayutas of Buddhas.

When a bodhisattva beholds the Buddhas, his heart is filled with great joy; with deep-seated love and reverence, he makes offerings of the requisites of a bodhisattva to the Buddhas and to the Sangha, dedicating all such merit toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Because this bodhisattva makes offerings to the Buddhas, the dharma of teaching and transforming sentient beings arises; they primarily gather in sentient beings through two of the four means of integration—namely, giving and kind speech—while regarding the latter two means of integration, they practice them only through the power of faith and understanding, as their practice has not yet been fully mastered or thoroughly penetrated.

"As this bodhisattva makes offerings to the Buddhas and teaches and transforms sentient beings according to their needs, they are able to receive and practice the dharmas of the pure stages. All such merits are naturally dedicated toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), becoming increasingly manifest and capable of being put to use."
For example, O Son of the Buddha!
Just as a goldsmith refines gold, tempering it with the power of fire until it becomes pliant and workable, and its luster and color are enhanced;

in the same way, as a Bodhisattva makes offerings to the Buddhas, teaches and transforms sentient beings, and receives and practices the pure dharmas of the various stages, all these merits naturally dedicate themselves toward *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), becoming increasingly brilliant and available for use according to one's will.
"Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha!

Regarding the characteristics and the attainment of the fruit within the first stage, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should consult, receive instruction from, and inquire of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends concerning the dharmas for accomplishing the stages; they should never grow weary of or neglect this."

This bodhisattva, while dwelling in the first stage, should consult with and question the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends regarding the characteristics and the fruits attained in the second stage, never becoming weary or satisfied.

Likewise, regarding the characteristics and the fruits attained in the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, they should consult with and question the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends concerning the dharmas that perfect these ten stages, without ever ceasing or becoming weary.

"This Bodhisattva should thoroughly understand the forward and reverse dharmas of all stages; thoroughly understand the formation and destruction of all stages; thoroughly understand the characteristics, causes, and effects of all stages; thoroughly understand the attainment and relinquishment of all stages; thoroughly understand the divisions of pure conduct in all stages; thoroughly understand the practice of proceeding from one stage to the next; thoroughly understand what is possible and what is impossible regarding all stages; thoroughly understand the shifting of the dwelling place in all stages; thoroughly understand the distinctions between the initial and subsequent matters of all stages; thoroughly understand the signs of non-retrogression in all stages; and furthermore, thoroughly understand all the dharmas of the pure stages of Bodhisattvas, up to thoroughly understanding the entry into the Tathāgata’s stage of wisdom."
"O Sons of the Buddha!

In this way, all Bodhisattvas skillfully know the characteristics of the stages—from the stage prior to setting forth through the first stage up to the tenth stage. Because they know them without obstruction and have attained the light of wisdom of the stages, they are able to attain the light of wisdom of all Buddhas."
“O Sons of the Buddha!

It is like a great caravan leader who, intending to lead many merchants to a great city, must first inquire about the road, the faults that lead to retreat, and the advantages and disadvantages encountered along the way.”

When first setting out, he knows the time for resting along the way, and he thoroughly understands how to reach that city; he is able to contemplate and deliberate with wisdom, providing all necessary provisions so that nothing is lacking, and he guides the multitude correctly to reach the great city, enabling both himself and the people to escape all hardships and calamities in the perilous path, remaining free from anxiety and distress.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

It is likewise for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: dwelling in the first stage (*bhūmi*), they skillfully know the dharmas of progression and regression through all the stages, up to skillfully knowing the dharmas that purify all the pure stages of a Bodhisattva, and skillfully knowing how to enter the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.”

"At that time, the Bodhisattva, having accumulated the great provisions of merit and wisdom, acts as a caravan leader for sentient beings, teaching them according to their needs to lead them out of the perilous and evil places of birth-and-death. He shows them the path of peace and security, even leading them to dwell in the great city of omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñā*), free from all decline and affliction."
Therefore, O Sons of the Buddha!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should always maintain a mind free from weariness and diligently cultivate the fundamental practices of the stages, until they skillfully know how to enter the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

This is called 'A Brief Explanation of the Gate for Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Entering the Stage of Joy. Were it to be explained in detail, there would be immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya matters."

"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling in this stage frequently become kings of Jambudvīpa, possessing noble status and sovereign power. They constantly protect the True Dharma and are able to gather in sentient beings through generosity. They skillfully eliminate the defilement of stinginess and greed in sentient beings, always practicing great giving without ever becoming exhausted."

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—all these merits are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never apart from mindfulness of the Dharma, never apart from mindfulness of the companions who are the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, never apart from mindfulness of the path practiced by the bodhisattvas, never apart from mindfulness of the pāramitās, never apart from mindfulness of the ten stages, never apart from mindfulness of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities, and even never apart from mindfulness of the perfection of all-knowledge.
One should constantly give rise to this thought:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the greatest, the most sublime, the highest, the unsurpassed, the guide, the general, the teacher, and the honored one; indeed, I shall become the one upon whom all sentient beings rely."
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas wish to leave the household life and practice with diligent vigor, in a mere moment they are able to renounce their home, wife, children, and the five desires within the Buddha-dharma."

Having gone forth, he practiced with diligent vigor; in a mere moment, he attained one hundred samādhis, beheld one hundred buddhas, and came to know the spiritual powers of one hundred buddhas. He was able to shake one hundred buddha-worlds, fly across one hundred buddha-worlds, illuminate one hundred buddha-worlds, and transform and teach the sentient beings of one hundred buddha-worlds. He could maintain his life for one hundred kalpas and know the events of one hundred kalpas each in the past and future worlds. He could skillfully enter one hundred dharma-gates and manifest one hundred bodies, and within each body, he could manifest one hundred bodhisattvas as his retinue. If he so desired, by the power of his vows, he could manifest even more than these numbers—indeed, hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, nayutas, beyond all calculation or knowledge.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"If there are sentient beings who have extensively cultivated and accumulated roots of goodness,
who have perfected the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*), and who have drawn near to the Buddhas,"
With great power of pure faith, And in accordance with a compassionate mind,
Such a person can give rise to The immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas.
The omniscience of all Buddhas Is of immeasurable power and purity.
With enduring strength and firm resolve, they accomplish all Buddha-dharmas;
with a compassionate heart they rescue the world, purifying the buddha-fields and proclaiming the turning of the wheel of Dharma— they thus give rise to this unsurpassed vow.
In a single thought-moment, one knows the three periods of time, yet there is no distinction between them;
the various differences of time are displayed for the sake of the world.
Briefly stated, this is the complete seeking of all the merits of the Buddhas.
Aroused from a vast mind, it is like empty space;
with compassion and wisdom as its head, practiced in union with skillful means,
and because of pure faith and a profound mind, its power is immeasurable.
With a mind directed toward non-obstruction, not following the teachings of others,
and being equal to all Buddhas, one gives rise to the Great Mind.
O sons of the Buddha, you should give birth to such a true mind.
One immediately leaves behind the conduct of ordinary beings and enters the sphere of the Buddhas’ activity;
one is born into the family of the Tathāgatas, free from all reproach or suspicion;
thus becoming equal to all Buddhas, one will surely attain the unsurpassed path.
When such a mind arises, one immediately attains the first stage (*bhūmi*).
That mind cannot be shaken, remaining as immovable as the king of mountains.
At that time, the Bodhisattva manifests the signs of great joy.
Their minds are ever pure and capable of receiving great matters.
Their hearts take no pleasure in strife or litigation; they do not delight in vexing sentient beings.
Free from anger and resentment, they rejoice in shame, modesty, and reverence.
Furthermore, one practices with a straightforward mind, guards the sense faculties, constantly remembers to save the world, and keeps in mind the quest for the wisdom of all Buddhas.
With a heart full of joy, one thinks: "I shall surely attain this."
Upon attaining the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), one immediately transcends five fears:
the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of death, the fear of ill repute,
the dread of the three evil realms, and the fear of being intimidated by the majesty of the great assembly.
Because they do not cling to a self, nor to what belongs to a self,
these sons of the Buddhas remain far removed from all fears.
They constantly practice a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, and always possess faith and reverence.
Equipped with the virtues of shame and remorse, one increases wholesome qualities day and night.
Delighting in the true benefit of merit, one does not delight in various sensual desires;
whatever Dharma one has heard, one is able to constantly contemplate it well.
Free from attachment in their conduct, they sever all thoughts of gain and offerings;
always delighting in Bodhi, they single-mindedly seek the Buddha’s wisdom.
Practicing the various pāramitās, they remain free from a mind of flattery and crookedness.
Acting in accordance with what they preach, they abide securely within truthful speech.
They do not defile the family of the Buddhas, nor do they abandon the training of a bodhisattva;
they distance themselves from worldly affairs and delight in benefiting the world.
Seeking the sublime Dharma without weariness, their diligence increases ever further;
such are the bodhisattvas, who delight in all meritorious virtues,
give rise to great vows, and desire to behold all Buddhas.
Protecting the Dharma, one goes to the Buddha’s presence; practicing the sublime conduct of a bodhisattva, one transforms all sentient beings and purifies all buddha-fields.
Within my buddha-field, it shall be filled with great bodhisattvas.
All Bodhisattvas are of one mind; seeing and hearing them is never in vain.
Within every atom of dust, all Buddhas attain the Way of Buddhahood.
From such as these, they give rise to vows that are immeasurable and boundless.
This vow is inexhaustible, like space, sentient beings,
the nature of phenomena, the world, nirvāṇa, the appearance of all Buddhas,
wisdom, the objects of the mind, the arising of knowledge, and the seeds; may my vow abide in this same way.
Having thus made this great vow, with a mind supple and well-disciplined,
able to believe in the Buddha’s merits, one contemplates sentient beings.
Knowing that they arise from causes and conditions, one then gives rise to a heart of compassion.
I shall rescue those sentient beings who suffer;
for the sake of these beings, I shall practice various kinds of giving, namely:
exquisite lands and the most sublime of all precious jewels.
Elephants, horses, and chariots; Retinues and the common people;
Head, eyes, hands, and feet; He gives his flesh and muscles without regret.
Seeking various scriptures, His mind never grows weary.
Having understood their meaning and intent, they are able to act in accordance with the world.
With a mind of shame and the capacity for receptivity, they cause these qualities to gradually increase;
with a heart of reverence, they make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.
Throughout day and night, the wise one constantly practices in this way;
their roots of goodness become clear and bright, like refined gold.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are able to fully understand the ten stages.
As one practices through successive stages, there shall be no obstacles whatsoever.
Just as a merchant leader, wishing to benefit his fellow traders,
first inquires about all the dangers and hardships along the road.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in the first stage, they should know the practices of all the stages without any hindrance, and are thus able to reach the stage of Buddhahood.
Abiding within this first stage, they frequently become kings of Jambudvīpa.
Skillfully understanding all phenomena, they constantly practice a heart of loving-kindness and compassion.
Guiding others in accordance with the Dharma, all come to have faith and respect;
they urge them to practice giving in order to seek the wisdom of the Buddha.
If a bodhisattva renounces their kingdom and leaves the household life to enter the Buddha-dharma,
practicing with diligent vigor, they will immediately attain a hundred samādhis,
behold a hundred buddhas, and cause a hundred lands to tremble.
His radiance illuminates a hundred lands; his flight through the air is likewise.
He transforms sentient beings in a hundred realms, enters a hundred dharma-gates, and recollects and knows the events of a hundred kalpas. He manifests a hundred kinds of bodies.
One can manifest a retinue of a hundred bodhisattvas;
yet by the power of their vows, they may exceed this number immeasurably.
Now, to clarify the meaning of the first stage, it is explained here only in brief.
If one were to explain it in detail, even ten million eons would not suffice.
This is the first bodhisattva stage, named "The Joyous";
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, it has now been analyzed and explained.
The entire assembly of bodhisattvas, having heard the teaching on the meaning of the higher stages,
their minds became pure and their joy was immeasurable. Each,
from their respective seats, leaped up and remained suspended in mid-air.
They stripped from their bodies exquisite garments and scattered them over Vajragarbha,
all of them praising him, saying: "Excellent, Vajragarbha!"
Possessing great wisdom and fearlessness, he skillfully expounds the stages of the bodhisattva.
The Great Being Vimukticandra, knowing that the minds of the assembly were pure and desiring to hear the description of the characteristics of the second stage, [addressed him].
He then requested Vajragarbha:
"O One of Great Wisdom!
We pray that you will explain the characteristics of the second stage; we all desire to hear it."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha spoke to the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have already fulfilled the first stage and desire to attain the second stage should give rise to ten mental states."

What are the ten? First, a supple mind; second, a harmonious mind; third, a receptive mind; fourth, a virtuous mind; fifth, a tranquil mind; sixth, a true mind; seventh, an unadulterated mind; eighth, a mind free from greed and stinginess; ninth, a joyful mind; tenth, a great mind.
If Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have already fulfilled the first stage and wish to attain the second stage, they should first give rise to these ten kinds of mind.
"O Sons of the Buddha!..."

A bodhisattva who wishes to dwell in this Stainless Ground (vimalā-bhūmi) has, from the very beginning, abstained from all killing, laid aside the sword and staff, been free from malice and resentment, and possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame.

Giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings and constantly seeking their well-being, one does not even harbor ill will to afflict them, let alone commit acts of cruelty.
One abstains from robbery and theft; regarding the necessities of life, one is always content with one's own possessions and does not destroy the wealth of others.

If an object belongs to another, is used by another, or is possessed by another, one does not take even a single blade of grass or a single leaf from among those objects without it being given; how much less so anything more?
Abstaining from sexual misconduct, one is content with the beauty of one's own wife, seeking no external desires nor the women of others;
one does not even give rise to such thoughts, much less engage in the act.
Abandoning false speech, one always speaks words that are true, real, truthful, and consistent; one does not engage in hateful or deceptive speech.
Even in dreams one does not speak falsely, let alone intentionally uttering falsehoods.

One abstains from divisive speech and harbors no intent to cause dissension; what one has heard here is not repeated there, and what one has heard there is not repeated here. Among those who are quarreling and estranged, one always delights in bringing about reconciliation.

They abandon harsh speech—whatever words are coarse, cruel, and malicious, which cause others to feel anger and distress; furthermore, they abandon such speech as that which, through hatred and pride, causes others to fear, suffer, and feel aversion or displeasure, thereby destroying both their own bodies and those of others. All such speech is completely relinquished.

All his speech is exceedingly delightful, beautiful and pleasing to the ear, capable of transforming the hearts of others, harmonious and gentle, loved by many, and able to bring joy and gladness to others; he always utters such words as these.

Free from frivolous speech, he constantly guards himself; regarding what should and should not be said, he always speaks at the proper time, speaks truthfully, speaks beneficially, speaks in accordance with the Dharma, and speaks with deliberation. He does not speak for the sake of amusement or sport, nor does he engage in frivolous speech even in jest, much less do so intentionally.
One does not covet the property of others; if there is something belonging to another, to which another is attached, or which is used by another, one does not form the thought: "I shall take it."

Free from thoughts of malice, resentment, and burning affliction, one should always maintain toward sentient beings a mind that seeks their well-being, a mind of affectionate moisture, a mind of benefit, and a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.

They abandon divination and physiognomy, practice right view, and with firm conviction believe in the causal conditions of sin and merit; they leave behind flattery and crookedness, faithfully take refuge in the Triple Gem, and give rise to a mind of certainty.
"The Bodhisattva thus constantly protects the wholesome paths, reflecting:
'That sentient beings fall into the various evil realms is entirely due to the causes and conditions of the ten unwholesome paths.'"
I shall now abide myself in the ten wholesome dharmas, and I shall also explain these wholesome dharmas to others and point them toward the place of right practice. Why is this?
It is impossible for one who does not practice wholesome deeds themselves to preach the Dharma to others and cause them to abide in wholesomeness.
"Furthermore, this bodhisattva again reflects deeply:
'By reason of practicing the ten unwholesome paths, one falls into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts;
by reason of practicing the ten wholesome paths, one is born among humans, and even as far as being born in the Peak of Existence.'"
Furthermore, these ten paths of wholesome action are practiced in conjunction with wisdom.

Those whose minds are weak and inferior, who delight in meager merit, who feel weary of and fear the triple world, and whose great compassion is thin, hear the Dharma from others and follow the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Furthermore, there are those who practice these ten paths of wholesome action, attaining knowledge of them spontaneously without hearing them from others; though they cannot fully perfect the skillful means of great compassion, they are able to penetrate deeply into the dharma of manifold causes and conditions and reach the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, there are those who practice these ten paths of wholesome action, pure and complete, with minds vast, immeasurable, and boundless.

Toward sentient beings, they give rise to great compassion and possess the power of skillful means; their vows are firm—because they do not abandon any sentient being, because they seek the great wisdom of a Buddha, because they purify the various stages of a bodhisattva, and because they are able to purify the various pāramitās—they are able to enter into profound and vast practices.

Furthermore, being able to purify one's conduct constitutes the ten paths of wholesome action, leading even to the attainment of the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four unhindered knowledges, great loving-kindness and great compassion, and ultimately the perfection of all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā), thereby gathering all the qualities of a Buddha.
"Therefore, we should practice the ten paths of wholesome action and constantly seek all-encompassing wisdom.
This bodhisattva further reflects: "These ten unwholesome paths:

the superior lead to the causes and conditions for hell; the middling lead to the causes and conditions for the animal realm; and the inferior lead to the causes and conditions for the hungry ghost realm."
Among these, the transgression of killing causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, a short lifespan; second, much illness.
The sin of robbery and theft likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, poverty; second, being unable to exercise mastery over shared wealth.
The sin of sexual misconduct likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, their wives will not be chaste and virtuous; second, they will obtain a retinue that does not accord with their wishes.
The sin of lying also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they are frequently slandered; second, they are constantly deceived by many people.
The sin of divisive speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they obtain wicked associates; second, they obtain discordant associates.
The sin of harsh speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they constantly hear unpleasant sounds; second, whatever they say is always met with dispute and litigation.
The sin of frivolous speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, people do not trust or accept whatever they say; second, they are unable to express themselves with clarity when speaking.
The fault of greed also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, having great desire, and second, never knowing contentment.
The sin of anger and resentment also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they are constantly sought out by others for their faults; second, they are constantly harmed and troubled by others.
The sin of wrong view also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, they are always born into families with wrong views; second, their minds are deceitful and crooked.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
In this way, the ten unwholesome paths are all causes and conditions for the great accumulation of suffering.
Then the Bodhisattva further reflects:
"Why is it that we do not distance ourselves from these ten unwholesome paths, practice the ten wholesome paths, and likewise cause others to practice these wholesome paths?

Having reflected thus, they immediately abandon the ten unwholesome paths, abide securely in the ten wholesome paths, and also inspire others to resolve their minds upon abiding in the wholesome paths.

"At that time, this bodhisattva gives rise toward all sentient beings a mind of peace, a mind of joy, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of compassion, a mind of pity, a mind of benefit, a mind of protection, a mind of teacher, a mind of great teacher, and a mind of 'this is my own. He forms this thought:

'These sentient beings have fallen into wrong views, follow after a perverted mind, and travel upon a wrong and perilous path; they are truly to be pitied. We should cause these sentient beings to abide in the path of right view and within the Dharma of reality.'"

"These sentient beings constantly harbor mutual anger and resentment, engage in strife and contention, and discriminate between self and other; we should cause these sentient beings to abide in unsurpassed great compassion."

These sentient beings are never satisfied; they constantly crave the wealth and property of others and perpetually sustain themselves through wrong livelihoods. We should cause these sentient beings to abide in pure actions of body, speech, and mind.

These sentient beings, following after the conditions of greed, hatred, and delusion, are constantly being burned by the great fires of various afflictions, yet they do not seek the means to escape them.
"We should cause these sentient beings to extinguish the great fires of their afflictions and establish them in a place of cool serenity.

These beings are constantly shrouded by the darkness of ignorance; they enter into great obscurity, remaining far removed from the light of wisdom, and they enter the perilous path of birth and death, following after various false views."

"We should cause these sentient beings to attain the unimpeded, pure eye of wisdom; by means of this eye, they shall know the true nature of all phenomena as it is, and obtain the unobstructed, all-encompassing knowledge of reality that does not depend on the teachings of others."

These sentient beings have fallen into the perilous path of birth and death; they are on the verge of falling into the deep pits of the hells, the animal realm, and the hungry ghosts; they have entered the net of evil and false views; they are shrouded by the thicket of various forms of ignorance; they follow the tracks of delusive and heterodox paths; they are perpetually blinded by folly; they are far removed from wise guides; they mistake what is not the way out for the essential means of liberation; they fall into the path of evil Māras; they comply with the intentions of Māra and distance themselves from the intent of the Buddha.

We should cause these sentient beings to cross over the perilous path of birth and death and reach the place of peace and security; we should establish them in the great city of fearlessness of the Omniscient One, free from all decline and affliction.

These sentient beings are submerged by the turbulent waters of the various afflictions; they are constantly swept away by the flow of desire, the flow of existence, the flow of views, and the flow of ignorance.

They perpetually follow the continuous succession of birth and death, entering the great river of craving, where they are devoured by the power of the afflictions and are unable to find the path that leads to liberation.
They are constantly harmed by the evil insects of sensual thoughts, thoughts of malice, and thoughts of harm.
Furthermore, they are seized by the water-dwelling insects and rākṣasas of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), entering into the deep, swirling currents and various perils of the five desires;
they are defiled by the mud of craving and attachment, withered by the parching land of pride (māna), and have no place of refuge.
They cannot escape from the village of enemies—the twelve sense bases (āyatana)—and do not encounter a guide who can lead them across safely.
