We should give rise to great compassion for these sentient beings and, by the power of our great roots of goodness, rescue and deliver them, enabling them to reach a place of peace and stability, free from all terrors and obscurations, and to dwell upon the jewel-island of all-encompassing wisdom.

These sentient beings are deeply attached in their hearts; they abound in anxiety, sorrow, suffering, affliction, and calamity. Bound by hatred and love, fettered by the shackles of desire, they enter the dense forest of ignorance within the triple world.
We should cause these sentient beings to distance themselves from all attachments within the three realms and establish them in the nirvana that is free from marks and unimpeded.

These sentient beings are deeply attached to "self" and "what belongs to self"; they cannot emerge from their own dens of the five aggregates, constantly follow the four inversions, rely upon the empty village of the six sense bases, are afflicted by the poisonous snakes of the four great elements, and are slain by the bandits of the various afflictions.

For those who undergo these immeasurable sufferings and afflictions, we should cause these sentient beings to be free from all attachment and establish them in the path of wisdom regarding emptiness and non-self—that is, nirvana—which severs all obstacles.
These sentient beings possess minds that are narrow and inferior; they delight in the lesser teachings and remain far removed from the unsurpassed, all-encompassing wisdom.
Because they are thus greedily attached to the mind of the Lesser Vehicle, they do not seek the method of deliverance through the bottomless Great Vehicle.
"We should cause these sentient beings to abide in the vast mind and the immeasurable, boundless teachings of all Buddhas—namely, the unsurpassed Great Vehicle.
"O Sons of the Buddha!"
By thus conforming to the power of upholding the precepts, this bodhisattva is well able to extensively generate great compassion.
Abiding in the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*), this bodhisattva beholds hundreds of buddhas, as well as tens of millions of billions of nayutas of buddhas;

having seen these buddhas, he makes offerings to them with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and the necessities of life, giving rise to a heart of reverence toward those buddhas, and further receives the ten paths of wholesome action.
Having received [this teaching], until they attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they shall never lose it midway.

Because these bodhisattvas have distanced themselves for many hundreds, many thousands, even up to many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas from the stains of stinginess, greed, and broken precepts, they purely cultivate generosity and uphold the precepts.
“O Sons of the Buddha!
It is like refined pure gold within a mineral ore; once all impurities are exhausted, it becomes even more brilliant and pure.

So too is the Bodhisattva: dwelling in this Stainless Bodhisattva Ground, for many hundreds, many thousands, even for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, because they have distanced themselves from the stains of stinginess, greed, and broken precepts, they purely cultivate generosity and ethical discipline.”
"At that time, among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the bodhisattva’s loving speech (*priyavāditā*) is predominant;

among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is preeminent—though it is not that the other perfections are not cultivated or accumulated, they simply increase in accordance with each respective stage."
“O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the second stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Stage Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he frequently becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin-rāja*), acting as a great Dharma King who extensively attains the power of the Dharma and accomplishes the seven treasures. Possessing power and sovereignty, he is able to remove the defilements of stinginess, greed, and broken precepts from all sentient beings. Through skillful means, he causes sentient beings to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action, performing great acts of giving that are inexhaustible.”

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never depart from mindfulness of the Dharma, never depart from mindfulness of their companions, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, never depart from mindfulness of the path practiced by bodhisattvas, never depart from mindfulness of the pāramitās, never depart from mindfulness of the ten stages, never depart from mindfulness of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique buddha-qualities, and so on, until they never depart from mindfulness of the perfection of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One should constantly give rise to this thought:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the greatest, the most sublime, the highest, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, the teacher, and the venerable one; indeed, I shall become the one upon whom all sentient beings rely."
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If these Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to leave the household life and practice with diligent vigor, they are able, in a mere moment, to renounce within the Buddha-dharma their home, wife, children, and the five desires."

Having gone forth, he practiced with diligent vigor; in a mere moment, he attained a thousand samādhis, beheld a thousand buddhas, and knew the spiritual powers of a thousand buddhas. He was able to shake a thousand buddha-worlds, fly across a thousand buddha-worlds, illuminate a thousand buddha-worlds, and transform and teach sentient beings in a thousand worlds. He could maintain his life for a thousand kalpas, know the events of a thousand kalpas each in the past and future, skillfully enter a thousand dharma-gates, and manifest as a thousand bodies, each of which could display a thousand bodhisattvas as its retinue. If he so desired, through the power of his vows, he could manifest even more freely than these numbers—hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, nayutas, beyond all calculation or knowledge.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more,
spoke these verses: "The Bodhisattva’s supple mind, The harmonious and receptive mind,
The virtuous mind, the mind of quiescence, The true mind, the unmixed mind."
Free from greed and stinginess, possessing a joyful mind and a great mind—
having attained these ten mental states, the bodhisattva enters the second stage.
Abiding in this stage, the bodhisattva accomplishes all meritorious qualities.
Always abstaining from taking life, not causing distress to any being,
always abstaining from stealing, and not giving rise to thoughts of sexual misconduct;
speaking truthfully, refraining from divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter.
Not giving rise to greed for the possessions of others,
not causing affliction to sentient beings, acting with a straightforward mind and right view,
being free from arrogance and devoid of a crooked or deceitful mind—
Being gentle and free from negligence, they uphold all the teachings of the Buddha.
"All intense suffering and affliction— the blazing bodies of those in the hells,
the animal realm, and the hungry ghosts— all arise from an evil mind."
I have now forever departed from such evil matters,
practicing the true principle of the wholesome dharma of quiescent extinction.
From the human realm up to the Peak of Existence, wherever there are places of experiencing pleasure—
The bliss of dhyāna and the bliss of the Three Vehicles all arise from the ten wholesome actions.
Having reflected thus, one’s mind is always free from negligence;
one personally maintains pure precepts and also teaches others to do so.
Observing all sentient beings, who undergo various forms of suffering and affliction, and having thus felt compassion for them, he gives rise to a heart of profound pity:
"Ordinary worldlings are truly pitiable; they have fallen into various wrong views."
Their minds harbor much resentment, they constantly delight in inciting disputes,
and they always take pleasure in the five desires; never satiated in their greedy seeking,
they give rise to the causes and conditions of the three poisons— I should deliver such as these.
Deeply shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, they fall into the perilous paths of birth and death;
ensnared in the great net of false views, they tumble into the cage of the world;
constantly assailed by the thieves of Māra, they are destroyed by the afflictions.
These are truly pitiable; I ought to deliver them.
Submerged in the deep waters of affliction, drifting and overwhelmed by the four currents, they fully experience within the three realms a hundred kinds of bitter poisons.
Dwelling in the deep thicket of the five aggregates, they give rise to the notions of "I" and "mine.
To deliver myself from this suffering, I shall diligently practice the Path.
Abandoning the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha, they give rise to inferior and base thoughts.
Causing them to abide in the great wisdom of the Buddha, they give rise to immeasurable diligence.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage, they accumulate immeasurable merit,
encounter all Buddhas, and serve and make offerings to them.
By these causes and conditions, their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure,
like fine genuine gold refined with alum.
The Son of the Buddha dwelling on this stage constantly acts as a Wheel-Turning King.
May all sentient beings alike Abide in the path of the ten wholesome actions.

From the moment they first resolve their minds [upon enlightenment], May all the merit they have cultivated and accumulated Be used to rescue the world, Causing them to attain the ten powers of a Buddha.
If one wishes to renounce the royal throne, Leave the household life to practice the Way,
And with a diligent mind practice energetic effort, One shall attain a thousand samādhis,
Behold thousands of Buddhas, And make offerings while listening to and receiving the Dharma.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are able to manifest such deeds; if,
by the power of their vows, they display various supernormal feats to liberate sentient beings,
those who are delivered exceed these numbers immeasurably.
"For those in all worlds who constantly and diligently seek what is wholesome, I have fully explained this; the Second Stage is hereby concluded.

When the bodhisattvas heard of these inconceivable practices,
their hearts were filled with great joy and they paid immeasurable respect. At that moment,
from the midst of the sky, a rain of various famous flowers and incenses fell.
Descending like clouds, they made offerings to Vajragarbha, and all praised him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent!"
Vajragarbha! You have well spoken of those great beings who uphold the practice of pure precepts;
among all sentient beings, they possess a heart of profound compassion.
I shall expound and explain this, the sphere of practice for the second stage.
The subtle and wondrous conduct of Bodhisattvas is truly without any difference;
it is the sphere of pure practice for all these Bodhisattvas.
For the sake of all sentient beings, He constantly seeks all that is good;
The second stage, Pure Clarity, Is now fully explained.
O you who are revered by devas and humans!
I pray you will explain the third stage, skillfully demonstrating the activities of wisdom and the conduct of Bodhisattvas.
I pray you will explain how these great beings practice generosity, ethical discipline, and patience;
how they exert diligence and cultivate meditative concentration.
"Wisdom and skillful means, as well as the mind of compassion—
how does one practice these dharmas to purify the conduct of a Buddha?
Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
“When a Bodhisattva reaches the third stage, with what kind of mind should they be endowed?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having practiced with a profound and pure mind in the second stage, desire to attain the third stage, they should enter the third stage by means of ten mental states.

What are the ten? First, the pure mind; second, the fierce and sharp mind; third, the mind of renunciation; fourth, the detached mind; fifth, the non-regressive mind; sixth, the firm mind; seventh, the radiant and flourishing mind; eighth, the insatiable mind; ninth, the swift mind; tenth, the great mind.

“O Sons of the Buddha! By means of these ten minds, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the third stage (*bhūmi*). He is able to contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) according to their true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), namely:

they are impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and impure; they are soon to perish and decay; they possess the characteristic of being untrustworthy; they arise and cease moment by moment, yet are neither arising nor ceasing; they do not come from the past limit (*pūrvānta*), they do not go to the future limit (*aparānta*), and they do not abide in the present.”

In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates the true nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), knowing that these phenomena are without action, without arising, and without coming or going.

Yet all sentient beings are bound by sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, hatred, and attachment; they have no place of accumulation and no fixed place of birth. They are merely incinerated by the fires of greed, anger, and delusion, increasing the mass of fires of suffering and affliction in future lives. They possess no real nature and are like illusions and transformations.
Having seen this, they become even more weary of and detached from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and proceed toward the wisdom of the Buddha.

"This Bodhisattva knows that the Tathāgata’s wisdom is inconceivable, immeasurable, possessed of great power, invincible, free from mixed characteristics, and devoid of the suffering of decay, affliction, sorrow, and lamentation; it can reach the great city of fearless security from which there is no returning, and it can save immeasurable sentient beings who are tormented by suffering."

Thus, seeing that the Buddha's wisdom is immeasurable and seeing that conditioned phenomena involve immeasurable suffering and affliction, one gives rise to ten superior states of mind toward all sentient beings.

What are these ten? Sentient beings are pitiable; they are solitary and without rescue; they are impoverished and have no place of reliance; the fires of the three poisons burn within them without ceasing; they are confined within the solid prison of the three realms of existence; they dwell constantly in the forest of various evil thorns that are the afflictions; they lack the power of right contemplation; their desire and delight for wholesome dharmas are meager; they have lost the sublime Dharma of the Buddhas and constantly follow along with the flow of the waters of birth and death; and they are terrified of nirvana.
Seeing that sentient beings thus suffer from so many misfortunes and afflictions, this bodhisattva arouses great diligence, thinking:

"I must rescue these sentient beings; I must liberate them; I must cause them to become pure; I must cause them to attain liberation; I must establish them in wholesome states; I must cause them to dwell in peace; I must cause them to rejoice; I must know what is appropriate for them; I must cause them to cross over; I must cause their suffering to be extinguished."

"Thus, the Bodhisattva skillfully remains far removed from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), deeply contemplates all sentient beings, and perceives that the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of all Buddhas possesses immeasurable benefits. Immediately desiring to be endowed with the Buddha’s wisdom in order to rescue and deliver sentient beings, he diligently practices the Bodhisattva path."

He reflects thus: "By what causes and conditions, by what skillful means, shall I pull these sentient beings out from within the great suffering and various afflictions, so that they may dwell forever in ultimate and eternal bliss?"
"Immediately one knows that this can only be attained by those who abide in unimpeded liberation and wisdom.
This unimpeded wisdom and liberation is not separate from the wisdom that penetrates all phenomena as they truly are, nor from the wisdom of non-active practice."
"From what is such illumination of wisdom obtained?
One should know that it is not apart from the definitive wisdom derived from extensive learning. He then further thought:
“What is the foundation of all Buddha-dharmas, such as the unhindered liberations?
They have not being separated from hearing the Dharma as their foundation.

Having reflected thus, the Bodhisattva redoubled his vigor whenever seeking the Dharma; day and night he constantly delighted in listening to the Dharma, never feeling satiated, and his mind never ceased.

Delighting in the Dharma, loving the Dharma, relying on the Dharma, following the Dharma, honoring the Dharma, taking the Dharma as ultimate, taking refuge in the Dharma, taking the Dharma as salvation, and practicing in accordance with the Dharma—thus does a bodhisattva skillfully seek the Dharma.

"Regarding all precious jewels, wealth, gold, silver, and so forth, their storehouses are never lacking or begrudged; they do not conceive thoughts of difficulty regarding these things, but rather conceive thoughts of how difficult it is to encounter those who preach the Dharma."
For the sake of seeking the Dharma, there is nothing among internal or external things that he cannot relinquish.

Of all things in the world that can be given as alms—namely, kingdoms, subjects, retinues, fields and estates, wealth and goods, mani-jewels, treasuries of gold and silver, elephants, horses, carriages, various precious necklaces, all manner of ornaments for the body, wives, children, and even his own limbs, hands, feet, ears, eyes, nose, and tongue—he gives his entire body away without any sense of attachment or regret.

Furthermore, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, one should wholeheartedly revere, make offerings to, and attend upon the teacher who expounds it; one must eliminate pride, self-conceit, and arrogance, as well as all evil afflictions and hardships, and be able to endure all unreasonable treatment and the like.
Because they seek the Dharma deeply, if they obtain even a single verse of a teaching never heard before, it is superior to obtaining treasures that fill a trichiliocosm;
and to hear a single stanza of the True Dharma is superior to attaining the positions of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, Śakra Devānām Indra, or Brahmā, and remaining there for immeasurable eons.
"If someone comes to this bodhisattva and says:
'I shall give you a single phrase of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, which can purify the path practiced by a bodhisattva; let me hear it from you. "
"If one can enter a great pit of fire and undergo such great suffering, I shall give it to you.
This bodhisattva then thinks:
"For the sake of receiving even a single phrase of the Dharma, I would cast myself from the Brahma Heaven down into a pit of fire as large as a trichiliocosm, let alone a small pit of fire."

"We who seek the Dharma should accept all things; we should seek the Dharma even at the cost of undergoing all the sufferings of the hells, let alone the various minor pains and afflictions of human life.
For the sake of seeking the Dharma, they give rise to such a mind.
Furthermore, regarding the Dharma as it has been heard, his mind is always joyful and he is able to contemplate it correctly.
Having heard all these dharmas, this bodhisattva subdues his mind and, in a secluded place, reflects thus:
"One who practices according to the teaching attains the Buddha-dharma; it cannot be attained merely by what is spoken with the mouth."

When a bodhisattva is thus able to abide in the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), they depart from all desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and the joy and happiness born of seclusion, they enter the first dhyāna.

With the subsiding of directed and sustained thought, through internal clarity and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of concentration, they enter the second dhyāna.

Through the fading away of joy, they dwell in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body; that which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindful, and happy," they enter the third dhyāna.

By abandoning both suffering and pleasure, and by first extinguishing sorrow and joy, one enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity and pure mindfulness.

This Bodhisattva, transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing all perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, perceives infinite space and thus enters the formless attainment of the sphere of infinite space;
transcending all perceptions of space, he perceives infinite consciousness and thus enters the formless attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Transcending all marks of consciousness, one knows there is nothing whatsoever and thus enters the formless meditative attainment of the sphere of nothingness;
transcending the sphere of nothingness, one knows the peace of that which is neither perception nor non-perception and thus enters the formless sphere of neither perception nor non-perception;
yet, because one acts in accordance with all dharmas, one does not take delight in or cling to them.

"This Bodhisattva, with a mind of loving-kindness that is lofty, vast, and immeasurable—free from anger, resentment, and malice—pervades one direction, two directions, three directions, and four directions by the power of faith and understanding; likewise for the four intermediate directions, the zenith, and the nadir."

With a mind of compassion, a mind of sympathetic joy, and a mind of equanimity—vast, exalted, and immeasurable; free from ill will and free from malice—one pervades one direction with the power of resolute faith, and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as the four intermediate points, the zenith, and the nadir.

"This bodhisattva possesses various supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*): he can shake the great earth; transform one body into many bodies and many bodies into one body; manifest disappearance and then reappear; pass unhindered through stone walls and mountain obstructions as if traveling through empty space; travel cross-legged through the air like a bird in flight; enter and emerge from the earth without difference from entering water; walk upon water as if on land; emit smoke and flames from his body like a great mass of fire; reach out his hand to touch and stroke the sun and moon despite their great divine merit and majestic power; and exercise mastery over his physical strength even as far as the Brahma world."
This bodhisattva, with the purified divine ear that surpasses the human ear, hears all sounds of humans and devas, whether near or far.

This bodhisattva, with the knowledge of others' minds, knows the minds of others as they truly are: he knows a defiled mind as a defiled mind, and a mind free from defilement as a mind free from defilement; a hateful mind and a mind free from hatred; a deluded mind and a mind free from delusion; a stained mind and a mind free from stain; a small mind and a great mind; he knows a distracted mind as a distracted mind, and a concentrated mind and an unconcentrated mind; a bound mind and a liberated mind; a surpassable mind and an unsurpassable mind, knowing a surpassable mind and an unsurpassable mind as they truly are; thus, by means of his own mind, he knows the minds of others.

This bodhisattva recollects and knows all places of birth in past lives—namely, one life, two lives, three, four, five lives, and so on up to ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and even up to a hundred lives, a thousand lives, ten thousand lives, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of lives.

For one kalpa, two kalpas, and even for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, he is able to recollect and know all the immeasurable periods of formation and destruction within those kalpas, as well as all the causes and conditions experienced throughout them: "I was born in that place; such was my lineage, such my name and surname, such my food and drink, such my suffering and joy, and such was the duration of my stay. Having died there, I was born here; having died here, I was born there."
In this way, he is able to recollect and know all such various signs and causes and conditions. This Bodhisattva’s divine eye is pure and surpasses that of the human eye;

he sees the birth and death of sentient beings, their physical forms—whether beautiful or ugly, good or evil, poor or wealthy—and their passage through the good and evil realms, receiving retribution according to their karma, all knowing them as they truly are. That is to say: these sentient beings have accomplished evil deeds of body, accomplished evil deeds of speech, and accomplished evil deeds of mind; they have opposed the noble ones and accepted the teachings of false views. Due to the causes and conditions of having given rise to sinful karma, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the evil realms and are born in hell.

These sentient beings, having accomplished wholesome bodily karma, wholesome verbal karma, and wholesome mental karma; not opposing the noble ones; and believing in and accepting right view—by reason of these causes and conditions of practicing wholesome karma, after death they are reborn in a good destination, in the heavens.

"This bodhisattva is able to enter and emerge from all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis, yet does not follow them into rebirth; rather, wherever there is a factor conducive to awakening, by the power of their vow, they are able to be born therein."

"When this bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Radiance (prabhākari-bhūmi), they behold hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of buddhas, and with reverence, offerings, respect, and praise—providing them with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites—they draw near to these buddhas to hear and receive the Dharma.
Having heard and received the Dharma, they practice according to their capacity."
"At that time, this bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing, existing only through a multitude of conditions.

Over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, the bonds of desire accumulated therein gradually become thin and weak; all bonds of existence and all bonds of ignorance likewise become entirely thin and weak, no longer being further accumulated.
Because they are not accumulated, he cuts off wrong greed, wrong hatred, and wrong delusion."
“O Sons of the Buddha!
Just as genuine gold, when refined and processed by a skilled smith, becomes increasingly exquisite and its radiance becomes doubly superior;

so too is it with the Bodhisattva: dwelling in the Stage of Illumination (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), because they do not accumulate the three bonds, they sever perverse greed, perverse anger, and perverse delusion, and all their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.”

This bodhisattva’s mind of patience, pliancy, excellence, indestructibility, immovability, lack of turbidity, neither elation nor depression, non-expectation of reward for all that is done, the arising of a mind of gratitude even for slight deeds by others, lack of flattery or crookedness, and lack of defilement or distraction, becomes increasingly superior, luminous, and pure.

"At that time, among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the Bodhisattva’s loving speech and beneficial conduct were predominant; among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of patience and the perfection of diligence increased further; and all other factors conducive to enlightenment became increasingly clear and pure."
“O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the third stage of illumination for all Bodhisattvas.

When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell in this stage, they frequently manifest as Śakra Devānām Indra; their wisdom is fierce and sharp, and through skillful means and conditions, they are able to transform sentient beings, causing them to leave behind lustful desire.”

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and so forth, up to never departing from mindfulness of the possession of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One should constantly give rise to this thought:
"When shall I become the foremost and the most honored among sentient beings, even to the point of becoming a refuge for all sentient beings?"

If this person desires to apply themselves with diligent vigor, they can, in a single moment, attain one hundred thousand samādhis, and even manifest a retinue of one hundred thousand bodhisattvas. According to their power of vows, their sovereign spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*) are incalculable, beyond reckoning for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to make this meaning even more clear, spoke these verses:
"By means of this mind, the bodhisattva can attain the third stage:
the pure mind, the fierce mind, the mind of renunciation, the detached mind, and the non-regressing mind."
With a firm mind, a patient mind, a receptive mind, a joyful mind, and a great mind—
by means of such minds as these, one enters the third stage.
The wise one, dwelling on the Stage of Radiance, contemplates conditioned phenomena as impure,
impermanent, and suffering; as having the characteristics of selflessness and decay,
lacking any solid nature, and perishing moment by moment before long.
Reflecting thus, one knows that there is no characteristic of coming or going.
Seeing all conditioned phenomena as like a disease, like an abscess or a sore,
one sees how they are bound by the fetters of craving and give rise to all manner of sorrow, lamentation, and suffering.
But being burned by the fierce fires of greed, hatred, and delusion,
from beginningless time until now, they have blazed on without ever ceasing.
At that moment, he conceived a sense of weary detachment toward everything within the three realms.
Contemning conditioned phenomena, the mind has no attachment.
It seeks only the wisdom of all Buddhas— immeasurable, boundless, profound,
inconceivable, pure, and free from all suffering.
Having thus perceived the Buddha’s wisdom and being free from all suffering and affliction,
he takes pity on all sentient beings who are impoverished and lack merit and wisdom,
whose fires of the three poisons burn constantly, and who have no one to protect them.
Falling into the midst of hell, one is tormented by a hundred kinds of suffering;
the heedless ordinary person sinks into a mass of afflictions,
blind and dark with no vision, having lost the precious jewels of all Buddha-dharmas.
Constantly following the waters of birth and death, they are without fear yet terrified by emptiness.
Toward these sentient beings, I shall diligently strive to deliver them;
through the pursuit of wisdom with vigor, I shall act as their benefactor.
Reflecting on what skillful means might provide protection and refuge,
I see that only the Tathāgatas possess profound, wondrous, and unimpeded wisdom.
What is the cause of this wisdom?
It arises solely from wisdom;
this wisdom is born only from extensive learning.
Having reflected thus, one should diligently seek the Dharma of extensive learning.
Day and night, always with diligent effort, they listen and receive the teaching without weariness;
they recite and delight in the Dharma, regarding the Dharma alone as precious.
For the sake of seeking the Dharma, they offer all manner of rare treasures and the like.
One’s beloved wife and children, all one's attendants as they please,
the kingdom and its cities, and all excellent goods for livelihood—
one gives these away with joy, the heart feeling no attachment or regret.
Head, eyes, ears, nose, and tongue, teeth as well as hands and feet,
limbs, joints, body, flesh, and blood, heart, liver, marrow, and brain—
giving these things away to others, he does not yet consider it difficult.
To hear the True Dharma is the most difficult of all things.
Suppose there were a person who said to this bodhisattva:
"If you can now enter this great mass of fierce flames,"
"Only then shall I grant you the Dharma taught by all the Buddhas.
Having heard this, he was immediately filled with joy and threw himself into the mass of fire.
"Even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with masses of fire,"
To descend from the Brahma world to Mount Sumeru is not difficult;
but to seek even a single phrase of the Dharma taught by all Buddhas,
which rescues beings from all suffering and affliction— to attain that is exceedingly difficult.
From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, until the attainment of the Buddha-way,
throughout this entire interval, for the sake of seeking all dharmas,
I have fully endured the sufferings of Avīci hell for as many eons as there are.
"How much more so for those in the human realm—how could they not overcome even minor sufferings?
Through the causal condition of hearing the Dharma, one is able to attain right mindfulness;
through the causal condition of right mindfulness, one is able to give rise to various meditative concentrations.
The profound and wondrous samādhis, as well as the five supernormal powers—these can all be successively aroused;
with mastery, they do not arise in dependence on birth.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are able, with a resolute mind, to...
Having made extensive offerings to many Buddhas and having heard and received the Dharma they taught,
one cuts off wrong views, craving, and hatred; other afflictions become thin and faint,
like refined gold that has been tempered until it reaches its proper state.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, the treasury of their merit is filled;
they frequently become kings of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, exercising sovereign power over sensual desires.
Out of love for the Buddha’s merit, they transform and guide immeasurable multitudes.
They are able to cause all beings to dwell securely within the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
When Bodhisattvas abide in this stage, they are able, with a supple mind,
to practice diligence with vigor and attain hundreds of thousands of samādhis.
They see all the Buddhas, their bodies adorned with the marks and signs;
their minds become increasingly sharp and keen, for those whose power of aspiration is preeminent.
They constantly act for the sake of all sentient beings, diligently seeking what is beneficial.
Having thus explained and analyzed this, the third stage, the Luminous, is complete.
When the sons of the Buddha heard this teaching on the characteristics and meanings of such a stage—
profound, wondrous, and immeasurable— their hearts were all filled with great joy.
They scattered various kinds of fragrant flowers as an offering to the Tathāgata.
The earth and the waters of the great ocean all shook violently,
while the celestial maidens in the sky above—
With voices likewise subtle and wondrous, they sang praises of this supreme Dharma.
The King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, hearing this, was filled with great joy;
he rained down mani-jewels, scattering them over the Buddha.
Leaping for joy, he praised him, saying:
"Excellent! A Buddha has appeared in the world; the treasury of his merit is spread abroad, bringing benefit to us."
Now that I have heard this exposition of the characteristics and meaning of the Bodhisattva stages,
a matter such as this, which is difficult to hear even in hundreds of thousands of kalpas, has been heard by me.
I pray that you will further explain the subsequent stages, for the benefit of all devas and humans.
All were joyful and desired to hear about the characteristics of the various practices for attaining the stages.
Bodhisattva Vimukticandra again entreated Vajragarbha:
"I pray that you will explain for the sake of all bodhisattvas the practices up to the fourth stage."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have fulfilled the pure practices of the third stage and wish to attain the fourth stage, they should enter this fourth stage by means of ten gateways of the illumination of Dharma."

What are the ten? First, the contemplation of the nature of sentient beings; second, the contemplation of the nature of phenomena; third, the contemplation of the nature of worlds; fourth, the contemplation of the nature of space; fifth, the contemplation of the nature of consciousness; sixth, the contemplation of the nature of the desire realm; seventh, the contemplation of the nature of the form realm; eighth, the contemplation of the nature of the formless realm; ninth, the contemplation of the nature of swift faith and understanding; tenth, the contemplation of the nature of the great mind.
"O sons of the Buddha!
By means of these ten gateways of the light of Dharma, bodhisattvas are able to enter the fourth stage from the third.
O sons of the Buddha!"

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the fourth bodhisattva stage, the Blazing Ground (Arciṣmatī), they gain increasing power within the family of the Tathāgata; because they have attained the internal dharma, they possess ten kinds of knowledge.

What are the ten? First, the non-retrogressive mind; second, the attainment of unshakable faith within the Three Jewels and ultimate pure wisdom; third, the cultivation of the contemplation of arising and ceasing; fourth, the cultivation that all phenomena are fundamentally unborn; fifth, the constant cultivation of practices for returning to and circulating within the world; sixth, the cultivation of knowing that birth exists due to the causes and conditions of karma; seventh, the cultivation of discerning the distinctions between the gates of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; eighth, the cultivation of the distinctions among the karmas of sentient beings; ninth, the cultivation of the distinctions between the past limit and the future limit; tenth, the cultivation of the practice of constant cessation and non-abiding in the present.
These ten wisdom-minds then cause one to be born into the family of the Buddha, gaining transformative power.
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this fourth bodhisattva stage, he contemplates the internal body as a body, practicing with diligence and single-mindedness to eliminate worldly greed and anxiety."
One contemplates the external body as a body, practicing diligent mindfulness with a concentrated mind to eliminate worldly greed and sorrow;
one contemplates the internal and external body as a body, practicing diligent mindfulness with a concentrated mind to eliminate worldly greed and sorrow;

one contemplates internal feelings, external feelings, and internal-external feelings; internal mind, external mind, and internal-external mind; and internal phenomena, external phenomena, and internal-external phenomena as phenomena, practicing diligent mindfulness with a concentrated mind to eliminate worldly greed and sorrow.
"This bodhisattva, for the sake of not arising unarisen evil and unwholesome states, generates desire, exerts effort, arouses the mind, and applies right abandonment;
for the sake of abandoning arisen evil and unwholesome states, he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses the mind, and applies right abandonment;
for the sake of arising unarisen wholesome states, he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses the mind, and applies right practice."

In order that the various wholesome dharmas already arisen may remain without being lost and may be cultivated and expanded, he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and practices correctly.
This Bodhisattva cultivates the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*):

the basis of psychic power consisting in concentration of desire and the cultivation of the formative forces of abandonment; relying on disenchantment, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, it is directed toward relinquishment.

The basis for power consisting in the cultivation of the basis of psychic power that is concentration of energy and accomplishment of the factors of exertion; the basis for power consisting in the cultivation of the basis of psychic power that is concentration of mind and accomplishment of the factors of exertion; and the basis for power consisting in the cultivation of the basis of psychic power that is concentration of investigation and accomplishment of the factors of exertion—these rely upon disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, and are dedicated toward equanimity.
"This bodhisattva practices the faculty of faith, relying on disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, and dedicating it toward equanimity;
likewise, they practice the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, relying on disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, and dedicating them toward equanimity."
"This bodhisattva practices the power of faith, relying on disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment;

he practices the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom, relying on disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, and dedicating them toward relinquishment."
“This bodhisattva practices the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, and dedicating it toward equanimity;

he practices the awakening factors of discrimination of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, relying on disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, and dedicating them toward equanimity.”
"This bodhisattva practices right view, relying upon disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, and dedicates it toward relinquishment;

he practices right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, relying upon disenchantment, detachment, and cessation, and dedicates them toward relinquishment."
"This Bodhisattva practices because he does not abandon the mind [set on] sentient beings;
because of the power of his original vows, he takes great compassion as the foremost and practices in conjunction with great loving-kindness;

for the sake of gathering all-knowledge, for the sake of adorning the Buddha-land, for the sake of possessing the various powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of a Buddha, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and the perfect voice; for the sake of conforming to the Buddha’s profound liberation, and for the sake of contemplating great wisdom and skillful means."
“O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in the Bodhisattva stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), all forms of attachment to the view of a self-body—including attachment to a self, attachment to sentient beings, attachment to persons or life-spanners, and attachment to knowers or perceivers—as well as attachment to the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements; all the resulting contractions and expansions, withdrawals and manifestations, the mental investigations of their own conduct, and the cherished clinging to what they perceive as a refuge or an island—all these are utterly extinguished.”

"This Bodhisattva’s factors conducive to enlightenment, which arise from wisdom and skillful means through even greater diligence, become increasingly supple and serviceable as they accord with their practice."
With a mind free from weariness, he further seeks the supreme Dharma, increasing his wisdom to save all the world.
He accords with his teachers, receiving their instructions with reverence, and practices exactly as they have taught.

"At that time, this bodhisattva knows kindness and knows how to repay it; his mind becomes increasingly gentle and harmonious, dwelling in peace and happiness with others, possessing a straightforward mind and a supple mind.
Free from crookedness, he practices the conduct of right concentration;
free from arrogance, he is easy to converse with."
By following these instructions, one grasps the intention of the teacher.
Thus, being endowed with a virtuous mind, a gentle mind, a tranquil mind, and a patient mind, one contemplates and practices the various dharmas of the pure stages.

"At that time, this bodhisattva becomes one whose diligence is irreversible: diligence that is not abandoned, indestructible diligence, tireless diligence, unfaltering diligence, vast diligence, boundless diligence, fierce and sharp diligence, unequaled diligence, diligence that rescues all sentient beings, and diligence that discriminates between what is the path and what is not the path."
"The mind and will of this bodhisattva are pure; he does not lose his profound resolve (*adhyāśaya*), and his faith and understanding are clear and sharp. All roots of goodness increase.
He remains far removed from worldly defilements, and disbelief, doubt, regret, and the like have all been extinguished."

Free from doubt and free from regret, they are fully endowed with presence; they never weary of nor abandon the matters of great faith and understanding regarding all Buddhas, naturally delighting in their practice, and an immeasurable mind is constantly manifest before them.

"When a Bodhisattva dwells in this fourth stage, the Radiant (*arciṣmatī*), they are able to see hundreds, thousands, tens of millions, billions, and nayutas of Buddhas. They make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise these Buddhas with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine; they draw near to the Buddhas and listen to the Dharma with a single mind.
Having heard and received the Dharma, they are able to faithfully accept, uphold, and practice it, frequently leaving the household life to cultivate the Path under the Buddhas."

"The resolve and profound intention of this bodhisattva are pure; their faith and understanding become increasingly clear and equal. Abiding for many kalpas—several hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, nayutas of kalpas—their roots of goodness become ever more excellent, lucid, and sharp."
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Just as pure gold used for ornamentation cannot be equaled by other gold, so too,

when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell in this Bodhisattva stage of Blazing Fire (*arcismatī*), their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and sharp, such that they cannot be equaled by Bodhisattvas of the lower stages."

"Just as the light of a mani jewel is pure and can illuminate the four directions, such that other jewels cannot equal it, and its radiance is not extinguished even when rained upon or drenched with water;

so too, when a Bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Blazing (Arciṣmatī), they cannot be equaled by Bodhisattvas of the lower stages, and neither any Māras nor any afflictions (kleśa) can destroy their wisdom."
"O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the brief explanation of the fourth stage, the Blazing Stage (Arciṣmatī), of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell in this stage, they frequently become the Heavenly King Suyāma, extensively teaching and transforming sentient beings to destroy their sense of self."

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never depart from mindfulness of the Dharma, and never depart from mindfulness of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas as their companions, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of the perfection of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
They constantly give rise to this thought:
"When shall I become the foremost and the most honored among all sentient beings, even to the point of becoming their refuge?"

“If this bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice such diligent vigor, in a single moment they will attain ten billion samādhis, and even manifest ten billion bodhisattvas as their retinue; yet, through the power of their vows, they can freely manifest even more than these numbers for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of incalculable kalpas.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"When the Bodhisattvas are fully endowed with it, Having cultivated and purified the Stage of Radiance (Prabhākārī),
They contemplate the nature of sentient beings, The nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and the nature of the world."
Through the nature of space, the nature of consciousness, and the nature of the three realms,
by means of resolute faith and the purity of the profound mind, one attains entry into the fourth stage.
Thus, within the family of the Tathāgata, they increase and attain power;
they do not regress from the Buddha-way, and their faith in the Three Jewels is indestructible.
Contemplating that arising and ceasing are without action, they know the revolving course of the world.
Birth arises from karma; thus saṃsāra and nirvāṇa differ.

Knowing the various karmas of sentient beings and observing the prior and subsequent limits of phenomena, one does not dwell in the marks of permanence or extinction—this is the power of birth within the Buddha’s family.
When the great bodhisattvas and others have attained such a Dharma as this,
out of compassion for all sentient beings, they practice the mindfulness of body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Relying on the four foundations of mindfulness— internal and external— they abide in disenchantment, detachment, and...
Relying likewise upon tranquility, one dedicates [merit] toward Nirvana.
Because evil dharmas are eliminated, wholesome dharmas increase;
one practices the four right efforts and cultivates the four bases of psychic power.
Practicing the five faculties and cultivating the five powers,
training in the seven factors of enlightenment and walking the eightfold noble path—
practicing such dharmas as these is solely for the sake of sentient beings.
Assisted by his original vows, with a mind of compassion as his foremost guide,
he seeks all-encompassing wisdom;
to purify all Buddha-fields, he accomplishes the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha.
All sounds and verbal expressions, the profound and wondrous Dharma,
as well as unimpeded liberation and great wisdom with its skillful means—
[these arise] from the view of a self as the foremost, along with the sixty-two views and the like.
The view of a sentient being, the view of a person, the view of a life-principle,
and the view of a knower— regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, which are the objects of attachment—
all these have been completely severed upon attaining this fourth stage.
As they sever afflictions and karma, their minds likewise become pure;
all the virtuous deeds they perform are for the sake of saving the world.
With supple and gentle hearts, the Bodhisattvas are never heedless.
With a steadfast mind, a straightforward mind, and a mind seeking the benefit of sentient beings—
one seeks these matters for the sake of the unsurpassed path.
For the sake of the station of great wisdom and to benefit the world, [one practices].
With a profound mind, they honor and support their teachers, Delighting in practicing according to their instructions.
Those who recognize kindness and repay it are easy to transform, Free from resentment and devoid of crookedness of mind;
Gentle and harmonious, they find joy in dwelling together.
Cultivating such dharmas with diligence and without turning back,
the Bodhisattva abides in this stage; their profound mind, straightforward mind,
pure mind, and resolute faith all become increasingly bright and clear.
All roots of goodness will increase;
such things as defilements, doubt, and remorse shall all be completely eliminated.
All bodhisattvas dwelling in this, the fourth stage, the Radiant (Arciṣmatī), encounter immeasurable buddhas;
they receive and uphold the teachings these buddhas proclaim.
Under these buddhas, they go forth into homelessness, their resolve being difficult to thwart or destroy.
Just as an ornament of pure gold cannot be surpassed by other gold,
so too when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, their profound resolve,
wisdom, and skillful means, as well as the pure path they practice, are unsurpassed.
Even a thousand billion Māras cannot destroy them.
Like a truly wondrous, bright pearl that is not ruined by water or rain,
the Bodhisattva dwelling on this stage is honored by gods and humans.
He frequently becomes King of the Yāma Heaven, Able to overturn all false views.
Whatever wholesome deeds he performs, They are all for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom;
His mind is always firm and steadfast, And cannot be moved or turned aside.
If one practices with diligent vigor, one attains ten billion samādhis and can see ten billion buddhas;
yet the power of one's vows exceeds even this.
Such is the fourth stage, pure and named "The Blazing Flame."
O you of immeasurable merit and wisdom!
This explanation of the practices for the fourth stage of the bodhisattvas has now been completed. Having heard this, the bodhisattvas—
Their hearts were filled with great joy, leaping for boundless delight.
They rained down a multitude of precious flowers, falling in dense drifts like snow,
as they all praised in unison:
"Excellent, Vajragarbha Mahāsattva!
You and the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, together with all your retinues,"
In the space above, their hearts were filled with great joy;
they emitted myriad wondrous radiances and performed various celestial musical performances,
singing praises of the Buddha’s virtues as well as those of the assembly of bodhisattvas.
The celestial maidens, each with a pure and wondrous voice,
praised the Buddha in unison, speaking these words: “World-Honored One,
after a long time has passed, you have fulfilled the vows sought through diligent toil.”
The unsurpassed, true, and perfect path—only now has it finally been attained.
One who benefits devas and humans—after a long time, he is finally seen today.
Śākyamuni Buddha has now arrived at the celestial palace.
From long ago until now, for the first time, signs of change have stirred;
from long ages past until now, for the first time, wondrous light has been emitted;
since beings existed long ago, for the first time, they have attained peace and happiness.
Only after a long time have I finally been able to hear the voice of great compassion;
having crossed to the shore of all merits, I have now, after a vast age, encountered it.
The Holy King is able to utterly destroy my mind of pride and the like.
Peerless one worthy of offerings, you now receive this worship;
you can open the path to the heavens and enable the attainment of all-knowledge.
The World-Honored One is exceedingly pure, immeasurable as space.
Untainted by worldly dharmas, like a lotus flower in the water;
standing loftily in the world, like Sumeru, the king of golden mountains,
amidst the great ocean— therefore, I joyfully prostrate before you.
Thus these goddesses, each with various wondrous voices,
having finished singing praises with reverent hearts, gazed upon the Buddha in silence.
Then the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra requested Vajragarbha to speak.
The Bodhisattva attains the fifth stage, the causal conditions for its characteristics.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!
When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already fulfilled the fourth stage and desire to attain the fifth stage, they are able to enter the fifth stage by means of ten kinds of impartial minds.

What are the ten? First, the equality of the Buddha-dharma of the past; second, the equality of the Buddha-dharma of the future; third, the equality of the Buddha-dharma of the present; fourth, the equality of purity of precepts; fifth, the equality of purity of mind; sixth, the equality of purity through the removal of views, doubt, and regret; seventh, the equality of purity through knowing the path and the non-path; eighth, the equality of purity through knowing conduct and insight; ninth, the equality of purity through the increasingly superior development of all factors of enlightenment; tenth, the equality of purity through the equal transformation of sentient beings.
O Sons of the Buddha!

By means of these ten pure minds of equality, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas fully attain entry into the fifth stage. Because they have skillfully cultivated the dharmas of enlightenment, because their profound mind is pure, and because they seek the ever-superior path, they are able to attain the Way of the Buddhas.

"This bodhisattva, having attained the power of great vows, does not abandon any being through a heart of compassion; having attained the power of the principles of mindfulness and wisdom, they cultivate merit and wisdom without relinquishing them."
They apply skillful means, desiring to attain the superior path of the higher stages;
they clearly contemplate the Dharma, receiving the protection of the spiritual power of all Buddhas;

they give rise to a mind of non-retrogression in meditative concentration, knowing as it truly is: "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering, this is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, this is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and this is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering."

"This bodhisattva skillfully knows the conventional truth, skillfully knows the ultimate truth, skillfully knows the truth of characteristics, skillfully knows the truth of distinctions, skillfully knows the truth of manifestation and accomplishment, skillfully knows the truth of phenomena, skillfully knows the truth of origination, skillfully knows the truth of exhaustion and non-arising, and skillfully knows the truth of entering the path; because they successively accomplish the various stages of a bodhisattva, they skillfully know the truth of practicing the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
At that time, because the Bodhisattva always abides in the One Vehicle, he thoroughly knows the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
because he accords with the inclinations of sentient beings and causes them to rejoice, he knows the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
and because he discerns the specific characteristics of all phenomena, he knows the truth of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-satya).
Because all phenomena are distinct from one another, one knows the truth of differentiation;
because one discerns the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, one knows the truth of manifestation and accomplishment;
and because of the suffering and affliction of body and mind, one knows the truth of suffering.
One knows the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) because all paths arise in continuous succession;
one knows the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya) because all afflictions and fevers are ultimately extinguished;
and one knows the truth of the path (mārga-satya) because the non-dual dharma is brought forth.

Because they know all phenomena through the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and thereby accomplish all bodhisattva stages, they skillfully understand the truth of practicing the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
yet, by the power of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*), they know that this is not the attainment of the wisdom of the inexhaustible truth.

"In this way, the bodhisattva, by means of this knowledge of the truths, knows all conditioned phenomena as they truly are: as false, deceptive, and subject to decay; as merely persisting for a moment to delude ordinary persons."

At that time, the bodhisattva’s great compassion toward sentient beings becomes increasingly predominant and manifests before them; he is able to give rise to the radiance of great loving-kindness and attains such power of wisdom that he does not abandon any sentient being, constantly seeking the wisdom of a Buddha, and observing the prior and subsequent limits of all conditioned phenomena as they truly are.
He knows that sentient beings arise from ignorance and craving since the beginningless past, transmigrating through birth and death;
unable to stir or depart from their abode within the five aggregates, they increase the mass of great suffering and affliction.
Within this, there is no self and nothing belonging to a self; there is no sentient being and no person; there is no knower and no life-principle;
and it is likewise for the future limit.
Thus, although there is nothing at all, they remain ignorant and their craving and attachment do not cease; they do not know that within the boundless, there is both emergence and non-emergence.
At that time, he reflects: "Ordinary beings are truly strange;
because of ignorance and delusion, they have experienced immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable bodies—those already extinguished, those now being extinguished, and those yet to be extinguished."

Thus constantly undergoing birth and death, they are unable to conceive a sense of weary detachment toward the body; instead, they further increase this mechanical body of suffering. Constantly drifting on the waters of birth and death, they cannot return to the house of the five aggregates, nor can they abandon them. They do not fear the four great poisonous snakes, nor can they pull out the arrows of pride and views, nor extinguish the flames of greed, anger, and delusion, nor destroy the ignorant darkness of ignorance, nor dry up the great ocean of craving and attachment. Failing to seek the Great Sage Teacher of the Ten Powers, they always follow the will of Māra within the city of birth and death, being frequently driven about by various evil thoughts and perceptions.

Thus, for these sentient beings who are afflicted by suffering, solitary, and destitute—having no savior, no refuge, and no ultimate path—I alone, without equal companion, shall cultivate and accumulate merit and wisdom. By means of these provisions, I shall cause all these sentient beings to abide in ultimate purity, even until they attain the Buddha’s power of unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena.

"Reflecting thus, from right contemplation there arises the power of wisdom. He makes a vow that all roots of goodness he performs shall be for the sake of delivering all sentient beings; for seeking what is excellent for all sentient beings; for seeking their peace and happiness; for benefiting all sentient beings; for liberating all sentient beings; for ensuring all sentient beings are free from suffering and affliction; for ensuring all sentient beings are free from coarseness and evil; for purifying the minds of all sentient beings; for subduing all sentient beings; and for extinguishing all the sorrows, afflictions, and sufferings of all sentient beings, thereby fulfilling their aspirations."
"At that time, this bodhisattva, dwelling in this fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā), is called 'one who possesses mindfulness' because they do not forget any dharmas;
they are called 'one who possesses wisdom' because their wisdom is decisive;
and they are called 'one who possesses the Path' because they know the sequence of the meaning of the scriptures."
Because they protect themselves and protect others, they are called those possessed of shame and remorse;
because they do not abandon the observance of the precepts, they are called those of firm resolve;
because they skillfully contemplate what is possible and what is impossible, they are called awakened ones.
Because they do not follow others, they are called those who follow wisdom;
because they skillfully discern the meanings of the chapters and phrases of all dharmas, they are called those who follow insight;
because they skillfully cultivate meditative concentration, they are called those who have attained supernormal powers.
Because they act in accordance with worldly dharmas, they are called "those who employ skillful means";
because they skillfully accumulate the provisions of merit, they are called "those who are never satiated";
and because they constantly seek the causes and conditions for wisdom, they are called "those who do not abandon."
Because they have accumulated the causes and conditions of great loving-kindness and great compassion, they are called those who are never weary;
because they always maintain right mindfulness, they are called those who are far removed from breaking the precepts;
because they seek with a profound mind the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and eighteen unique qualities, they are called those who constantly contemplate the Buddha-dharma.
Because they constantly cause sentient beings to leave evil and cultivate goodness, they are called "those who adorn the Buddha-land";
because they plant various merits to adorn the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, they are called "those who perform various wholesome deeds";
because they seek to adorn the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind, they are called "those who always practice diligence."
Because he makes offerings to all Bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma, he is called "One Who Delights in Great Reverence";
because his mind is free from anger or obstruction amidst all the worldly skillful means of the Bodhisattvas, he is called "One Whose Mind Is Unobstructed";
and because he always delights in teaching and transforming sentient beings, he is called "One Who Day and Night Remains Far Removed from Other Minds."
"When a bodhisattva practices in this manner, they practice giving and also transform sentient beings;
through kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation, they likewise transform sentient beings."
Furthermore, they teach and transform sentient beings by manifesting in physical forms; they also teach and transform sentient beings by preaching the Dharma;

they also teach and transform sentient beings by demonstrating the practices of Bodhisattvas; they also teach and transform sentient beings by demonstrating the great deeds of the Buddhas; they also teach and transform sentient beings by demonstrating the faults and evils of birth and death; and they also teach and transform sentient beings by demonstrating the benefits of the Buddhas' wisdom.
The Bodhisattva practices in this manner, employing great supernormal powers and various causes, conditions, and skillful means to transform sentient beings.

Although this Bodhisattva utilizes these diverse causes, conditions, and skillful means, his mind remains constantly fixed upon the Buddha’s wisdom without ever losing his roots of goodness; furthermore, he perpetually seeks further superior methods for the benefit of sentient beings.

For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he displays all the worldly scriptures, arts, literature, mathematics, and treatises on names and natures; medical prescriptions for treating illnesses—namely, those for wasting diseases, childhood ailments, demonic possession, poisoning by *gū* spirits, leprosy, and so forth; treatises on music, song, dance, theater, laughter, and entertainment;

and [treatises on] kingdoms, cities, towns, villages, houses, gardens, pavilions, ponds, springs, flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, forests, trees, gold, silver, *maṇi* jewels, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, *musāragalva*, and *aśmagarbha*;
as well as the sun, moon, five planets, twenty-eight lunar mansions, divination of good and bad fortune, earthquakes, dream books, and strange omens.

Within his body are all the marks: generosity, upholding the precepts, subduing the mind, meditative concentration and supernormal powers, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless attainments; all matters that do not afflict sentient beings and all matters that bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, arising out of compassion for them, so as to lead them into the unsurpassed Dharma of all Buddhas.

"When a Bodhisattva dwells in this Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (Duranjaya-bhūmi), they encounter hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and billions of Buddhas, making offerings to them, honoring and praising them with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine; they draw near to them to hear the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma, they leave the household life;

having left the household life, they receive and uphold the sūtras and teachings from those Buddhas and become Dharma-preachers. By preaching the Dharma for the benefit of others, they attain an increasingly superior and vast store of learning and the accumulation of samādhi, such that even after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, they do not forget these matters. At that time, all the Bodhisattva’s merits and roots of goodness become increasingly superior, radiant, and pure."
“O Son of the Buddha!
It is like refined pure gold that, when polished with musaragalva, its radiance becomes even more excellent.

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, by the power of skillful means and wisdom, their roots of merit and virtue become increasingly pure, bright, and superior, surpassing those of the lower stages.”
Furthermore, just as the sun, the moon, the constellations, and the celestial palaces of the various devas are sustained by the wind so that they move without losing their proper course,
so it is, O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Ground Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā), because they contemplate with skillful means, their roots of merit and goodness become increasingly bright and pure; yet they do not take realization as a final goal, nor do they hasten toward the path of Buddhahood.
“O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the ‘Difficult-to-Conquer’ stage (*sudurjayā bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, which has now been briefly explained.
When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell in this stage, they frequently become kings of the Tuṣita Heaven; their faculties are sharp and keen, and they are able to subdue all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)."

Whatever deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of their bodhisattva companions, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of the perfection of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"When shall I become the foremost, the most honored, and even the refuge among all sentient beings?
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If this bodhisattva wishes to practice such diligent effort, they can, in a single moment, attain ten billion samādhis, and even manifest ten billion bodhisattvas as their retinue; yet if they employ the power of their vows, their sovereign spiritual power exceeds these numbers, reaching hundreds of thousands of millions of billions that cannot be fully known.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke again in verse:
"When the bodhisattvas have fully perfected The practices of the fourth stage, They contemplate the Buddhas of the three times:
Their morality is equal, and their minds are likewise equal."
Having removed views, doubt, regret, and so forth— such as [the confusion between] the path and what is not the path,
and [erroneous] practice— and having contemplated all things as equal, one enters the fifth stage.
With the four foundations of mindfulness as the bow and the faculties as sharp arrows,
With the four right efforts as horses, the four bases of power as the chariot,
and the five powers as armor, they shatter the thieves of all afflictions;
courageous and unretrogressive, they enter directly into the fifth stage.
The stainless garments of shame and modesty, Pure precepts as incense,
The seven factors of enlightenment as flower garlands, Meditative concentration as unguents,
Wisdom and skillful means— Adorned with various forms of mindfulness.
Thus one enters the groves of all dhāraṇīs:
The four bases of psychic power are its feet, Right mindfulness is its neck,
Compassion is its clear and pure eyes, And sharp wisdom is its tusks.
With the roar of emptiness and non-self, he destroys the thieves of all afflictions;
such a lion among men is able to enter the fifth stage.
This bodhisattva, having reached it, dwells in the fifth stage.
They turn to cultivate the supreme, pure dharmas, all for the sake of the Buddha-way.
They constantly practice the mind of loving-kindness and compassion, never experiencing weariness;
they do so solely to cultivate these practices of the fifth stage.
Having deeply accumulated the two provisions— merit and wisdom—
and through various powers of skillful means, one desires to attain the supreme clear observation.
Constantly protected by the Buddhas, one shall achieve mindfulness and wisdom.
One can skillfully contemplate in successive order, knowing the various truths as they truly are:
the ultimate truth, the conventional truth, the truth of differentiation, the truth of establishment,
phenomena, arising, cessation, the truth of the path, and the truth of reaching the unobstructed.
Observing the truths in this way, the mind becomes subtle and pure.
Although one has not yet attained unobstructed liberation,
by virtue of possessing wisdom and the power of faith, [one attains it].
Surpassing all the wisdomes of the world, one thus contemplates the truths:
that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are false,
deceptive, and fraudulent, and that not a single one possesses any solid reality.
Able to attain a portion of the compassionate light of all Buddhas,
for the sake of all sentient beings, he single-mindedly seeks the Buddha-wisdom.
Knowing the sequence of the conditioned, he deeply pities sentient beings.
Falling into the darkness of ignorance, bound by the causal conditions of craving—
this Bodhisattva is able to uproot the world’s suffering and affliction,
knowing that all phenomena are devoid of a life-principle, just like grass and trees.
Sentient beings are constantly bound by two things;
Due to the causes and conditions of afflictions, They come from past lives, And so it shall be in future lives as well.
This continuity remains unbroken, And they cannot reach the end of suffering.
Feeling compassion for them in this state, I shall deliver them:
Without emerging from the house of the five aggregates, without fearing the harms of the four great elements,
without extracting the arrows of various perversions, and without extinguishing the flames of the three poisons.
Having realized that they have not destroyed the darkness of ignorance, have fallen into the great ocean of craving,
lack the light of wisdom, and are separated from the Great Teacher,
one should apply oneself with even greater diligence and vigor.
Whatever deeds one undertakes, they are all for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
Constantly maintaining right mindfulness and wisdom, practicing the Way with a sense of shame and remorse,
and possessing firm resolve and insight, one causes them to increase further and further.
Cultivating merit and wisdom without weariness, maintaining the precepts without weakness,
seeking extensive learning without fatigue, and correctly practicing to purify Buddha-fields.
Planting the seeds of the marks and signs, as well as the voice, one never feels satiated with these causes and conditions.
Whatever wholesome deeds one performs, they are all for the benefit of sentient beings.
For the sake of benefiting the world, one composes scriptures and treatises, names, lineages,
and medical prescriptions for demonic illnesses, as well as songs, dances, and humorous performances.
The methods for halls, pavilions, gardens, and groves; clothing, various foods and drinks;
and the display of diverse heaps of jewels, all intended to bring joy to the multitude;
as well as the calculation of the sun, moon, five planets, and the twenty-eight lunar mansions.
The signs of earthquakes and auspicious or inauspicious omens; dream books and various strange occurrences;

generosity, observance of precepts, and so forth; the cultivation of meditative concentration free from desire, the four immeasurables, and supernormal powers—for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to the world.
The Bodhisattvas of Great Wisdom, having attained this stage difficult to surpass,
make offerings to billions of Buddhas; from these Buddhas they hear the Dharma and cultivate all roots of goodness, until they have all attained clarity and purity.
Like a conch-shell gem polished upon pure gold;
like a precious palace that remains according to the wind without losing its nature;
unstained by the benefits of worldly dharmas, like a lotus flower in the water.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage, they often become kings of Tuṣita;
their faculties become increasingly sharp and keen, and they shatter the views of all non-Buddhists.
All the various wholesome deeds they perform are dedicated solely to the wisdom of the Buddha.
Attaining the powers and fearlessnesses of a Buddha, they are able to deliver all sentient beings.
These bodhisattvas, through diligent cultivation, further increase their power of vigor;
they are able to attain thousands of myriads of kotis of profound and wondrous samādhis.
They make offerings to a thousand billion Buddhas and can shake a thousand worlds;
according to the power of their vows, they surpass these numbers immeasurably.
Such is the fifth stage, with its various skillful means.
The Great Being of Supreme Wisdom has finished explaining according to the Dharma.
*The Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, Scroll 20 (or Scroll 3).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Later Qin.
Chapter Six: The Ground of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
When the bodhisattvas hear the explanation of the characteristics of the higher grounds, they [realize] the Ground of Presence.
Abiding in the midst of space, raining down various wondrous treasures and emitting pure radiance,
they made offerings to the World-Honored One and all praised him, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Vajragarbha!
At this time, immeasurable billions of devas are all filled with joy.”
In the empty space above, a rain of various precious powdered incenses falls;
its radiant forms interlace in exquisite patterns, subtle and most delightful.
A rain of manifold fragrant flowers, necklaces, banners, and canopies falls upon the Buddha.
The King of Paranirmita-vaśavartin, together with his retinue,
rained down a multitude of exquisite treasures, falling in dense clouds like mist.
They sang praises and made offerings to the Buddha, extolling Vajragarbha.
They all praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent! How well this has been spoken!
