Then, ten million billion celestial maidens, in the sky above, [uttered these words].
They performed various celestial music and sang praises of the Buddha’s virtues, all saying these words:
“That which the Tathāgata has taught is subtle and immeasurable; it is able to extinguish all afflictions.”
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty; there is not even a hair’s breadth of characteristic mark.
This emptiness is without discrimination, identical to space.
It has no characteristic of going or staying, nor is there any conceptual proliferation.
Primordially and eternally pure, suchness is free from discrimination.
If a person can thoroughly penetrate the nature of all phenomena,
their mind will remain unshaken amidst both existence and non-existence.
But out of great compassion, for the sake of delivering all sentient beings,
they are called children of the Buddhas, born from the Dharma of the Buddha’s mouth.
They constantly practice giving, benefiting all sentient beings.
Though fundamentally pure and virtuous, one maintains the precepts with a steadfast mind;
though knowing that dharmas are beyond harm, one practices patience;
though knowing the nature of dharmas is detached, one practices diligence.
Although he has already extinguished afflictions, he enters into the various dhyānas;
although he has already understood the emptiness of phenomena, he discriminates among all dharmas.
Although his wisdom of quiescent extinction is vast, he seeks to benefit the world.
One who can extinguish all evils is called a Great Man.
After these celestial maidens had offered praise and songs with hundreds of thousands of kinds of exquisite voices,
they all fell silent and gazed upon the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"By what characteristics shall one attain the sixth stage?
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha replied:
“O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already fulfilled the practices of the fifth stage and wish to enter the sixth stage, they should enter the sixth stage by means of ten dharmas of equality.”
What are the ten? First, all phenomena are equal because they lack intrinsic nature;
second, all phenomena are equal because they are devoid of conceptualization.
3. All phenomena are equal because they are unarisen;
4. All phenomena are equal because they are unceasing;
5. All phenomena are equal because they are primordially pure.
Sixth, all phenomena are equal because they are free from conceptual proliferation;
seventh, all phenomena are equal because there is neither grasping nor rejecting;
eighth, all phenomena are equal because they are detached.
Ninth, all phenomena are equal because they are like illusions, dreams, echoes, reflections of the moon in water, images in a mirror, mirages, and magical transformations;
tenth, all phenomena are equal because existence and non-existence are non-dual.
O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas fulfill the practices of the fifth stage, they are able to enter the sixth stage by means of these ten dharmas of equality.
O Sons of the Buddha!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus contemplate the nature of all phenomena and endure them with compliance, they attain the sixth stage;
although the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena has not yet manifested before them, their mind is already clear and sharp, having accomplished the patience of compliance.

"This Bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as having such characteristics; with great compassion as the foremost, he increases and fulfills it, and further uses superior contemplation to observe the characteristics of arising and ceasing in the world."
Therefore, he forms this thought:
"All places in the world where one receives a body and takes birth exist because of attachment to a self; if one were free from attachment to a self, there would be no place for birth in the world."

All ordinary persons are blinded by ignorance and attached to a self; they constantly delight in seeking existence and always follow wrong thoughts to travel upon false and delusive paths. They habitually give rise to the three types of formations—formations of evil, formations of merit, and imperturbable formations—and because of these formations, they produce the seeds of the "heated" mind.

Because of a mind characterized by outflows (*āsrava*) and grasping (*upādāna*), the body of birth-and-death arises. That is to say: karma serves as the ground, consciousness (*vijñāna*) as the seed, ignorance (*avidyā*) as the covering, and the water of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as the moisture; irrigated by the "I-making" (*ahaṃkāra*) and nourished by various views (*dṛṣṭi*), it causes the sprout of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) to grow.
Due to name-and-form, the sense-faculties (*indriya*) arise;
through the conjunction of the sense-faculties, contact (*sparśa*) is produced.
From contact arises feeling;
because of pleasant feeling, craving arises;
because craving increases, there are the four types of clinging.
Due to the causal condition of the four graspings (*upādāna*), karma arises within existence (*bhava*);

the arising of the body of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) is called birth; the decay and transformation of the five aggregates is called old age; and the cessation of that decay is called death. With old age and death as causal conditions, there is a massing together of many sufferings, including sorrow, lamentation, and feverish affliction.
These twelve links of dependent origination have no one who assembles them; they assemble spontaneously.
They have no one who disperses them; they disperse spontaneously.
When causes and conditions conjoin, they exist; when causes and conditions disperse, they cease to exist.
"Thus, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination in accordance with reality within the sixth stage, and further reflects:
'Because one does not know the ultimate truth of the various realities as they truly are, ignorance covers the mind;
the karmic fruit of ignorance is called "formative action" (saṃskāra); based upon formative action, there arises initial consciousness (vijñāna)."
Co-arising with consciousness are the four aggregates of clinging; dependent upon these aggregates of clinging is name-and-form;
through the fulfillment of name-and-form are the six sense bases; because the faculties engage with their objects, there is consciousness; from this conjunction arises tainted contact;
co-arising with contact is feeling.
Clinging with delight to sensations is called craving;
the intensification of craving is called grasping;
from grasping arises karma associated with outflows.
The existence of karma and the five aggregates as its retribution is called birth;
the maturation of the five aggregates is called aging;
the disintegration of the five aggregates is called death.

At the time of death and separation, the feverish mind of the foolish person attached to objects is called sorrow and lamentation (*śoka-parideva*), and the utterance of wailing cries is called weeping.

The five consciousnesses are called suffering (*duḥkha*), the mental consciousness is called grief (*daurmanasya*), and the proliferation of this grief and suffering is called despair (*upāyāsa*). In this way, there is merely the production of a great tree of suffering and a great mass of suffering.
"In this way, the mass of suffering consisting of the twelve links of dependent origination is without self and without what belongs to a self;
it has no agent and no instigator. The Bodhisattva then reflects:
"If there were an agent, then there would be an action performed."
"If there is no agent, then there is no action.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is neither agent nor action. He further thought:
"The three realms are illusory; they are created solely by the mind.
"The Tathāgata has said that all twelve links of dependent origination depend entirely upon the mind. Why is this so?"
The arising of a mind of craving in accordance with an object is itself consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The object is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); because these formations delude the mind, they are called ignorance (*avidyā*).
The locus upon which consciousness relies is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The entry [of the sense bases] that gives rise to a mind of craving is called the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana);
the coming together of the three factors is contact (sparśa);
that which arises simultaneously with contact is sensation (vedanā).
Clinging to what is experienced is called craving;
not relinquishing craving is called grasping;
through the conjunction of these, it is called becoming.
The continued succession of this existence and further existence is called birth;
the transformation and maturation of that which has been born is called aging;
the disintegration of aging is called death.
"In this context, ignorance has two functions:
first, it is delusion regarding the objects of perception; second, it serves as the cause for the arising of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Volitional formations also have two functions:"
First, it produces the retribution of future lives; second, it acts as the cause for consciousness.
Consciousness also has two functions:
first, it enables the continuity of existence (*bhava*); second, it acts as the cause for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Name-and-form also has two functions:
first, they mutually support and accomplish one another; second, they act as the cause for the six sense bases.
The six sense bases also have two functions:
First, it can take the six sense objects as its object; second, it can act as the cause for contact (*sparśa*).
Contact also has two functions:
first, it can contact the object; second, it can act as the cause for sensation (*vedanā*).
Feeling also has two functions:
first, it perceives objects of aversion and attraction; second, it acts as the cause for craving.
Craving also has two functions:
First, it gives rise to a mind of greed toward that which can cause defilement; second, it acts as the cause for grasping (*upādāna*).
Grasping also performs two functions:
first, it is able to increase afflictions (*kleśa*); second, it acts as the cause for existence (*bhava*).
Existence (*bhava*) also has two functions:
first, it enables rebirth in other realms; second, it acts as the cause for birth (*jāti*).
Birth also has two functions:
First, it can give rise to the five aggregates; second, it acts as the cause for old age.
Old age also has two functions:
first, it causes the sense faculties to mature; second, it acts as the cause for death.
Death also has two functions:
first, it destroys the body of the five aggregates; second, because there is no seeing or knowing, it causes the continuity [of existence] to remain unbroken.
"In this context, regarding 'ignorance conditions volitional formations,' ignorance causes volitional formations not to cease by assisting in their formation;
'volitional formations condition consciousness' means it causes consciousness not to cease by assisting in its formation;
'consciousness conditions name-and-form' means it causes name-and-form not to cease by assisting in its formation."
...up to birth being the condition for old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, because it produces and assists their uninterrupted continuity.
Through the cessation of ignorance, then volitional formations cease; and so on, up to old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, which likewise cease.
In this context, if ignorance were absent, volitional formations would also not exist; when the cause ceases, the result ceases, and the same applies to the remaining factors.
Among these, ignorance, craving, and grasping constitute the three links that perpetuate the path of afflictions;
volitional formations and existence constitute the links that perpetuate the path of karma.
The remaining causal factors constitute the uninterrupted path to the cessation of suffering.
Because they continue uninterruptedly from the prior limit to the subsequent limit, these three paths are uninterrupted.
These three paths are devoid of self and what belongs to self, yet they undergo arising and ceasing; like two bamboo poles leaning against one another, they appear solid though they lack solidity.
“The formations conditioned by ignorance refer to matters of the past;
consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling refer to matters of the present;
craving, grasping, becoming, birth, aging, and death refer to matters of the future—thus the three periods of time emerge.”
Because ignorance ceases, the formative forces cease; this is called the teaching on the cessation of the continuity [of suffering].
"The twelve links of dependent origination are said to consist of the three types of suffering:
ignorance, formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases are termed the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkha);..."
Contact and sensation are called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
craving, grasping, becoming, birth, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair are called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
Because ignorance ceases, the formative forces cease, and so on up to old age and death; this is called the teaching on severing the continuity of the three types of suffering.
“With ignorance as cause, volitional formations arise;
the rest are likewise.
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, because the intrinsic nature of volitional formations is empty.”
The rest are also like this.
"Ignorance is the condition for volitional formations; this is explained by way of bondage through birth;
the rest are also like this."
"Because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease"—this is taught by way of the cessation of bondage.
The rest is also like this.
"Volitional formations have ignorance as their condition"—this is taught by way of the contemplation of non-existence.
"With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease"—this is the teaching on the contemplation of cessation in accordance with the sequence;

the others are likewise so. "In this way, one contemplates the twelve factors of dependent origination in ten ways, both in direct and reverse order: namely, by way of the sequential order of the causal links; by what is comprised within body and mind; by the dharma of self-assistance and accomplishment; by their mutual inseparability; by following the course of the three realms; by distinguishing the prior and subsequent limits; by the differentiation of the three types of suffering; by arising from causes and conditions; by the bondage of birth and cessation; and by the contemplation of the exhaustion of non-existence."

"At that time, the Bodhisattva, in accordance with the twelve links of dependent origination, contemplates the absence of self, the absence of sentient beings, and the absence of a life-span; he contemplates the emptiness of human nature, the departure from an agent and one who causes another to act, the absence of a master or owner over the aggregates, and the non-existence of causes and conditions."
"When observing in this way, the liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa-mukha*) manifests before one;
because these phenomena are extinguished and no longer continue, the liberation door of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa-mukha*) manifests;

knowing that these two types of existence will not arise again—except for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings with great compassion—the liberation door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa-mukha*) manifests."

"When a bodhisattva practices these three gates of liberation, they become detached from the marks of self and other, detached from the marks of agent and recipient, and detached from the marks of existence and non-existence; thus, their compassionate heart increases further."
Out of profound compassion, he practices with diligent vigor, desiring to fulfill those factors conducive to enlightenment that are not yet complete.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"Because conditioned phenomena arise through combination, they increase; when they disperse, they cease."
Because the various conditions are complete, they increase; because they are incomplete, they cease.

Now that I know conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) have many faults, I should not bring about the completion of their causes and conditions, yet I do not utterly extinguish conditioned phenomena, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva thus knows that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) abound in faults and lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), being free from the mark of solidity, unborn and unceasing, and when they harmonize with great compassion (*mahāmaitrīkaruṇā*) without abandoning sentient beings, they immediately attain the unobstructed *prajñāpāramitā*, and its radiance manifests before them."

Having attained such wisdom and fully cultivated its accumulation, he grasps the causes and conditions for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* yet does not dwell together with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). He contemplates the nature of conditioned phenomena as being characterized by quiescence (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*), yet he does not abide therein, because he desires to fulfill the factors conducive to unsurpassed enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), they attain the samādhi of swift emptiness, the samādhi of essential emptiness, the samādhi of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the samādhi of the foremost emptiness, the samādhi of great emptiness, the samādhi of combined emptiness, the samādhi of the emptiness of arising, the samādhi of emptiness that is non-conceptual as it truly is, the samādhi of inclusive emptiness, and the samādhi of the emptiness of detachment and non-detachment.
In this way, ten thousand gates of emptiness-samādhi manifest before him;
the same is true for the signless and wishless samādhis.

As this bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), because such minds as the resolute mind, the determined mind, the wondrous mind, the profound mind, the non-reverting mind, the non-abandoning mind, the vast mind, the boundless mind, the mind that delights in wisdom, and the mind harmonized with wisdom and skillful means become increasingly superior and grow ever more expansive, he accords with *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and no teacher of external paths can shake or move him.

Entering the stage of wisdom, they transcend the levels of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, becoming definitively oriented toward the Buddha-wisdom, such that they cannot be restrained by any māras or afflictions.

Abiding securely within the luminosity of a bodhisattva’s wisdom, they skillfully cultivate the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and single-mindedly employ the practice of wisdom and skillful means to assist the factors conducive to enlightenment.

"When this Bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), they attain a progressively superior practice within the *prajñāpāramitā* and attain the third, the 'Superior Accordant Patience' (*anulomikī kṣānti*).

Because they accord with these dharmas without opposition, while dwelling in this Stage of Presence, the Bodhisattva comes to see hundreds, thousands, and even hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; they make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise them, providing robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine. They draw near to these Buddhas and listen to the Dharma at their abodes.
Having heard the Dharma, because they follow the light of wisdom as it truly is, they act according to what has been taught, thereby bringing joy to all the Buddhas."

This person becomes increasingly superior, coming to know the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas; even throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, their various roots of goodness become ever more wondrous, luminous, and pure.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

Just as genuine gold, when polished with lapis lazuli, becomes increasingly brilliant in its luster and color, so too do the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva dwelling in this Stage of Presence become increasingly superior through the application of wisdom and skillful means; they become luminous, pure, and quiescent, surpassing those of all other stages.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Just as the bright moon can cause the bodies of sentient beings to attain purity, such that the four winds cannot obstruct or extinguish it;

so too, when Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell in this Stage of Presence (Abhimukhī), their roots of goodness become increasingly superior, enabling them to extinguish the fires of affliction of immeasurable sentient beings, and remaining indestructible by the four kinds of Māras."
"O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas’ Stage of Presence (Abhimukhī).

When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage, they frequently become Śakra, Lord of the Suyāma Heaven. Their wisdom is fierce and sharp; they are able to shatter all those with overweening pride, and no interrogations from Śrāvakas can exhaust their depth."

In whatever they do—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or collaborative work—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of their fellow bodhisattvas, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
He constantly makes this vow:
"May I be the foremost and the most honored among all sentient beings, even unto being the one upon whom all sentient beings rely."

If this bodhisattva wishes to practice with diligent vigor, they can, in a single moment, attain one hundred trillion samādhis, and even manifest a retinue of one hundred trillion bodhisattvas. If they employ the power of their vows, they can exceed these numbers for hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of kalpas beyond measure.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to make this meaning clear, spoke these verses:
"The Bodhisattvas have already attained The full realization of the fifth stage;
They know all phenomena are signless, Signless and without arising or ceasing."
Originally and eternally pure, free from all conceptual proliferation;
by cultivating and gathering such wisdom, one enters the sixth stage.
All phenomena are eternally devoid of marks; they are neither grasped nor abandoned.
The nature of things is empty like an illusion, free from duality and without discrimination.
If one can accord with such a subtle principle,
and the mind has no opposition toward it, one attains entry into the sixth stage.
Abiding in the patience of benefit and conformity, and having attained mastery through wisdom,
he observes all the characteristics of arising and ceasing within the world.
He fully knows that all worlds emerge entirely from the darkness of ignorance.
If the darkness of delusion is extinguished, then there are no worldly realms.

Contemplating and discerning the law of causes and conditions, one accords with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) without destroying dependent retribution, karmic actions, or conventional designations (*prajñapti*).
Just as there is truly no agent, nor is there any recipient;
so one should contemplate conditioned phenomena as being without substantial reality, like clouds.
Not knowing the meaning of ultimate truth is called ignorance.
From this, volition arises, and through the actions of body and speech, retribution is obtained.
From action comes consciousness, which gives rise to name-and-form;
thus is the world produced, leading to birth, death, and the mass of suffering.
To understand that the three realms exist solely from the mind,
and to know that the twelve links of dependent origination reside within the single mind—
thus, birth and death arise solely from the mind.
If the mind is extinguished, then birth and death are likewise extinguished.
Ignorance performs two functions: it produces delusion and it produces karma;
thus proceeding through old age and death, it shatters and destroys the five aggregates.
From this very source, suffering and affliction arise;
if this source is exhausted, then suffering and affliction are likewise exhausted.
If ignorance is fully present, the continuity of existence will not be severed.
If the causes and conditions are not complete, then the continuity is severed.
Ignorance, craving, and grasping constitute the path of afflictions;
volitional formations and existence constitute the path of karma; the remainder constitutes the path of suffering.
Ignorance extending to the six sense bases is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*);
contact and sensation are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*); the remaining factors are the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
When the continuity of these three types of suffering is extinguished, there is no longer any self.
Ignorance and the formative forces constitute the past;
consciousness and sensation constitute the present;
and suffering arising from craving constitutes the future.
If ignorance is extinguished, then there is no suffering.
Delusion arises from a multitude of conditions, and thus the various fetters are born;
if those conditions are extinguished, then the fetters are extinguished.
From causes arises the fruit; when the cause ceases, the fruit ceases.
Observing all phenomena in this way, their intrinsic nature is entirely empty.
Following along with ignorance, the world comes into being.
If one opposes ignorance, then existence is severed.
From this there is that; if this is absent, that is absent.
These ten kinds of contemplation constitute the profound law of dependent origination.
Contemplating the continuity of causes and conditions—past, future, and present—they do not depart from a single mind;
yet, through discrimination, there appear to be three paths.
From the contemplation of the three kinds of suffering, as well as the nature of arising and ceasing, [the three realms are distinguished].
Exhausted in non-existence, they are able to practice the contemplation of the inverse and the direct order.
Thus do Bodhisattvas enter the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination;
they know it to be empty like an illusion, like a dream, and like a shadow.
Like a mirage and like a magical illusion, it is deceptive and has no creator, nor is there any recipient; it merely deludes the foolish.
Observing dependent origination in this way, the wise cultivate emptiness.
Without conditions there are no marks; know that these two are empty and false.
Regarding all that exists, one has no aspiration therein, yet for the sake of compassionately delivering sentient beings, one acts solely out of a heart of great compassion.
Thus these great beings cultivate the gates of liberation;
with a heart of compassion they love the Buddha and his immeasurable virtues.
They know that all conditioned phenomena arise solely from a combination of causes.
One immediately attains the ten thousand concentrations of emptiness; signlessness and wishlessness are likewise so.
Wisdom increases further and further as one enters the supreme conformative patience, attaining the unconditioned wisdom-liberation of all bodhisattvas.
Thus these roots of goodness become increasingly superior, luminous, pure, and beneficial;
they make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and are praised by all Buddhas.
Always in the presence of the Buddhas, they leave the household life to study the Buddha-way.
Upon reaching the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas, their roots of goodness increase further;
it is like using lapis lazuli gems to polish pure gold,
whereby its radiance becomes increasingly pure— the analogy is just so.
Just as when the full moon’s light is pure in the midst of space,
And cannot be obstructed or extinguished by the four winds;
So too the light of a bodhisattva’s wisdom Extinguishes the heat of all afflictions.
The four Māras cannot subdue them; the analogy is likewise so.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage, they mostly become benevolent universal monarchs (*cakravartin*);
their faculties are all sharp and keen, and they are able to destroy overweening pride.
All the various wholesome deeds they perform accord with wisdom;
even the challenges posed by the śrāvakas cannot exhaust them.
If these sons of the Buddha desire to exert themselves with such diligence, [they shall attain this].
They are able to attain hundreds of thousands, Even billions of various samādhis;
They are able to see hundreds of thousands, Even billions of Buddhas of the ten directions.
Just as when spring is clear and bright, The light of the sun is pure.
Thus the sixth stage, profound and subtle, difficult to know or see,
which the śrāvakas do not comprehend— this the Great Being has briefly explained.
At that time, the hosts of devas remained in the midst of the void.
Raining down fragrant flowers and precious jewels, like clouds dispersing over the Buddha, they leaped for joy and uttered wondrous sounds, all praising him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Vajragarbha! You who well know the ultimate truth,
a mass of immeasurable merit, a lotus among men.
He preached these sublime practices to benefit all the worlds.
The King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven rained down flowers of radiant light and incense,
offering them in profusion to the one who has removed sorrow and affliction.
The devas and the celestial kings uttered these words in sublime voices:
"If one hears the meaning of this ground, one shall attain great benefit.
At that time, let there be hundreds of thousands of kinds of most excellent musical performances."
The celestial maidens, skilled in song, by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power, proclaimed:
“The Buddha is the most profoundly tranquil; he can transform evil into good.
He is universally revered by all the worlds.”
Though they have transcended the world, they manifest worldly dharmas;
knowing that the body is identical to the true mark (*dharmatā*), they manifest various kinds of bodies;
though using all manner of speech and sounds, they expound the dharma of quiescent extinction.
While understanding language, they perceive no characteristic of sound.
Able to traverse hundreds of thousands of lands, they present sublime offerings to all Buddhas.
Knowing that the body is the Buddha-land, they abandon characteristics and attain mastery of wisdom.
Though they transform and guide sentient beings, they harbor no notions of "self" or "other";
they extensively accumulate great merit, yet do not give rise to attachment therein.
Because of grasping at signs through views, the fires of the three poisons burn the world.
Not grasping at any signs, he arouses diligence through compassion.
The gods and goddesses joyfully present offerings;
having thus offered praise, they remain silent and gaze upon the Buddha.
At that time, Vimukticandra addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
"The great assembly is entirely pure; I pray that you will explain the characteristics of the seventh stage.
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied:
“O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have fully perfected the practices of the sixth stage and wish to enter the seventh Bodhisattva stage, they give rise to ten sublime practices from skillful wisdom.”
What are these ten?
This bodhisattva skillfully cultivates emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet dwells among sentient beings with a heart of compassion;
he accords with the equal Dharma of all Buddhas, yet does not cease making offerings to the Buddhas.
They constantly delight in contemplating the gateway of the wisdom of emptiness, yet they extensively cultivate and accumulate the provisions of merit;
they remain far removed from the triple world, yet they are able to adorn the triple world;

they have ultimately extinguished the flames of all afflictions, yet they are able to give rise for sentient beings to the Dharma that extinguishes the flames of the afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion.

They accord with all phenomena—being like illusions, dreams, shadows, echoes, transformations, the moon reflected in water, and images in a mirror—and though they are non-dual in nature, they give rise to various afflictions through conceptual discrimination without losing the retribution of karmic results;
they know that all Buddha-lands are empty like space and that all lands are devoid of marks, yet they initiate practices to purify Buddha-lands;
they know that the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas is bodiless, yet they initiate the adornment of themselves with the physical body, the thirty-two major marks, and the eighty minor characteristics.

They know that the voices of all Buddhas possess an ineffable nature; they have faith and understanding that the voice of the Tathāgata is by nature originally quiescent, yet it gives rise to various kinds of adorned sounds in accordance with all sentient beings.

They know that in a single thought-moment, all Buddhas penetrate the events of the three periods of time, perceiving their various characteristics, various times, and various kalpas, and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; yet, because they accord with the mental inclinations and faith-understandings of sentient beings, they speak in such ways.
O Sons of the Buddha!
These are called the ten sublime practices born from wisdom and skillful means.
Once Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have fulfilled the practices of the sixth stage, they cultivate these sublime practices and thereby enter the seventh stage.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Thus, because skillful means and wisdom manifest before one, it is called 'entering the seventh stage.
This bodhisattva, dwelling within the seventh stage, enters into the nature of immeasurable sentient beings and enters into immeasurable dharmas..."
The Buddha’s method for transforming sentient beings; entering the nature of immeasurable worlds; entering the immeasurable pure lands of all Buddhas;
entering the distinctions among immeasurable dharmas; entering the immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas to attain the Unsurpassed Way;
entering the calculation of immeasurable kalpas; and entering the immeasurable Buddhas’ penetration of the three periods of time.
...entering the distinctions in the faith and inclinations of immeasurable sentient beings; entering the differences in the form-bodies of immeasurable Buddhas;
entering the distinctions in the faculties, conduct, and roots of immeasurable Buddhas and sentient beings;

entering the immeasurable voices and languages of the Buddhas that bring joy to sentient beings; and entering the mental activities of the minds of immeasurable sentient beings as manifested by the Buddhas.
The distinctions: entering the wisdom-conduct that follows the infinite Buddhas; entering the demonstration of the faith and understanding of the infinite Śrāvaka vehicles;
entering the infinite teachings on the causes and conditions of the path spoken by the Buddhas to inspire faith and understanding in sentient beings;
entering the cultivation and perfection of the infinite wisdom of the Pratyekabuddhas; and entering the infinitely profound wisdom taught by the Buddhas.
...entering the immeasurable paths of practice of all bodhisattvas, and entering the immeasurable matters of the Great Vehicle compendia taught by all Buddhas so that sentient beings may enter them.
The bodhisattvas form this thought:

"Thus, these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess immeasurable and boundless great power, which cannot be known through calculation even over hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas."

I should gather all such powers of the Buddhas; they are not accomplished through forceful discrimination between this and that, but are accomplished by means of non-discrimination and non-apprehension of signs.

This bodhisattva, through such wisdom and skillful reflection, constantly cultivates great skillful means and wisdom, causing them to abide securely within the knowledge of the Buddha-way by virtue of the immovable dharma.

If one wishes to constantly give rise to various paths for delivering sentient beings without obstruction—arising both when coming and when going, and being able to give rise to the Path while sitting, lying down, standing, or walking—and to deliver and liberate sentient beings from all hindrances (āvaraṇa), remaining in all modes of deportment (īryāpatha) never departing from such contemplation; [then one should practice as follows].
"This Bodhisattva, in every thought-moment, fulfills the ten perfections of a bodhisattva and the ten stages of a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because this Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in every thought-moment, practices all Buddha-dharmas with great compassion as the foremost, dedicating them all toward the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
Regarding the ten pāramitās:
because the roots of goodness cultivated by a bodhisattva seeking the Buddha-way are shared with all sentient beings, this is the dāna-pāramitā;
because it can extinguish the heat of all afflictions, this is the śīla-pāramitā.
To have compassion as one's primary concern and to cause no harm toward any sentient being is the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā);
to seek ever-superior roots of goodness without weariness is the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā);
and for the mind that cultivates the path not to be distracted but to always incline toward omniscience is the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).
To endure the gate of the prior non-arising of all phenomena is the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā);
to be able to give rise to the gate of immeasurable knowledge is the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā);
to aspire toward the turning of ever-superior wisdom is the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
That which cannot be obstructed or destroyed by any non-Buddhists or māras is the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*);
that which is established in accordance with reality regarding the characteristics of all phenomena is the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*).
In this way, within every moment of thought, they fulfill the ten pāramitās.

When these bodhisattvas fulfill the ten pāramitās, within every moment of thought they also fulfill the four means of integration (saṃgrahavastu), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma), and the three gates of liberation (vimokṣamukha).
"To state it in brief: all dharmas that assist toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are fully present in every single thought-moment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
“Does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva fulfill the factors conducive to awakening only within the seventh stage,
or does he also fulfill them in all stages?
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva replied:
“O Son of the Buddha!
Within the ten stages, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas fully possess all the factors conducive to enlightenment; however, it is because the seventh stage is preeminent that it receives this name.”
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, having fulfilled their practices and deeds within the seventh stage, have entered the path of wisdom and the supernormal powers.
"O Son of the Buddha!
In the first stage, the bodhisattva makes vows; because they take all Buddha-dharmas as their object, they fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment.
In the second stage, because they eliminate the defilements of the mind, they fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment.
In the third stage, because their vows increase further and they attain the light of the Dharma, they fulfill the factors conducive to enlightenment.
In the fourth stage, because one enters the Path, one fulfills the factors conducive to enlightenment;
in the fifth stage, because one acts in accordance with worldly dharmas, one fulfills the factors conducive to enlightenment;
in the sixth stage, because one enters the profound gateways of the Dharma, one fulfills the factors conducive to enlightenment.
In this seventh stage, because one gives rise to all Buddha-dharmas, one is fully endowed with the factors conducive to enlightenment. Why is this?
O Sons of the Buddha!
In this stage, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains the path derived from all wisdoms; by the power of this, the eighth stage is spontaneously accomplished.
“O Son of the Buddha!
It is, for example, like two trichiliocosm worlds, one entirely pure and one entirely defiled; it is difficult to pass through the space between these two.
Only by means of the power of great diligence, the power of great supernormal abilities, and the power of great vows can one pass through.”
O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas travel upon such a manifold path, it is difficult to pass beyond;
yet, by virtue of the power of their great vows, the power of their great wisdom, and the power of their great skillful means, they are able to pass beyond.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked:
"Is the seventh bodhisattva stage one of pure conduct,
or is it one of defiled conduct?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"From the first stage, the Stage of Joy, onward, all that the bodhisattva practices is free from afflictions and sinful karma. Why is this?"
Because they dedicate [their merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, their conduct is pure according to each stage and cannot be called a transgression.
Son of the Buddha!

It is like a wheel-turning sage king who rides a great precious elephant and travels through the four continents; though he knows there are those suffering in poverty and distress, the fault does not lie with the king, yet the king cannot avoid his human body.

If one relinquishes the royal body to be born in the Brahma-world, dwelling in a Brahma palace and traveling through a thousand worlds to manifest the power of a Brahma King, only then does one leave behind the human body.
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is the same for the Bodhisattva: from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, while riding upon the vehicle of the various *pāramitās*, they know the mental activities and the defilements of all sentient beings, yet they are not stained by those defilements. Because they ride upon the path of goodness, this is not called a transgression.

However, when a Bodhisattva relinquishes all the paths of practice they have cultivated and enters the eighth stage from the seventh, at that time they are said to be riding upon the pure vehicle of the Bodhisattva; they fully know all the defilements of the world but are not stained by those defilements, and this is also called a transgression.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this seventh stage, they have largely transcended the multitude of afflictions such as desire and the like.
In this seventh stage, they are neither called those who possess afflictions nor called those who are free from afflictions."
Why is this? Because they do not give rise to any afflictions, they are not called "those with afflictions";
yet because they seek the wisdom of the Tathāgata and their vows are not yet fulfilled, they are not called "those without afflictions."
"When a Bodhisattva dwells in this seventh stage, they accomplish profoundly pure physical action, profoundly pure verbal action, and profoundly pure mental action.
This Bodhisattva has completely transcended all unwholesome courses of action that are censured by the Buddhas and associated with the defilements of the secondary afflictions;
as for all wholesome courses of action praised by the Buddhas, these they constantly practice."

Furthermore, as described in the context of the fifth stage, he spontaneously masters worldly scriptures and arts; within a trichiliocosm, he is the most rare and becomes a great teacher. With the sole exception of the Tathāgata and Bodhisattvas who have entered the eighth stage, there is no sentient being whose profound mind and wondrous conduct can equal his.

Although this bodhisattva has not yet attained the full retribution of his meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis, he is born with mastery over them according to his will.

Abiding in this Far-Reaching Stage (*Dūramgamā-bhūmi*), in every thought-moment, he fully cultivates and accumulates the power of skillful means and wisdom (*upāya-prajñā-bala*), as well as all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), becoming increasingly more perfect.

Abiding in this Ground of Far-Going (*dūramgamā*), one is able to enter the Bodhisattva samādhi of Excellent Discernment, the samādhi of Well-Contemplated Meaning, the samādhi of Benefiting the Mind, the samādhi of Discerning the Treasury of Meanings, the samādhi of Discerning Dharmas According to Reality, the samādhi of Firmly Rooted Abiding, the samādhi of Knowing the Gateways of Supernormal Powers (*abhijñā*), the samādhi of the Nature of Phenomena (*dharmatā*), the samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Benefit, the samādhi of the Treasury of Various Meanings, and the samādhi of Not Tending Toward Saṃsāra or Nirvāṇa.
Thus, by being fully endowed with a million bodhisattva samādhis, one is able to purify and cultivate this stage.

Because this bodhisattva has attained these samādhis, and because their wisdom and skillful means are perfectly pure and they have deeply realized the power of great compassion, they are said to have transcended the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and entered the stage of the Buddha’s wisdom.

When this bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they engage in immeasurable physical actions of signlessness, immeasurable verbal actions of signlessness, and immeasurable mental actions of signlessness; because these are the pure practices of this bodhisattva, they illuminate the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva abides in the first stage, possessing immeasurable physical actions, immeasurable verbal actions, and immeasurable mental actions, has he already been able to transcend the stages of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"It is by virtue of the Great Dharma that one is able to transcend, not through the power of actual practice;
yet this seventh stage, by the power of its own actual practice, cannot be destroyed by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like being born into a royal family; one immediately surpasses all the ministers and officials. Why is this?
By the power of the Great Honored One, their bodies have grown large and their wisdom has been established; they have truly attained victory.
O Sons of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva first resolves on the path, they have already surpassed all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas because they have made great vows and their profound resolve is pure;
now, by abiding in this stage, they surpass them through the power of their own wisdom.
O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas abide in the seventh stage, they attain the profound, detached, and non-active karma of body, speech, and mind; yet they continue to seek the supreme Dharma without ever abandoning it.
"Because of this increasingly superior mind, although he practices within the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), he does not realize the limit of reality.
Vimukticandra said: "O Son of the Buddha!"
"From which stage does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva come to be able to enter into cessation?
Vajragarbha replied,
"A bodhisattva-mahāsattva comes from the sixth stage to be able to enter into cessation."

Now, abiding in this stage, they are able to enter into quiescence in every thought-moment without realizing quiescence; this is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of inconceivable actions of body, speech, and mind, which reach the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without realizing the limit of reality.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a person who boards a ship and enters the great ocean; because they skillfully practice the methods of navigation and thoroughly understand the characteristics of the water, they are not harmed by the perils of the sea.

In this way, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in this seventh stage, riding upon the ship of the various pāramitās, they are able to traverse the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) without realizing the limit of reality.

"By means of such great power of aspiration, by attaining the power of wisdom, and by generating the power of great skillful means from meditative concentration and wisdom, the bodhisattva, though deeply loving *nirvāṇa*, manifests within the cycle of birth and death; though surrounded by a retinue, his mind is always detached; and though taking birth in the triple world through the power of his vows, he is not defiled by worldly dharmas."
Their minds are always perfectly tranquil, yet through the power of skillful means they cause them to blaze forth again, though without being consumed.
Following the movement of Buddha-wisdom, they transcend the stages of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; they attain the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas while manifesting within the realm of Māra;
and though they have transcended the paths of the four Māras, they manifest the conduct of Māra.
Although he manifests the practices of various non-Buddhists, his profound mind never abandons the Buddha-dharma;
although he manifests a body in all worlds, his mind always dwells in the supramundane dharma;

and while his adornments surpass those of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, the four heavenly kings, Śakra-devendra, and Brahmā-devaputra, he does not abandon his delight in the Dharma or his love for the Dharma.

"When a Bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom and dwells in this stage of Far-Going (Dūramgamā), they encounter hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, making offerings to, revering, honoring, and praising them. Having provided these Buddhas with robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites, they uphold the teachings of those Buddhas; their wisdom cannot be destroyed by the challenges and interrogations of any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
Because this bodhisattva has compassion for sentient beings, their patience regarding phenomena (dharmakṣānti) becomes increasingly pure;
through immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, their roots of goodness become increasingly superior and pure.
“O Son of the Buddha!

It is like refined pure gold that has been smelted and purified; when it is interspersed and adorned with various excellent jewels, it becomes even more brilliant and beautiful, such that other jewels cannot surpass it.”
O Sons of the Buddha!
It is the same for the Bodhisattva.

Abiding in the Bodhisattva stage of Far-Going (Dūramgamā), all roots of goodness born from skillful means and wisdom become increasingly superior, luminous, and pure, such that no one can destroy them.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like the light of the sun, which no stars or moonlight can equal, and which is able to dry up all the mud and water within Jambudvīpa.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: dwelling in the stage of Far-reaching (Dūramgamā), their roots of goodness become increasingly superior, such that they cannot be equaled by any Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, and they are further able to dry up the muddy sludge of the afflictions of sentient beings.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the seventh stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Stage of Far-Reaching Travel (*dūraṃgamā*).

When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwell in this stage, they frequently become kings of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), possessing sharp and keen faculties, and are able to generate the wholesome conditions for sentient beings to awaken to the Way.

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, never depart from mindfulness of the Dharma, and never depart from mindfulness of their companions, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, up until they never depart from mindfulness of the perfection of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
One should constantly give rise to this thought:
"When shall I become the foremost and the most honored among all sentient beings, even unto becoming the one upon whom all sentient beings rely?"

If this bodhisattva wishes to practice such diligent effort, they will, in a single moment, attain hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of samādhis, and even manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattva retinues. If the bodhisattva employs the power of their vows, they can freely manifest even more than these numbers, beyond what could be calculated even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"With a mind of profound wisdom and concentration, Having fully practiced the six stages,
Simultaneously giving rise to skillful means, Wisdom enters the seventh stage."
Practicing emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet cultivating a heart of compassion;
following the Buddha’s impartial Dharma, yet making offerings to all Buddhas;
though observing emptiness with wisdom, yet practicing merit without weariness.
Thereafter, one is able to enter the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūramgamā).
Though capable of adorning the triple world, the mind delights in seclusion;
though the mind is ever in a state of tranquil extinction, it continues to extinguish the afflictions.
Practicing the non-dual dharma of emptiness, Which is like an illusion or a dream,
Yet practicing with a heart of compassion, One attains entry into the seventh stage.
Though one contemplates all lands, They are empty, just like space.
Yet they are able to skillfully adorn and purify all Buddha-fields;
though they know that the bodies of all Buddhas are identical to the signless nature of dharmas,
they nevertheless plant the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor signs of excellence.
Although they know that the characteristics of all Buddhas are ineffable,
they adorn the voices of the Buddhas in order to bring joy to the world;
although they know that all Buddhas attain enlightenment within a single thought-moment, they...
Yet they manifest the number of eons and kalpas to guide all sentient beings.
Knowing the Dharma in this way, they attain the illumination of the Dharma;
a bodhisattva who acts thus enters the seventh stage.
Abiding in this stage, one is able to contemplate the conduct of immeasurable sentient beings;
one also knows that the power of all Buddhas is likewise immeasurable;
and that both the worlds and the number of kalpas, as well as the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), are all immeasurable.
Furthermore, knowing the desires and inclinations of all sentient beings, he knows that the teaching of the three vehicles is in every way immeasurable. [He thinks:
"I should transform and guide these sentient beings so as to bring them to fulfillment."
Through such reflection, with the union of skillful means and wisdom,
one constantly practices this path amidst the four modes of conduct.
In every single moment of thought, one is able to fulfill the factors that assist toward enlightenment.
These ten kinds of dharmas, such as the pāramitās:
the merit cultivated by these bodhisattvas is all shared with all sentient beings; this is called dānapāramitā.
To eliminate the defilements of the mind is called the *śīla-pāramitā*;
Not being harmed by the six sense objects is the *kṣānti-pāramitā*;
Being able to give rise to ever-superior dharmas is the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
Thus, the non-movement of the Path is named the Dhyāna-pāramitā;
the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena is named the Prajñā-pāramitā;
and the dedication toward the Buddha-way is named the Upāya-pāramitā.
Seeking ever more excellent dharmas is called the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā);
being incapable of being defeated by anyone is called the perfection of power (bala-pāramitā);
being able to understand and explain according to reality is called the perfection of wisdom (jñāna-pāramitā).
These are the factors that assist awakening; In every thought-moment they are able to be gathered, For they give rise to vast vows And take great matters as their object.
The merit within the first stage Is designated as "complete."
The second stage is named "Removing All Evil Defilements of the Mind";
the third is "Increasing the Radiance of Vows";
the fourth stage is "Abiding in the Path."
Fifth, acting in accordance with the world;
sixth, entering the profound Dharma and attaining the stage of the mark of non-arising, gradually increasing therein;
seventh, gathering all things and being endowed with the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
It can give rise to all merits and all vows.
Through such merits, all practices within the subsequent eighth stage will naturally attain purity.
The Stage of Far-Reaching Travel is difficult to traverse; it is accessible only through great power of wisdom.
Like the space between two kingdoms, it is difficult to cross over.
Abiding within the seventh stage, one remains unstained like a noble universal monarch.
Abiding in this path, one is not said to possess any faults.
Upon reaching the eighth stage, the Bodhisattva’s ground of wisdom,
at that time one transcends the realm of mind and abides in the activity of gnosis.
Just as the Brahma King is not called a human when observing the world,
so the Bodhisattva is not defiled by faults, like a lotus flower in the water.
When the Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they transcend all manner of afflictions.
They are not said to possess afflictions, nor are they said to have exhausted afflictions.
Having entered this true path, they possess no afflictions;
yet because they aspire to seek the Buddha-way, they are not said to have exhausted afflictions.
Within all the worlds, regarding scriptures, arts and crafts,
literary compositions, and incantations, he naturally understands them all.
Cultivating all meditative concentrations, as well as the various supernormal powers and immeasurable states of mind that benefit the world— all such matters he is able to bring forth.
At that time, this bodhisattva surpasses the practices of the two vehicles.
Abiding in the seventh stage among all the practices of a bodhisattva,
they were previously superior due to the power of their great vows at the time of first generating the mind;
now, in this stage, they are superior due to the power of their wisdom.
Just as a prince, though in his youth, possesses a noble nature that excels;
later, through the perfection of merit, he becomes superior among all men.
Abiding here, one attains profound wisdom and further arouses supreme diligence.
Moment by moment they enter into quiescence, yet they do not realize [nirvana] therein.
It is like a person riding in a boat who enters the great ocean;
though they travel through deep and perilous waters, they are not harmed by the water.
The Bodhisattva’s practice becomes ever more sublime through skillful means and wisdom;
his merits are fully perfected, yet they remain difficult for all in the world to know.
Having made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, his mind is utterly pure.
Like pure gold interspersed with various jewels, Adorned by their alternating brilliance;
So too, having attained the light of Buddha-wisdom, One dries up the moisture of all craving.
Just as the radiance of the sun Evaporates the mud and mire.
When the Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, he becomes a King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations;
all his faculties are sharp and keen, and he thoroughly penetrates the fruits of all paths.
If he desires to apply himself with diligent vigor, he perceives hundreds of thousands of millions of [Buddhas].
The number of Buddhas of the nayutas is even greater than this due to their power of vows.
The purity of wisdom on the seventh stage is difficult for all in the world and those of the two vehicles to know; it has now been briefly explained.
The King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, along with all the devas and bodhisattvas,
upon hearing this account of supreme conduct, were filled with great joy in their hearts.
They made offerings to the Buddha and his sons, raining down exquisite flowers and incense.
Necklaces, various banners and canopies, powdered incense, and many precious robes,
along with exquisite maṇi jewels and all manner of ornaments for the body,
descended from the sky like clouds, scattering over the Buddha and the great assembly.
In the midst of the sky, the goddesses performed various kinds of music as offerings to the Tathāgata and all the Bodhisattvas;
with exquisite voices, they sang praises of their manifold virtues:
“The Omniscient One, most honored among all sentient beings,
out of compassion for the world, the Buddha manifests supernormal powers;
from flowers, incense, precious jewels, and the like, such sounds as these issue forth.”
Upon every hair, mote, and grain of sand, He manifests nayutas of Buddhas,
Infinite in number, preaching the Dharma therein;
Within the tip of a single hair, One beholds immeasurable Buddha-lands.
Mount Sumeru, the Iron Ring Mountains, and the oceans— though present, they do not crowd the world;
yet within the tip of a single hair, the three evil realms exist, where devas, humans,
and asuras each undergo the retribution of their karma.
In all the Buddha-fields, I see the sublime voices of all Buddhas turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma,
arising in accordance with the thoughts of sentient beings;
within those Buddha-worlds, the bodies of sentient beings are of various kinds.
The land contains sentient beings, and within the bodies of sentient beings there is the land.
All devas and humans alike must first be separated from their shared dwellings;
only after the Buddha has observed this does he preach the Dharma for them.
In lands as minute as motes of dust, the mental conceptions of sentient beings are subtle;
because the lands are coarse, the mental conceptions of sentient beings are coarse.
The Buddha manifests such various supernormal powers as these.
If one were to speak for the sake of sentient beings, these matters could never be exhausted.
Thus, with wondrous voices, they praised the World-Honored One;
their hearts were filled with great joy, and they gazed upon the Buddha in silence.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra requested of Vajragarbha, saying:
"Son of the Buddha, you should now explain the characteristics of entering the eighth stage.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha replied:
“O Son of the Buddha!

These Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, having already practiced the subtle conduct of the seventh stage, the path of wisdom and skillful means, and having gathered the pure and wholesome factors that assist the path, their minds abide without cessation due to the power of their great vows.”

Protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas and having gained strength through their roots of goodness, they constantly mindfully accord with the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities; with a joyful mind and a profound mind, they skillfully and purely accomplish the power of merit and wisdom.
By virtue of great compassion, they do not abandon any sentient beings; they cultivate the path of immeasurable wisdom and are able to enter into all dharmas.
These are fundamentally without birth or cessation, without marks, without emergence, without loss, without departure, without return, and of a nature of non-existence;
they are equal in the beginning, middle, and end, no different from the Tathāgata’s non-conceptual wisdom.

When all mind, mentation, and consciousness, as well as recollections and conceptualizations, are free from attachment, and one enters into the nature of all phenomena as being like space, this is called a bodhisattva attaining the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and entering the eighth stage; at that moment, they attain this eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), and are termed a Bodhisattva of Profound Practice.

It is difficult to know and impossible to discern; it is free from all marks and free from all perceptions and all attachments; it is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable; it cannot be destroyed by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; profound and vast, it stands manifest in detachment.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

It is, for example, like a bhikṣu who has attained supernormal powers and mastery over the mind, who enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in due order, whereby all stirring thoughts, recollections, conceptualizations, and the activities of the mental factors are entirely extinguished."

The Bodhisattva is also like this: dwelling in this stage of Far-Going (dūraṅgamā), all immediate activities are instantly extinguished; he attains the absence of activity of body, speech, and mind, and dwells in great seclusion.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
It is as if a person, while dreaming, wishes to cross deep water; at that time, they exert great diligence and employ great skillful means, desiring to cross this water.
Before they have crossed, they suddenly awaken, and realizing that the skillful means used for the crossing were merely a matter of haste, they immediately let them all go."
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: from the very beginning, having aroused great diligence and extensively practiced the Path until reaching the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), they completely relinquish all urgent affairs, do not engage in dualistic thoughts, and no further recollections or conceptualizations appear before them.
"Just as one born in the Brahma-world does not have the afflictions of the desire realm manifest before them, so it is, O Sons of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this Immovable Stage, all mind, thought, and consciousness do not manifest before them; even the mind of a Buddha, the mind of enlightenment, and the mind of nirvāṇa do not manifest, let alone the arising of a worldly mind."
"O Sons of the Buddha!
These Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accord with this stage by virtue of the power of their original vows.
Furthermore, the Buddhas manifest their bodies for them, abiding within the flow of the Dharma of all stages, acting as the causal conditions for the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
All the Buddhas spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
"You have attained this foremost patience, which accords with all the teachings of the Buddhas. Good son!
I possess the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities, which you have not yet attained."
To attain these various merits, you should apply yourself with diligent effort and never abandon this gate of patience.
Son of good family!

Although you have attained this foremost, most profound liberation of quiescence, ordinary beings are unwholesome, lack quiescence, constantly give rise to various afflictions, and are harmed by various discursive thoughts; you should take pity upon these sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family!
You should call to mind your original vow: the desire to bring great benefit to sentient beings and the desire to attain the inconceivable gate of wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The nature of all phenomena and the characteristics of all phenomena remain eternally constant and unchanging, whether a Buddha exists or does not exist.
It is not because of attaining these dharmas that the Tathāgatas are called "Buddhas"; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are likewise able to attain this quiescent, non-conceptual dharma.

"Good son! Observe our immeasurable and pure physical forms, immeasurable wisdom, and immeasurable pure lands; observe our immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable skillful means, immeasurable circular halos, and immeasurable pure voices. You should now likewise give rise to such matters."
Furthermore, son of good family!
You have now just attained this one illumination of the Dharma, namely, the illumination of the Dharma that all phenomena are quiescent, without discrimination, and unarisen.
"What we have attained is immeasurable and boundless, such that it cannot be known even by calculation throughout many hundreds of millions of kalpas.
For the sake of attaining this, you should give rise to this Dharma."

"Good son! Observe the immeasurable lands, immeasurable sentient beings, and immeasurable distinctions among all phenomena in the ten directions; you should penetrate these matters as they truly are and accord with such wisdom."
“Regarding this bodhisattva, all Buddhas grant such immeasurable and boundless gateways that serve as causes and conditions for the arising of wisdom;
by means of these immeasurable gateways, this bodhisattva is able to give rise to immeasurable knowledge and differentiated activities, all of which are fully accomplished.”
“O Sons of the Buddha!

I shall now explain this for you: if the Buddhas did not cause these bodhisattvas to abide in such a gateway of wisdom, those bodhisattvas would at that time ultimately enter parinirvāṇa, thereby abandoning the benefit of all sentient beings.

Because the Buddhas provide these bodhisattvas with such immeasurable and boundless causes and conditions for the arising of wisdom, the wisdom produced in a single thought-moment is such that the wisdom from the first stage up to the completion of the seventh stage does not equal even one hundredth part of it; it does not equal one ten-thousandth, one millionth, one billionth, nor even one *nayuta* of hundreds of thousands of millions, nor even an immeasurable, boundless, *asaṃkhyeya* part of it—not even can it be reached by calculation or analogy.”

Why is this? Previously, one practiced the Way and accumulated merit with a single body; now, within this stage, one attains immeasurable bodies to cultivate the bodhisattva path. This is because one employs immeasurable sounds, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable birthplaces, immeasurable pure lands, and immeasurable means of teaching and transforming sentient beings; because one makes offerings to and serves immeasurable Buddhas; because one accords with immeasurable Buddha-dharmas; because of immeasurable supernormal powers; because of the distinctions among immeasurable great assemblies; and because one accumulates all the practices of the bodhisattvas through immeasurable actions of body, speech, and mind, by virtue of the dharma of immovability.
“O Son of the Buddha!
It is like one who boards a ship intending to enter the great ocean; before reaching the great ocean, they must exert much effort, whether by manual labor or physical strength.
Once they have reached the great ocean, they no longer exert such effort, but proceed solely by the power of the wind.”
If one were to travel across the great ocean for a single day using one's original power, one could not reach it even in a hundred thousand years.
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas: having accumulated a vast store of the provisions of roots of goodness, they board the ship of the Great Vehicle and reach the great ocean of wisdom where Bodhisattvas practice. In a mere instant, without exerting effort, they can draw near to the wisdom of all Buddhas; whereas the effort originally exerted—even over one kalpa, or a hundred thousand million kalpas—could never reach it.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas reach the eighth stage, they give rise to effortlessness from the fundamental wisdom of skillful means. Abiding upon the path of the bodhisattvas, they contemplate the power of the Buddhas’ wisdom, namely:

knowing the arising of worlds, the cessation of worlds, the destruction of worlds, and the formation of worlds; knowing by what causal conditions of karma worlds are destroyed, and knowing by what causal conditions of karma worlds are formed.”

“This bodhisattva knows the small characteristics of the nature of earth, knows the great characteristics of the nature of earth, knows the immeasurable characteristics of the nature of earth, and knows the differentiated characteristics of the nature of earth;
he likewise knows the small, great, immeasurable, and differentiated characteristics of the natures of water, fire, and wind.”

"They know the subtle characteristics of atoms; they know the distinct characteristics of atoms. They are able to know all the distinctions among the atoms within a single world-system; they are able to know exactly how many atoms constitute the earth in this world-system;
they are able to know exactly how many atoms constitute the water, fire, and wind therein."

“They know the differences between the weights and atoms of various precious substances, and the atoms of the bodies of various sentient beings, as well as the atoms of all things within worlds; they discern the coarse bodies and subtle bodies of sentient beings, and fully comprehend how the bodies of hell-beings arise from such-and-such atoms, how the bodies of animals arise from such-and-such atoms, how the bodies of hungry ghosts arise from such-and-such atoms, how the bodies of asuras arise from such-and-such atoms, how the bodies of devas arise from such-and-such atoms, and how the bodies of humans arise from such-and-such atoms.”

"When this bodhisattva enters such wisdom that discerns subtle atoms, he knows the destruction of the desire realm and knows the formation of the desire realm; he knows the destruction of the form realm and knows the formation of the form realm; he knows the destruction of the formless realm and knows the formation of the formless realm;
he knows the formation and destruction of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm."

He knows the minor characteristics of the desire realm, the major characteristics of the desire realm, the immeasurable characteristics of the desire realm, and the distinctive characteristics of the desire realm;
he likewise knows the minor, major, immeasurable, and distinctive characteristics of the form realm and the formless realm.
To know the three realms in this way is called the Bodhisattva’s stage of the illumination of wisdom that aids in teaching and transforming sentient beings.

Being skilled in discerning the bodies of sentient beings and skillfully observing the places where they should be born, he assumes a body in accordance with the birthplaces of sentient beings and in accordance with their bodies.

This Bodhisattva manifests a body that pervades the trichiliocosm, assuming various distinct forms according to the bodies of sentient beings, just as the sun reflects its image in all waters. Whether it be two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty trichiliocosms; or a hundred trichiliocosms; or a thousand, ten thousand, a million, ten million, a hundred million, or a hundred thousand million nayutas of worlds—their bodies pervade them all.

Even throughout immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and ineffable trichiliocosms, their bodies fill them entirely, assuming forms in accordance with the differences among the bodies of sentient beings.

“Having accomplished such wisdom, this bodhisattva remains with his body unmoving in a single world, yet manifests his physical form in the great assemblies of all Buddhas throughout unspeakably many Buddha-worlds, according to the bodies of sentient beings and according to what they believe and delight in.”

If, within an assembly of śramaṇas, he manifests the form and appearance of a śramaṇa; within an assembly of brahmins, he manifests the form and appearance of a brahmin; within an assembly of kṣatriyas, he manifests the form and appearance of a kṣatriya; within an assembly of householders, he manifests the form and appearance of a householder; within the assemblies of the Four Great Kings, Śakra, Māra, and the Brahmās, he manifests the form and appearance of a Brahmā; and even within the assemblies of the Akaniṣṭha devas, he manifests the form and appearance of an Akaniṣṭha deva;
for those to be delivered by the Śrāvaka vehicle, he manifests the form of a śrāvaka; for those to be delivered by the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, he manifests the form of a pratyekabuddha.
For those to be delivered by the Bodhisattva Vehicle, he manifests the form and color of a bodhisattva;
for those to be delivered by the Buddha-body, he manifests the form and color of a Buddha.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

In all the unspeakably many Buddha-lands, he manifests the assumption of bodies according to the differences in the physical forms and inclinations of sentient beings; yet in reality, he is far removed from the distinctions of bodily characteristics, eternally abiding in the equality of all bodies.

“This bodhisattva knows the body of sentient beings, knows the body of the land, knows the body of karmic retribution, knows the body of śrāvakas, knows the body of pratyekabuddhas, knows the body of bodhisattvas, knows the body of Tathāgatas, knows the body of wisdom, knows the body of Dharma, and knows the body of space.”

"In this way, the Bodhisattva knows the inclinations of the deep minds of sentient beings. He may take the body of a sentient being and make it his own body; or he may take the body of a sentient being and make it the body of a land, the body of karmic retribution, the body of a śrāvaka, the body of a pratyekabuddha, the body of a bodhisattva, the body of a Tathāgata, the body of wisdom, the body of Dharma, or the body of space. Or he may take the body of a land and make it his own body, the body of karmic retribution, or even the body of space. Or he may take the body of karmic retribution and make it his own body, or even the body of space. Or he may take his own body and make it the body of a sentient being, the body of a land, the body of karmic retribution, the body of a śrāvaka, the body of a pratyekabuddha, the body of a bodhisattva, the body of a Tathāgata, the body of wisdom, the body of Dharma, or the body of space."

“This bodhisattva knows the bodies of sentient beings accumulated through karma, the retribution body, the affliction body, the form body, and the formless body; he knows the small characteristics, large characteristics, defiled characteristics, pure characteristics, immeasurable characteristics, vast characteristics, inverted characteristics, level characteristics, crooked characteristics, square characteristics, and the characteristics of spatial differentiation of all Buddha-lands; and he knows the distinctions in the conventional designations of the karmic retribution body, the distinctions in the conventional designations of the śrāvaka body, the distinctions in the conventional designations of the pratyekabuddha body, the distinctions in the conventional designations of the bodhisattva body, and the distinctions of the Tathāgata body.”
