He skillfully discriminates and explains, according to reality, the characteristics of all bodies: the Bodhi-body, the vow-body, the transformation-body, the body that receives supernatural powers, the body adorned with the primary and secondary marks, the body of power, the mind-made body, the merit-body, the wisdom-body, and the Dharma-body.

They know that the bodies of all phenomena possess the characteristic of equality and indestructibility; they know that the body of space possesses the characteristics of being immeasurable, all-pervasive, and formless.

"When these bodhisattvas skillfully know how to manifest such various bodies, they attain mastery over life, mastery over mind, mastery over material wealth, mastery over karma, mastery over birth, mastery over vows, mastery over resolute belief and understanding, mastery over the supernatural powers, mastery over wisdom, and mastery over the Dharma."
When this bodhisattva attains these ten masteries of a bodhisattva, he immediately becomes one possessed of inconceivable wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, vast wisdom, and indestructible wisdom.

“The Bodhisattva, following such wisdom that is ultimately and eternally pure, gives rise to faultless bodily, verbal, and mental actions; his bodily actions follow the movement of wisdom, his verbal actions follow the movement of wisdom, and his mental actions follow the movement of wisdom. With the perfection of wisdom as the sovereign and great compassion as the foremost, he skillfully cultivates expedient means, skillfully gives rise to various vows, and is skillfully protected by the supernatural powers of all Buddhas. He never abandons the practice of the wisdom that benefits sentient beings, fully knowing the diverse affairs within boundless worlds.”
O Sons of the Buddha!
To state the essentials: when Bodhisattvas dwell in the Immovable Stage (*acalā bhūmi*), all actions performed through their body, speech, and mind are capable of gathering all the Buddha-dharmas.
"When this bodhisattva reaches this stage, because they are free from all afflictions, they dwell well within the power of the pure mind;
because their mind never departs from the Path, they dwell well within the power of the profound mind;
and because they do not abandon sentient beings, they dwell well within the power of great compassion."
For the sake of saving all the world, they are well-established in the power of great compassion;
because they do not forget the teachings they have heard, they are well-established in the power of dhāraṇī;
and because they discern and select all Buddha-dharmas, they are well-established in the power of all eloquence.
Because they traverse boundless and diverse worlds, they dwell securely in the power of supernormal knowledges;
because they do not abandon any of the practices of bodhisattvas, they dwell securely in the power of vows;
because they cultivate and accumulate all Buddha-dharmas, they abide securely in the power of the perfections.
Because they have skillfully given rise to the knowledge of all modes, they abide within the powers of a Tathāgata.
Having attained such power of knowledge, these bodhisattvas demonstrate that all their actions are free from fault.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Because this stage of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas cannot be destroyed, it is called the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi);
because their wisdom does not regress, it is called the Non-regressive Stage (Anivartanīya-bhūmi).
Because it is difficult for all the worlds to fathom or know, it is called the Stage of Majestic Virtue (*tejo-bhūmi*);
because it is free from the faults of a household, it is called the Stage of the Prince (*kumāra-bhūmi*);
and because one possesses sovereign mastery according to one's will, it is called the Stage of the Birth of Bodhisattvas (*bodhisattva-janma-bhūmi*).
Because one no longer creates [new karma], it is called the Ground of Accomplishment;
because of skillful discernment and knowledge, it is called the Ground of Culmination;
because of the skillful arousal of great vows, it is called the Ground of Transformation.
Because they do not harbor any dharmas, it is called the Stage of the Victorious Abodes;
because they skillfully cultivate the arising of the prior path, it is called the Stage of Effortlessness.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain such wisdom, it is called "entering the realm of the Buddhas," "being illuminated by the merits of the Buddhas," and "acting in accordance with the majestic deportment of the Buddhas. They advance toward the Buddha-dharma, are constantly well-protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas, are always welcomed by the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, Brahmā Devānām Indra, and others, and are constantly guarded by the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapatis.

They are well able to give rise to all profound meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and can constantly manifest immeasurable varieties of bodies; within each of these bodies they possess sovereign power, attaining great rewards and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). They attain mastery over boundless samādhis and receive immeasurable prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), manifesting the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* according to the place where sentient beings are brought to fulfillment.

"This Bodhisattva enters into such great wisdom, skillfully penetrating all phenomena, constantly radiating the light of great intelligence, and traversing the path of the unobstructed nature of reality (*dharmatā*). He skillfully knows the distinctions between the paths of worldly phenomena, can manifest all merits at will with sovereign ease, and has a thorough understanding of the past and future limits."

They are able to enter the wisdom that revolves within the paths of Māra and enter the sphere of activity of the Tathāgatas; they are able to practice the bodhisattva path in infinite worlds because they do not manifest the characteristic of turning back.
For this reason, this stage is called "The Immovable.
O Sons of the Buddha!

Because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwelling in the Immovable Stage have well-generated the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they are never separated from the vision of boundless Buddhas, yet they do not abandon coarse offerings and services to those Buddhas.

In each and every eon, throughout all worlds, this bodhisattva beholds hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable buddhas; he makes offerings, pays homage, respects, and praises them, providing every requisite for worship as an act of offering, drawing near to these buddhas and receiving from them the various clarifications of the dharmas pertaining to the mundane world and so forth.

This person penetrates ever deeper into the Tathāgata’s treasury of Dharma; regarding the matters of the distinctions among the natures of the world, there is no one who can exhaust their inquiry, such that even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, they could not be fully expounded.
Furthermore, all roots of goodness become increasingly superior, bright, and pure.

"It is like refined, purified gold that a skilled craftsman fashions into a jeweled necklace; once it is fastened around the neck of the ruler of the four continents, no one in Jambudvīpa is able to seize it."
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: dwelling in this Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), all their roots of goodness become increasingly superior, luminous, and pure, such that they cannot be destroyed by any Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or even Bodhisattvas of the seventh ground.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, because they possess the gate of wisdom that skillfully discriminates, the light of their wisdom extinguishes the afflictions and fevers of sentient beings.
"It is like this, O Son of the Buddha!"
If the Great Brahmā King, Lord of a thousand worlds, can at one time diffuse a mind of loving-kindness to fill a thousand worlds, he can also emit light that shines everywhere throughout them.
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas: dwelling in the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), they are able to emit bodily light that reaches as many worlds as there are atoms in one hundred thousand triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems, and furthermore, they are able to extinguish all afflictions and fevers, causing sentient beings to attain refreshing coolness.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
This is a brief explanation of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*); were it to be explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even in the course of immeasurable eons."
"When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they frequently become Mahābrahmā, lord of a thousand worlds, with faculties that are sharp and keen.
They provide inexhaustible causes and conditions for all sentient beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the path of the perfections for bodhisattvas;
and in explaining the distinctions among the natures of the world, none are able to refute them."

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of their companions, the bodhisattvas, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of the knowledge of all modes.
They constantly give rise to this thought:
"When shall I become the foremost and the most honored among sentient beings, even unto becoming the one upon whom all sentient beings rely?"

If this bodhisattva wishes to practice with diligent vigor, they can, in a single moment, attain as many samādhis as there are atoms in ten million trichiliocosms, and even manifest a retinue of bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms in ten million trichiliocosms. If, however, by the power of their vows, their supernormal powers are sovereign, they can exceed these numbers, reaching hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of kalpas beyond measure.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"When a bodhisattva dwells in the seventh stage, Having already attained wisdom and skillful means,
And having well accumulated the factors conducive to enlightenment, They are bound by their great vows."
Protected by the spiritual power of all Buddhas, their roots of goodness are fully perfected;
because they seek supreme wisdom, they are able to enter the eighth stage.
Having well accumulated merit and possessing profound compassion, they proceed.
Free from all conditioned states of mind, the mind becomes equal to space.
Within the Dharma as it has been taught, the mind attains the power of certainty;
thus one attains the sublime patience of non-arising, which is the state of peace.
All phenomena from the very beginning Are neither born nor extinguished;
They are without marks and do not emerge, Neither lost nor proceeding.
In the beginning, middle, and end of all phenomena, They are non-different from suchness.
There is no mental activity, equal and like empty space.
Having accomplished such patience, free from all conceptual proliferation,
one attains this Immovable Ground, the practice of profound quiescence.
All the worlds cannot fathom it; all characteristics of the mind have been utterly destroyed.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, their consciousness is free from discrimination.
As when one enters the meditative absorption of cessation, there is no thought, perception, or discrimination.
It is like a person in a dream who suddenly wishes to cross a river;
upon waking, the mind is vast and open, and one knows for oneself that nothing was actually done.
Having attained this profound patience, all conceptual thoughts are extinguished;
like the Brahma kings, they are free from the afflictions of the desire realm.
Previously protected by the power of their vows, the Buddhas now exhort them, saying:
"Such is this foremost patience, the rank of all Buddhas.
We possess profound power of wisdom, fearlessness, and the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma);
since you lack these, you should apply yourself with diligent vigor."
Although you have now extinguished all the fires of affliction,
you should observe that throughout the world, afflictions are constantly ablaze.
You should remember your original vow, which was the desire to benefit all sentient beings.
Thoroughly and universally knowing all dharmas, they extensively deliver all beings.
The true nature and characteristics of all dharmas are eternally abiding and without change;
even those of the two vehicles attain this, yet they do not receive the name of "Buddha" on its account.
Only because he has attained unimpeded, profound, and subtle wisdom,
and has thoroughly penetrated the three periods of time, is he named Buddha.
He is one who is peerless among all peers, revered by devas and humans alike.
Opening these gates of manifold wisdom, They cause entry into all Buddha-dharmas.
Accomplishing boundless depths And immeasurable, wondrous wisdom,
All dharmas previously practiced Do not equal even a single thought-moment of this.
Thus these bodhisattvas, having attained the stage of wondrous wisdom,
are able within a single thought-moment to have their bodies pervade the ten directions.
Entering this gateway of wisdom, they traverse the path swiftly and without obstruction.
Just as one travels upon the great ocean, where the power of the wind causes swift progress;
so too, free from all effortful mental activity, one abides solely in the work of wisdom,
contemplating the worlds of the ten directions— their formation, destruction, and duration.
One can know that the four great elements are one, and also know their various differences—
their small, large, and immeasurable characteristics, as well as all their manifold distinctions;
one can count and know the atoms within the three thousandfold world system.
He also knows the bodies of sentient beings, numbering as many as the atoms of the four great elements;
he fully and universally perceives the various celestial bodies composed of myriad jewels,
distinguished by their countless atomic particles, and he knows all other things in the same way.
By reason of wisdom, the mind becomes transformed and pliant;
for the benefit of all sentient beings, his body pervades all worlds.
Within the bodies of sentient beings, he manifests himself as their own self.
As well as the worlds of all Buddhas, And all other various bodies— Just as the sun and moon follow the wind, Their reflections appearing in all waters;
So too is the Bodhisattva: Following the wind of wisdom, they manifest accordingly.
Abiding eternally in the nature of phenomena, serene and unmoving,
he manifests his physical form to sentient beings with pure minds.
According to the inclinations of their hearts, he appears to take birth.
Within the assemblies of gods and humans, they manifest their bodies to all;
the Bodhisattva possesses mastery amidst the convergence of causes and conditions,
even able to manifest the body of a Buddha according to their will.
Sentient beings, the body of the land, the bodies of karma-retribution and of the noble ones,
the wisdom-body, and the dharma-body— knowing that all are equal and identical,
by these causes and conditions, one attains the supernormal power of mastery over wishes.
To bring joy to the world, they manifest various bodies.
They are able to attain ten kinds of wondrous and great sovereign wisdom;
their actions follow the movement of that wisdom, in accord with a mind of compassion.
One can skillfully cultivate all the dharmas of the Buddhas,
Abiding within the three pure karmas, as immovable as Mount Sumeru.
One will attain the ten powers possessed by the great Bodhisattvas.
All the hosts of Māras are unable to turn them back.
They are constantly protected by all Buddhas and revered by Śakra and Brahmā;
the Guhyapada Vajrapāṇi spirits always follow and guard them.
When a Bodhisattva attains this stage, their merit is immeasurable;
even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, it could not be fully described.
They draw near to countless Buddhas and further increase all their roots of goodness.
Like pure gold and various jewels, adorning the neck of a king;
so the Bodhisattva on this stage often becomes a Great Brahmā King,
presiding over a thousand lands, with immeasurable wealth of merit.
Able to employ the teachings of the three vehicles without end,
the light of their compassionate mind shines universally, destroying the heat of all afflictions.
If one wishes, in a mere moment, they can attain hundreds of thousands of [realms].
The number of great trichiliocosms, And the various samādhis of subtle atoms—
One can see as many Buddhas in the ten directions As there are such [atoms],
Yet by the power of their vows, They exceed this and are immeasurable.
Now I have briefly explained the wondrous characteristics of the eighth stage;
were I to expound them in detail, they would not be exhausted even in a thousand billion kalpas.
*Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, Scroll Three.
The Scripture on the Ten Stages, Scroll Four, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Later Qin Dynasty. 9.
The Stage of Wondrous Virtue (Sādhumatī-bhūmi), the Ninth.
When the Son of the Buddha expounded this sublime meaning of the Eighth Ground,
by the Buddha’s spiritual power, immeasurable lands were shaken.
From the body of the All-Knowing One, immeasurable, subtle, and wondrous rays of light issued forth.
Illuminating the realms of the ten directions, may all sentient beings attain peace and happiness.
Countless bodhisattvas, numbering in the millions, dwell in the midst of the void,
presenting a multitude of wondrous offerings such as no devas possess.
The Great Lord Maheśvara King, together with the King of Paranirmita-vaśavartin,
joyfully presented various wondrous offerings to the Buddha of Ocean-like Merit.
Countless tens of millions of celestial maidens, all filled with reverence and delight, paid their respects.
With voices equally subtle and wondrous, they sang in praise of the Buddha’s virtues:
“By the Buddha’s spiritual power, such sublime Dharma is brought forth;
He who practices well and dwells in tranquility has no evil thoughts whatsoever.”
Each remaining in their respective lands, they skillfully cultivate the bodhisattva practices;
for the sake of benefiting the world, they travel everywhere throughout the ten directions.
They demonstrate the Buddha-way to all beings, their minds equal to space and unimpeded.
The supernatural powers of the bodhisattvas and their most sublime offerings surpass those of the humans and devas of the ten directions; these are brought about by the power of merit.
These sons of the Buddha, who delight in wisdom, manifest this through the power of the Buddha.
Without moving from a single land, he manifests in all places to benefit the world, like the full moon, bright and pure.
He extinguishes all sounds, speech, and all conceptual thoughts.
Yet with various sounds and voices, he preaches the Dharma like an echo.
To those of inferior capacity whose minds are weary and despondent,
he demonstrates and teaches the path of the śrāvaka, causing them to emerge from all sufferings.
According to all sentient beings, for those whose faculties are dull and who delight in the Dharma of causes and conditions, he preaches the Pratyekabuddha path;
according to those with sharp faculties who benefit sentient beings, [he preaches the Mahāyāna].
Possessing a heart of great compassion, he preaches the Bodhisattva Dharma;
if there is a supreme great mind that resolutely delights in the Great Matter,
he manifests the Buddha-body for them and expounds the immeasurable teachings of the Buddhas.
Just as a master of illusions displays various forms and colors,
so too these physical characteristics have no substantial reality. In this way,
the sons of the Buddha, being skilled in the arts of wisdom, [perceive all things as such].
He is able to demonstrate all modes of conduct, his mind detached from existence and non-existence.
Tens of millions of celestial maidens sing praises with exquisite voices;
having thus offered their hymns of praise, they fall silent and gaze upon the Buddha.
Furthermore, Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
This great assembly is pure and desires with single-minded devotion to hear about the correct practice that transcends the eighth stage."
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said: "O Son of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have thus skillfully observed the path of the Buddhas with such immeasurable wisdom, they desire to further seek the even more excellent, profound, and tranquil liberation; they desire to further contemplate the wisdom of the Tathāgata; they desire to enter the deep and secret Dharma of the Tathāgata; they desire to select and grasp inconceivable great wisdom; they desire to select various dhāraṇīs and samādhis and cause them to be doubly purified; they desire to cause their supernormal powers to become vast; they desire to act in accordance with the differentiated activities of the world; they desire to cultivate the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha that cannot be destroyed; they desire to accord with the power of all Buddhas in turning the wheel of Dharma; and they desire not to abandon the great compassion and great vows they have undertaken—thereby they attain entry into the ninth stage."

"When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage, they know, as it truly is, the activity of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas; they know the activity of out-flowing (sāsrava) and non-out-flowing (anāsrava) dharmas; the activity of mundane and supramundane dharmas; the activity of conceivable and inconceivable dharmas; the activity of conditioned and unconditioned dharmas; the activity of the dharmas of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; the activity of the dharmas of the Bodhisattva path and the dharmas of the Tathāgata stage."

“In accordance with such wisdom, one knows as they truly are the difficulty of the practice of the bodhicitta; the difficulty of the various afflictions; the difficulty of karma; the difficulty of the faculties; the difficulty of aspirations and inclinations; the difficulty of nature; the difficulty of the resolute mind; the difficulty of the profound mind; the difficulty of birth; the difficulty of residual impressions; and the difficulty of the distinctions among the three groups.”

He knows, exactly as they are, the various distinctions among the minds of sentient beings: the mind’s characteristic of being variegated; its characteristic of lightness and movement; its characteristic of being broken or unbroken; its characteristic of being formless; its characteristic of being boundless, pervasive, and sovereign; its characteristic of pure differentiation; its characteristic of defilement; its characteristic of being stainless; its characteristic of bondage; its characteristic of liberation; its characteristic of crookedness and artifice; its characteristic of integrity and straightforwardness; and its characteristic of following the Path. He knows all these things in accordance with reality.

“This bodhisattva knows the deep characteristics of afflictions and their shallow characteristics; he knows the characteristics of the mind’s companionship with afflictions and its non-separation from them; he knows the distinct characteristics of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); he knows the characteristics of what is associated with and dissociated from this mind; he knows the characteristics of obtaining retribution at the time of birth; he knows the distinct characteristics within the three realms; he knows the characteristics of craving, delusion, and views penetrating deeply like arrows; he knows the characteristics of the heavy offenses of pride and delusion; he knows the characteristics of the uninterrupted causal conditions of the three karmas; and, in brief, he knows as they truly are the distinctions among the eighty-four thousand modes of affliction.”

“This bodhisattva knows the characteristics of all karmas—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; the characteristics of the distinguished and the undistinguished; the characteristics of being companions to the mind;
the characteristics of not being separated [from the mind]; the characteristics of natural exhaustion; the characteristics of exhaustion through the practice of the path;

the characteristics of the seeds; the characteristics of accumulation; the characteristics of the non-forfeiture of retribution; the characteristics of succession; the characteristics of having retribution; and the characteristics of having no retribution...”

The characteristic of retribution; the characteristic of black karma with black retribution; the characteristic of white karma with white retribution; the characteristic of black-and-white karma with black-and-white retribution;

the characteristic of karma that is neither black nor white which can exhaust all karma; the characteristic of knowing the origin of the arising of karma; the characteristic of the distinct differences in the dharmas of experiencing karma;
the characteristic of knowing the arising of karma through immeasurable causes and conditions; and the characteristic of knowing the distinction between mundane karma and supramundane karma.
The characteristics of distinct marks, the characteristics of present retribution, the characteristics of retribution in the next life, the characteristics of retribution in subsequent lives,

the characteristics of certainty according to various karmas, and the characteristics of uncertainty; briefly stated, up to knowing, as they truly are, the eighty-four thousand differentiating characteristics of all karmas.

“This bodhisattva knows the characteristics of the distinctions between dull, middling, and sharp faculties; he knows the characteristics of the differences between the past and future limits, as well as their non-differentiation; he knows the characteristics of superior, middling, and inferior; he knows the characteristics of the companionship of afflictions and their inseparability; he knows the characteristics of being fixed according to the various vehicles, the unfixed, the matured, and the immature; he knows the characteristics of following the movements of the mind, the easily broken, the deeply grasped, the predominant, the indestructible, the transformative, and the non-transformative; he knows the characteristics of the distinctions among the three periods of time, and the characteristics of the profound, hidden, and co-arising distinctions—in brief, he knows the characteristics of the eighty-four thousand distinctions among all faculties as they truly are.”

"This Bodhisattva knows the characteristics of the various desires and inclinations of sentient beings—whether they be weak, middling, or sharp—and, to speak briefly, he knows the distinctions among the eighty-four thousand types of desires and inclinations as they truly are."

“This bodhisattva knows the characteristics of the weak, middling, and sharp faculties of all natures; briefly stated, he knows the characteristics of the eighty-four thousand distinctions among these natures as they truly are.

This bodhisattva knows the characteristics of the weak, middling, and sharp faculties of the profound mind; briefly stated, he knows the characteristics of the eighty-four thousand distinctions among the profound minds as they truly are.”

"This Bodhisattva discriminates and knows all fetters (*saṃyojana*): those that arise with a companion in the mind and those that do not; those associated with the mind and those dissociated from the mind; their characteristics of deep penetration; their characteristics of having followed and afflicted sentient beings since beginningless time; their opposition to all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); their firm binding; their connection to the three realms (*tridhātu*) such that they remain latent within the immeasurable mind without manifesting; their opening of the gates of various karmas; and their characteristics of being without anything to be known as an antidote, being non-existent, having no fixed objective reality, being non-different from the Noble Path, and having the characteristic of extinguishing movement."

“This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, the various distinctions among births: namely, the distinctions between hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, humans, and devas; the distinctions between the realm of form and the formless realm; and the distinctions between those with perception and those without perception.”

Karma is the field, craving is the water, ignorance is the darkness, and that which covers consciousness is the seed. The subsequent body is the sprout of birth; name-and-form arise together and are not separate from one another. One knows as it truly is the characteristic of delusion and craving, the characteristic of continuity, the desire to be born, the desire to act, and the desire for love; the characteristic of sentient beings who do not depart from pleasure, the characteristic of the distinctions between the three realms, and the characteristic of the continuity of the three modes of existence. All these are known according to reality.

“This bodhisattva knows, as they truly are, all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): whether with remainder or without remainder; the habitual tendencies present in the place of birth; the habitual tendencies present in dwelling together with sentient beings; the habitual tendencies present in karma and afflictions; the habitual tendencies present in the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; the habitual tendencies present in the state of detachment from desire; the habitual tendencies present in the subsequent body; and the habitual tendencies that follow in succession.”

They penetrate deeply into the characteristic of the severance of the path and the characteristic of maintaining afflictions; they know, in accordance with reality, that when these are abandoned, there is no such dharma.

"This bodhisattva knows, in accordance with reality, the characteristics of sentient beings who are fixed and unfixed: those fixed in the right [path], those fixed in the wrong [path], and those who are unfixed; as well as those fixed in the wrong path among those with wrong views, and those fixed in the right path among those with right views, and those who are unfixed apart from these two."

Each of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) is the mark of wrong certainty (*mithyātva-niyata*); the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are the mark of right certainty (*samyaktva-niyata*). The state of error is wrong certainty, and the state of correctness is right certainty; because one no longer acts [in those ways], that which is apart from these two states is the mark of non-certainty (*aniyata*).

He knows, as they truly are, the characteristics of those deeply entrenched in the wrong assembly who find it difficult to turn back; the characteristics of the causes and conditions for cultivating the unsurpassed path; and the characteristics of the protection of sentient beings within the indeterminate assembly and the wrong-determined assembly.
“O Son of the Buddha!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accord with such wisdom are said to be ‘dwelling securely in the stage of sublime goodness.

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they know the various characteristics of the differences in the activities of sentient beings, and provide them with the causes and conditions according to their respective liberations.”
"This Bodhisattva knows the method for transforming sentient beings and knows the method for delivering sentient beings; knowing them as they truly are, he preaches the Dharma for them.

He knows, as they truly are, the characteristics of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the Bodhisattva vehicle, and the stage of the Tathāgata; according to the causes and conditions of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma for them."
They preach the Dharma according to differences in mental states, faculties, and inclinations;
furthermore, they preach the Dharma according to the spheres of conduct and the spheres of wisdom;
knowing all spheres of conduct, they preach the Dharma accordingly.
They preach the Dharma by entering deeply into difficult places in accordance with the natures of sentient beings;
they preach the Dharma by turning according to the paths, births, afflictions, and habitual tendencies;
and they preach the Dharma in order to bring about liberation through the various vehicles.

"When this bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they become a great Dharma teacher, guarding the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas. Having entered into the profound and subtle meanings of a great Dharma teacher, they employ immeasurable wisdom and skillful means, as well as the four types of unimpeded knowledge, to give rise to the speech of a bodhisattva and preach the Dharma."
"This Bodhisattva constantly accords with the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) without making conceptual distinctions. What are these four?

First, unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); second, unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); third, unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); and fourth, unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)."

"This bodhisattva, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of dharmas (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), knows the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), knows the distinctions between all phenomena; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), knows how to teach all phenomena without conceptual differentiation; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), knows the uninterrupted succession of all phenomena."

"Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the characteristics of arising and ceasing of all phenomena; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one knows that all phenomena are provisional names and yet continues to speak using those provisional names; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one follows those provisional names to provide infinite discourse without impairment."

"Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinct characteristics of all phenomena in the present; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinct characteristics of all phenomena in the past and future; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one explains the phenomena of the past, future, and present without discrimination; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one speaks because one attains the boundless characteristics of phenomena within each respective age."

"Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions among all phenomena; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions among the meanings of all phenomena; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma in accordance with various languages and sounds; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one preaches the Dharma in accordance with what beings delight in and understand."

"Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of dharmas (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions among all phenomena through the knowledge of dharmas (*dharmajñāna*); by means of skillful means, one knows that all phenomena are without distinction.
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions among all phenomena as they truly are through inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one explains the distinctions among all phenomena through conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)."
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one knows the excellent exposition of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one knows that all phenomena possess a single, indestructible characteristic;

by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), one skillfully enters into the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), truths (*satya*), and the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression, they become the refuge for all the world because of their subtle and wondrous voice;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence, their discourse becomes ever more excellent, enabling sentient beings to attain boundless illumination of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that all phenomena are without differentiation and are subsumed within the Single Vehicle;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one enters the various gates of differentiating phenomena;
and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one is able to explain the non-differentiated meaning of the various vehicles."
"By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one explains infinite dharmas through a single dharma-gate.

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one is able to enter into all bodhisattva practices, wisdom practices, dharma practices, and practices that accord with wisdom;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), one is able to analytically explain the distinctions among the meanings of the ten stages (*bhūmi*)."
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), one explains without discrimination the paths and stages that accord with the various levels;
by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one explains the infinite characteristics of all practices.

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one knows that all Buddhas attain enlightenment within a single thought-moment; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions between various times and places; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression, one explains according to the distinctions in the events of the Buddhas' attainment of the Way; and by means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence, one can explain a single phrase of the Dharma for infinite eons without exhaustion.

"Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows all that the Buddhas have spoken: all the powers of the Buddhas, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), great loving-kindness and great compassion, the unimpeded knowledge, and the turning of the wheel of Dharma, thereby conforming to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

By means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one issues eighty-four thousand [teachings] from the voice of the Tathāgata according to the minds of sentient beings, according to their faculties, and according to the differences in their inclinations.
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one explains all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) through the voice of the Tathāgata without making distinctions."
"By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence and through the power of the wisdom of all Buddhas, they preach according to the sounds and inclinations of sentient beings.
O Children of the Buddha!"

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thus well understands unimpeded wisdom and dwells securely in the ninth stage, they are said to have attained the treasury of all Buddha-dharmas and become a great Dharma-preacher. They attain the *dhāraṇīs* of manifold meanings, the *dhāraṇīs* of manifold dharmas, the *dhāraṇī* of the arising of wisdom, the *dhāraṇī* of manifold luminosities, the *dhāraṇī* of noble intention, the *dhāraṇī* of manifold riches, the *dhāraṇī* of renown, the *dhāraṇī* of majestic power, the *dhāraṇī* of non-obstruction, the *dhāraṇī* of boundless revolution, and the *dhāraṇī* of the treasury of diverse meanings. Having attained such millions of *asaṃkhyeya* *dhāraṇīs*, they preach the Dharma by means of immeasurable gateways of eloquence, employing appropriate skillful means.

“Having attained such immeasurable dharanī-gates, this bodhisattva is able to hear the Dharma from immeasurable Buddhas; having heard it, they do not forget it, and they are able to expound the Dharma as they have heard it for others through immeasurable methods of differentiation.”

"This bodhisattva, at the site of a single Buddha, hears and receives a million *asaṃkhyeya* dhāraṇīs of the Dharma; as it is from one Buddha, so it is from all other immeasurable and boundless Buddhas."

“The Dharma-illumination gate that this bodhisattva hears when paying homage to the Buddha cannot be received, upheld, or mastered even by a highly learned śrāvaka endowed with the power of dhāraṇī, even in the course of one hundred thousand kalpas.”

"By virtue of having attained such power of dhāraṇī, the various unimpeded knowledges, and the power of eloquence, this bodhisattva, while seated upon the Dharma throne for the purpose of preaching the Dharma, teaches the Dharma according to the inclinations of all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm."

"This bodhisattva, seated upon the Dharma throne—save for the Buddhas and those bodhisattvas who have received their office—is the most preeminent among all; within his mind, he has attained immeasurable illumination of the Dharma."
When this bodhisattva sits upon the Dharma-seat, he may cause the entire great assembly to fully understand through a single sound, and they immediately understand;
or he may cause the entire great assembly to each attain realization through various sounds, and they immediately attain realization;
or he may remain silent and simply emit light, causing the entire great assembly to each understand the Dharma, and they immediately understand the Dharma.

Alternatively, the sound of the Dharma issues from every single pore; or the sound of the Dharma issues from all material and immaterial things throughout the trichiliocosm; or, with a single voice, it pervades the entire world-system, causing all beings to attain understanding.

"Suppose all sentient beings in this trichiliocosm were to pose questions and challenges simultaneously, and each single being were to do so with an infinite and boundless variety of vocal distinctions—such that what one person asked was different from what the others asked—the Bodhisattva would receive all such questions and challenges within a single thought-moment and, using only a single voice, cause them all to attain understanding and liberation."

In this way, when he extensively preaches the Dharma for sentient beings filling two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred trichiliocosm worlds; or a thousand trichiliocosm worlds; or ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, or a billion trichiliocosm worlds; or ten billion, a hundred thousand million, ten thousand million, or a nayuta of trichiliocosm worlds; up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of trichiliocosm worlds, he—relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power—is able to perform extensive Buddha-works for sentient beings, becoming doubly more diligent as he gathers such luminous wisdom.

"If within a single hair-tip there were great assemblies as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably unspeakable worlds, and the Buddha were to preach the Dharma therein; and if the Buddha, according to the minds of various sentient beings, preached the Dharma so that each and every sentient being in their hearts attained various immeasurable dharmas;
as it is with one Buddha, so it is for all Buddhas preaching the Dharma within such great assemblies."

Just as it is with the tip of a single hair, so it is with all worlds throughout the ten directions; within this, one should generate a power of great mindfulness, such that in a single thought-moment, one receives the illumination of all dharmas from all Buddhas without losing even a single phrase.

"If, as in this great assembly filled with sentient beings listening to the Dharma, one were to expound it therein using the light of the definitively pure Dharma to bring about understanding and realization, causing all those sentient beings to attain joy in a single thought-moment—how much more so for the sentient beings in various worlds?"

"When this bodhisattva dwells in this stage, their roots of goodness become increasingly superior; day and night they have no other thoughts, deeply entering the sphere of action of all Buddhas, constantly meeting with all Buddhas, and deeply penetrating the liberation of bodhisattvas."

The Bodhisattva, conforming to such wisdom, constantly beholds all Buddhas; within each and every eon, they make offerings to the Buddhas with immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of exquisite articles of worship. At the abodes of these Buddhas, they pose various questions and challenges, thereby attaining mastery over all dhāraṇīs; thus, the roots of goodness of this Bodhisattva become increasingly superior, luminous, and pure.
"In this way, O Son of the Buddha!
Just as the jeweled crown of a Cakravartin King, when fully adorned with refined gold, or his necklace, cannot be taken away by any minor kings or the people of the four continents; so it is."
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas: dwelling in this stage of Sublime Virtue (*sādhumatī*), their various roots of goodness become increasingly superior, bright, and pure, such that they cannot be destroyed—neither by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, nor by Bodhisattvas of the other stages.
“The roots of goodness of this bodhisattva become increasingly bright, able to illuminate the difficult places of the afflictions of sentient beings; having illuminated them, they draw them back in.
Son of the Buddha!
It is like the Great Brahma King, who can illuminate all the difficult places within the entire trichiliocosm.”
The Bodhisattva is also like this.

Abiding in this stage of the Bodhisattva’s wondrous goodness, their roots of virtue are bright and pure; they illuminate the difficult places where sentient beings dwell in affliction, and having illuminated them, they draw them back into [the fold].
"O Sons of the Buddha!

This is called a brief explanation of the ninth Bodhisattva stage, the Stage of Sublime Virtue (*Sādhumatī*), for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas; if explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even in immeasurable and boundless eons."
"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this stage, he frequently becomes a Great Brahmā King, presiding over a trichiliocosm, such that none can surpass him."

One who understands the meaning as it truly is attains mastery within mastery; they are well able to proclaim the *pāramitās* of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, such that no questioning or challenging by sentient beings can ever exhaust them.

Whatever wholesome deeds they perform—whether through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, or cooperation—they never depart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of their bodhisattva companions, up to and including never departing from mindfulness of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
They constantly give rise to this thought:
"When shall I become the foremost and the most honored among sentient beings, even unto becoming the one upon whom all sentient beings rely?"

If this bodhisattva wishes to practice such diligent effort, in a single thought-moment they attain as many samādhis as there are atoms in ten million *asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms, and can even manifest as many bodhisattva retinues as there are atoms in ten million *asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms. If, however, by the power of their vows, their spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*) are sovereign, they exceed even these numbers, being beyond description for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta* kalpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses: "The Bodhisattvas,
in accordance with their immeasurable and profound power of wisdom,
possess a supreme and most subtle state that is difficult for all the world to know."
Those who benefit sentient beings can reach the ninth stage and enter the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
They attain the most sublime and wondrous samādhis and dhāraṇīs.
With vast and great supernormal powers, skillfully entering the characteristics of the world;
with the certainty of the power of wisdom, able to contemplate all Buddha-dharmas;
with great vows and pure compassion, one attains entry into the ninth stage.
Practicing these higher stages, those who uphold the treasury of all Buddhas are able to penetrate all phenomena—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
whether with outflows or without outflows; and whether mundane or supramundane.
This is both conceivable and inconceivable; knowing that dharmas are determinate or indeterminate,
one contemplates and discerns these characteristics of the three vehicles,
as well as the characteristics of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Arising the knowledge of such dharmas, one destroys the darkness of all ignorance;
following this mind of wisdom is the foremost excellence.
Fully knowing all sentient beings and their various perilous and difficult mentalities, [one acts accordingly].
The flickering and easily shifting mind, the boundless and sovereign mind,
the characteristics of the depth and shallowness of afflictions, and the mental associates that never leave the mind; furthermore,
knowing the characteristics of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the enveloping fetters (*paryavasthāna*), which follow and continue through existence.
Knowing that karmic actions are manifold and diverse, each with its own distinct characteristics,
and that while causes perish, their fruits are never lost— one thoroughly penetrates such matters. Furthermore,
one knows the faculties of sentient beings— whether they be dull, middling, or sharp.
The distinctions of vastness and so forth, the characteristics of the prior and subsequent limits,
the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, as well as all manner of desires and pleasures—
even those numbering eighty-four thousand— he is able to know them all completely.
The nature of the world is likewise: it is a difficult place where afflictions and views abound, uninterrupted since beginningless time.
All latent tendencies of the mind accompany the mind; they bind the mind and are difficult to sever.
One knows that all fetters and afflictions are merely false conceptualizations and discriminations;
they have no location or place, nor do they possess fixed characteristics.
They are not separate from the body, yet they are difficult to perceive.
The power of meditative concentration can obstruct it, and the diamond path can sever it.
Furthermore, one can know that sentient beings enter the distinctions of the six realms;
covered by the waters of craving and the darkness of ignorance, karma is the field and consciousness is the seed.
Born from the sprout of a future body, name-and-form grow together;
since beginningless birth and death, they have continued in succession within the three realms.
Furthermore, one understands that for devas, nāgas, and others, it is the afflictions, various karmas, and the mind [that constitute existence].
If one were apart from the mind, then nothing at all would exist.
All sentient beings abide within the three categories:
some are submerged in various false views, while others dwell upon the path of wisdom.
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they fully know the minds of sentient beings,
their faculties, and their inclinations, along with all their various distinctions.
With profound intent and skillful reflection, they preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
Having attained unimpeded wisdom, they skillfully expound with eloquent speech.
As Dharma-teachers, Bodhisattvas are like the lion king, the bull king, and the king of mountains; they dwell securely in fearlessness.
Throughout all worlds, they rain down the exquisite flavor of ambrosia,
just as a great dragon king can rain down to fill the vast ocean.
These bodhisattvas possess excellent knowledge of the unimpeded [mastery] of phenomena, meaning, expression, and eloquence.
Skillfully able to practice in accordance [with the Dharma], endowed with the power of eloquence,
they are able to attain a million *asaṃkhyeya* dhāraṇīs;
they can receive all the Buddha-dharmas, just as the ocean receives the rain from the dragons.
When a bodhisattva attains such profound, wondrous, and pure,
immeasurable dhāraṇīs through the power of various samādhis,
they are able, within a single thought-moment, to behold immeasurable Buddhas.
Having heard this, with a pure Brahma-voice, they proclaim the jewel of the sublime Dharma.
These Bodhisattvas may teach the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm according to their mental faculties and inclinations, preaching the Dharma so that they may rejoice.
In this way, throughout immeasurable trichiliocosm worlds,
he applies himself with ever-deepening diligence and reflects thus:
"Within the tip of a single hair, immeasurable Buddhas preach the Dharma."
The Buddha expounds the wondrous Dharma for all kinds of people;
these Bodhisattvas receive it all, just as the earth receives all seeds.
They further make this vow:
"All sentient beings throughout all the lands in the ten directions, may they gather together as one assembly.
In a single thought-moment, may you know their minds entirely;
by preaching the Dharma with a single voice, may you cause them all to sever the net of doubt."
When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they become a Dharma King among humans and devas;
acting as a great Dharma teacher, they accord with the minds of sentient beings.
Constantly, throughout day and night, they gather together with all the Buddhas.
Able to abide in the profound and wondrous, In the liberation of the wisdom of cessation;
Having made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, Their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure,
Just like a Wheel-Turning King, Adorned with a crown of genuine gold.
The light shines upon sentient beings in the perilous places of affliction,
like the radiance of the Brahma King illuminating the great trichiliocosm.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage, they act as the [protectors] of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.
The Great Brahmā King of the World, with all his faculties fully sharp and keen,
skillfully uses the Dharma of the Three Vehicles to instruct and awaken all sentient beings;
all the wholesome karmas he performs are in accord with right mindfulness.
Within a single thought-moment, one can attain immeasurable,
profound, and wondrous samādhis, as numerous as the atoms within all worlds.
One shall behold the Buddhas of the ten directions preaching the Dharma with subtle and wonderful voices.
Beholding the Buddha’s great supernormal power, they further give rise to immeasurable vows.
Thus, this ninth stage—the sphere of activity for those of great wisdom—is profound, subtle, and difficult to perceive; it has now been briefly explained.
As he spoke of the unsurpassed deeds performed by the great bodhisattvas—
numbering countless nayutas— the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens in the sky above were all filled with great joy in their hearts.
With hearts full of reverence, they made manifold and wondrous offerings to the Buddha.
Countless nayutas of bodhisattvas were filled with immeasurable joy;
they burned all manner of exquisite incense, extinguishing all afflictions.
The King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, together with the great assembly of devas,
dwelt in the midst of space; their hearts were filled with great joy,
and with minds of profound reverence, they all prepared various kinds of offerings.
Each scattered various precious garments, which descended while swirling in the air.
Immeasurable billions of celestial maidens, their faculties filled with joy and delight,
offered worship to the Buddha from the void above with hearts full of reverence.
They simultaneously produced immeasurable billions of *nayuta* musical instruments, and from among all those objects, there issued forth these sounds:
“The Buddha sits here; he pervades everything everywhere.”
Within the lands of the ten directions, Buddhas likewise appear everywhere.
With immeasurable billions of various marks and signs adorning their bodies,
they are exquisitely beautiful beyond compare, filling the worlds.
From within a single pore, he emits immeasurable rays of light,
extinguishing all the fires of affliction throughout the world.
These number as many as the motes of dust in the ten directions, beyond all calculation or measure.
The radiance from a single pore is likewise inexhaustible;
each beholds a Buddha-body, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Sometimes one sees the Buddha in various forms, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitude;
sometimes one sees him in Tuṣita Heaven, teaching and transforming the devas.
Sometimes one sees him descending from Tuṣita to enter a womb.
Some see him at the time of his birth; some see him leaving home at night;
some see him sitting at the site of enlightenment and accomplishing the unsurpassed path;
some see him turning the wheel of Dharma; and some see him entering parinirvāṇa.
In immeasurable lands, they manifest in various ways;
for the sake of delivering sentient beings, such things occur everywhere.
It is like a skillful illusionist who is well-versed in the arts of illusion.
He manifests to all sentient beings Various and diverse bodies.
Within such Buddha-wisdom, He is skillful in manifestation,
Transforming all bodies To pervade every world.
Just as all phenomena are empty and quiescent, having been devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics from the outset,
and being identical to space, so too is the Great Teacher.
Having attained entry into the ultimate truth, he possesses this subtle and wondrous nature and characteristic.
In accordance with the characteristics of the Dharma-nature, The Buddha displays his great supernormal powers.
The nature practiced by all Buddhas— All sentient beings abide within this very nature;
Their characteristics are identical to the characteristic of sameness.
All phenomena are equal, entering into the foremost state of the meaning of quiescent extinction; they are entirely devoid of marks.
If one wishes to attain the Buddha-wisdom, one should abandon all conceptualizations.
Thoroughly penetrating both existence and non-existence, he swiftly became a Teacher of Gods and Humans.
The hosts of celestial maidens all produced such myriad wondrous sounds—
ten million kinds in all— as they gazed upon the Buddha in profound stillness.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, seeing that the assembly was entirely tranquil,
addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha of Great Renown!
“From the ninth stage up to the tenth stage,
please briefly explain now the various great supernormal powers of the Bodhisattvas.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
“O Son of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas possess such immeasurable wisdom and have skillfully practiced the Buddha-way up to the ninth stage (*navamī bhūmi*), having well accumulated all pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) and gathered immeasurable factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), protected by great merit and wisdom, extensively practicing great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), deeply understanding the distinctions in the nature of the world, penetrating the difficult places where sentient beings dwell, reaching the sphere of activity of all Tathāgatas, and recollecting the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice of quiescence (*nirvāṇa*), they proceed toward the powers (*bala*), fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of all Buddhas; holding fast to these without relinquishing them, they attain the station of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).”
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas practice in accordance with this wisdom and approach the stage near the rank of a Buddha, they attain the Bodhisattva Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement, which manifests before them."

Furthermore, there appeared before him a million *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis, such as: the samādhi of entering the distinctions of the dharma-nature; the samādhi of adorning the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); the samādhi of raining down the light of flowers upon all worlds; the samādhi of the ocean-treasury; the samādhi of the ocean-seal; the samādhi of the vastness of space; the samādhi of discerning the nature of all dharmas; the samādhi of following the mental activities of all sentient beings; the samādhi of discerning all dharmas according to reality; and the samādhi of attaining faith in the wisdom of the Tathāgata. All such samādhis manifested themselves.
This bodhisattva enters all these samādhis and thoroughly understands the distinctions among their functional applications. The final samādhi is named "Benefiting the Stage of All-Knowledge.

When this samādhi manifests before him, a great jewel lotus-king emerges, its circumference equal to a million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems. It is adorned with an interlacing of every kind of precious gem, surpassing everything in all worlds. It is born from supramundane roots of goodness, accomplished through the wisdom of the emptiness of nature and the practice that all phenomena are like illusions; its radiance is able to illumine all worlds.
Its stem is made of great precious lapis lazuli, surpassing all that belongs to the various heavens and being immeasurable;
its pedestal is made of king-candana sandalwood, its filaments are made of great agate jewels, and its petals are made of the golden light of Jambūnada gold;
within it are infinite radiances, and all manner of exquisite jewels are contained therein.
A net of jewels covered it from above, surrounded by as many lotuses as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms.
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s body was exquisite and beautiful, perfectly matching the flower seat.
Because this bodhisattva has attained the power of the samādhi of the stage of all-knowledge, his body is now present upon a great lotus throne.

Immediately, each of his retinue members is likewise upon a lotus, surrounding him; each of these bodhisattvas, seated upon their lotuses, attains one million samādhis and, with single-minded reverence, gazes up at the Great Bodhisattva.

"When this bodhisattva ascends the lotus throne, all worlds currently existing in the ten directions tremble greatly; all evil realms are completely stilled; light universally illuminates the worlds of the ten directions; all worlds become entirely adorned and purified; and all are able to see and hear the great assemblies of all Buddhas."

Why is this? As this bodhisattva sits upon the great lotus throne, there immediately issue forth from beneath his feet a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light, which illuminate the Avīci hells and other realms throughout the ten directions, extinguishing the suffering and affliction of sentient beings;
from his two knees, he emits various rays of light that fully illuminate all animals throughout the ten directions, eliminating their suffering and affliction.
From his navel, he emitted various rays of light that illuminated all hungry ghosts throughout the ten directions, extinguishing their suffering and affliction;
from his left and right flanks, he emitted various rays of light that illuminated the bodies of humans throughout the ten directions, bringing them peace, stability, and happiness;
and from both his hands, he emitted various rays of light that illuminated the palaces of the devas and asuras throughout the ten directions.
From his two shoulders, he emitted various rays of light that illuminated the śrāvakas of the ten directions;
from his neck, he emitted various rays of light that illuminated the pratyekabuddhas of the ten directions;
and from his mouth, he emitted various rays of light that illuminated the bodies of all bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, up to those dwelling in the ninth stage.

From his white tuft of hair, he emitted various rays of light that illuminated the bodies of Bodhisattvas who had attained their positions throughout the ten directions; all the palaces of Māra were thus eclipsed and became invisible.

From the crown of his head, he emitted as many rays of light as there are atoms in a million *asaṃkhyeya* triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems, illuminating the great assemblies of Buddhas throughout the ten directions. These rays circled the worlds ten times, remained suspended in the void to form a network of light—lofty, vast, brilliant, and pure—as an offering to all the Buddhas.

Such an offering surpasses all offerings made by Bodhisattvas from their first aspiration up to the ninth stage; it is not matched by even a hundredth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-billionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.

"This great net of radiant light surpasses all the flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, ointments, garments, banners, canopies, various jewels, necklaces, and mani-gems used as articles of worship throughout the worlds of the ten directions, because it arises from supramundane roots of goodness."
In each of the great assemblies of the Buddhas, a rain of various jewels fell like massive clouds.
If there are sentient beings who perceive and understand such offerings, you should know that they are all certain to attain the unsurpassed Great Way.
When these rays of light had thus rained down great offerings and returned, they circled the great assemblies of the Buddhas ten times and entered beneath the feet of the Buddhas.
At that time, the Buddhas and the great bodhisattvas knew that in a certain world, a certain bodhisattva mahāsattva was practicing such a path and had achieved the reception of his office.
“O Sons of the Buddha!

At that moment, bodhisattvas from the ten directions—beginning with those who have reached the ninth stage and extending to infinite numbers—all came to surround him. They presented great offerings and, with single-minded reverence, gazed upon and paid homage to him, each attaining ten thousand samādhis.”

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained their offices emitted from their vajra-adorned chests a great light named "Destroyer of Mara’s Thieves," accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of subsidiary rays. It illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, manifesting immeasurable spiritual powers, and likewise entered the chests of these great Bodhisattvas.
When this light has vanished, these Bodhisattvas immediately attain great power, with their supernormal knowledges and wisdom increased a hundred thousand millionfold.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

At that time, all the Buddhas emitted from the white tuft between their eyebrows a ray of light named "Augmenting the Stage of All-Knowledge. It was accompanied by an infinite and boundless retinue of radiance, illuminating all worlds in the ten directions without exception. It circled all worlds ten times, manifesting the great supernormal powers of all Buddhas, exhorting and encouraging immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas. All worlds in the ten directions shook in six ways; the sufferings and afflictions of all evil realms were extinguished;

and all the palaces of Māra were eclipsed and no longer appeared. It manifested the places where all Buddhas attained the Way, and it displayed the magnificent arrays of the great assemblies of all Buddhas—vast as the Dharma-nature and ultimate as space.

Having illuminated all worlds, they gathered in the void, circumambulated [the Bodhisattva] to the right, and displayed great miraculous transformations and adornments before entering the crown of this Bodhisattva’s head;

the lights of their respective retinues entered the crowns of the heads of the lotus-born Bodhisattvas in those retinues, whereupon each of those Bodhisattvas immediately attained ten thousand samādhis never before obtained.
This radiance enters the crown of this bodhisattva’s head as if it were the light of a single Buddha;
the same is true for the lights of all Buddhas.

When the radiant light of all Buddhas in the ten directions enters the crown of this bodhisattva’s head, it is called "attaining office" and "entering the realm of all Buddhas"; he becomes endowed with the ten powers of a Buddha and shall henceforth be reckoned among the number of Buddhas.
“O Sons of the Buddha!
It is like the eldest son of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, born of the principal queen, who has perfected the marks of a Wheel-Turning King.

The Wheel-Turning Sage King commands his son to take the waters of the four great oceans upon a throne of Jambūnada gold atop the precious white elephant. Above, a canopy is spread, and it is adorned with various banners, pennants, and musical performances. Holding a golden vessel of fragrant water, [the king] pours it over the crown of the son’s head; he is then named the Anointed Great King. Because he fully possesses and turns the ten paths of wholesome action, he receives the name ‘Wheel-Turning Sage King.’”
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas: when they receive their office, all Buddhas pour the water of wisdom upon the crown of this Bodhisattva’s head, naming him a Crowned Dharma King; because he is fully endowed with the ten powers of a Buddha, he is reckoned among the ranks of the Buddhas.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the office of great wisdom of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
By virtue of this office, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas undergo immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of difficult practices and hardships.
Once these bodhisattvas have attained this office, they abide on the Bodhisattva stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), and their immeasurable merit and wisdom increase ever further.
"O Sons of the Buddha!..."

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), they know, as it truly is, the accumulation of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the accumulation of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the accumulation of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). They know, as it truly is, the accumulation of the nature of the world, the accumulation of the nature of sentient beings, the accumulation of the nature of consciousness, the accumulation of the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the accumulation of the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the accumulation of the nature of space, the accumulation of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the accumulation of the nature of nirvāṇa, and the accumulation of the nature of all afflictions and false views. They know, as it truly is, the various worldly modes of activity and the modes of returning [to the source]. They know, as it truly is, the accumulation of the path of the śrāvaka, the accumulation of the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the accumulation of the path of the bodhisattva; the accumulation of the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) of all Buddhas; the accumulation of the form body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*); and the accumulation of all wisdom.
In this way, he accumulates the attainment of the Buddha-way, the accumulation of turning the wheel of Dharma, and the accumulation of manifesting parinirvāṇa.
To state the essentials: he knows and demonstrates, in accordance with reality, the distinctions among all dharmas.

“This Bodhisattva, through such wisdom that accords with the practice of enlightenment, penetrates ever more deeply according to reality; he knows the transformation of sentient beings, the transformation of karma, the transformation of afflictions, the transformation of views, the transformation of the nature of the world, the transformation of the nature of phenomena, the transformation of Śrāvakas, the transformation of Pratyekabuddhas, the transformation of Bodhisattvas, the transformation of Tathāgatas, the transformation of all things, and the transformation of discrimination and non-discrimination—entering into all of these exactly as they truly are.”

At that time, this bodhisattva knows, as it truly is, the sustenance by the power of the Buddha; knows, as it truly is, the sustenance by the locus of phenomena; knows, as it truly is, the sustenance by karma, the sustenance by afflictions, the sustenance by time, the sustenance by vows, the sustenance by past lives, the sustenance by conduct, the sustenance by the lifespan of an eon, and the sustenance by wisdom.

"When this Bodhisattva dwells within the ten stages, they know as they truly are all the subtle wisdoms of the Buddhas, namely: the subtle wisdom of birth and death, the subtle wisdom of the world, the subtle wisdom of renunciation, the subtle wisdom of attaining the Way, the subtle wisdom of mastery over supernormal powers, the subtle wisdom of turning the wheel of Dharma, the subtle wisdom of maintaining the life-span, the subtle wisdom of manifesting parinirvāṇa, and the subtle wisdom of the long endurance of the Dharma; such subtle wisdoms as these are all known according to reality."

"Furthermore, he knows as they truly are all the secret realms of the Buddhas, namely: the secret of body, the secret of speech, the secret of mind; the secret of discerning the proper and improper time; the secret of bestowing predictions upon Bodhisattvas; the secret of gathering and subduing sentient beings; the secret of the distinctions between the various vehicles; the secret of the eighty-four thousand distinctions among faculties; the secret of the actual performance of karma according to reality; the secret of practice; and the secret of attaining enlightenment. All such secrets he knows as they truly are."

“This Bodhisattva, regarding all the Buddhas’ wisdom for entering into eons—namely, that one eon subsumes incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), incalculable eons subsume one eon; the finite subsumes the infinite, and the infinite subsumes the finite; a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) subsumes immeasurable ages, and immeasurable ages subsume a single thought-moment; an eon subsumes what is not an eon, and what is not an eon subsumes an eon; eons with Buddhas subsume eons without Buddhas, and eons without Buddhas subsume eons with Buddhas; past and future eons subsume the present eon, and the present eon subsumes past and future eons; future and past eons subsume the present eon, and the present eon subsumes future and past eons; long eons subsume short eons, and short eons subsume long eons—he knows all such conceptualizations of eons as they truly are.”

"This Bodhisattva enters, as they truly are, the wisdom of the hair-pores entered by all Buddhas; the wisdom of entering into atoms; the wisdom of lands; the wisdom of body and mind; the wisdom of attaining the Way; the wisdom of sentient beings' bodies and minds attaining the Way; the wisdom of the conduct of sentient beings; the wisdom of attaining the Way; the wisdom of traversing the Buddha-way everywhere; the wisdom of manifesting through conforming conduct; the wisdom of manifesting through contrary conduct; and inconceivable wisdom—which the world cannot know, which Śrāvakas cannot know, which Pratyekabuddhas cannot know, and which Bodhisattvas cannot know, but which only a Tathāgata can know."
"O Sons of the Buddha!
The wisdom of all Buddhas is vast, immeasurable, and boundless; when a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are able to enter into such wisdom."
"O Sons of the Buddha!

As these Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas practice according to this stage, they attain the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable liberation, the Bodhisattva’s unimpeded liberation, the liberation of purified conduct, the liberation of universal-gate illumination, the liberation of the Tathāgatagarbha, the liberation that accords with unimpeded discourse, the liberation of entering the three periods of time, the liberation of the treasury of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the liberation of the light of liberation, and the liberation free from differentiation."
O Sons of the Buddha!
These Bodhisattvas, taking the ten liberations as their foremost, attain in this stage immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* liberations;

they likewise attain hundreds of thousands of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis, hundreds of thousands of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* dhāraṇīs, and hundreds of thousands of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

“Having accomplished such wisdom, this bodhisattva accords with bodhi and achieves immeasurable power of mindfulness; in a single moment, they can reach the presence of immeasurable Buddhas in the ten directions, receive immeasurable illumination of the Dharma and immeasurable rains of the Dharma, and is able to receive, uphold, and master them all.”
For example, just as the great rain poured down by the Dragon King Sāgara cannot be sustained by any land except for the great ocean,
so too, O Sons of the Buddha,
do the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, because they receive the great rain of the Dharma, are able to enter the secret realm of the Tathāgata.

This great rain of Dharma cannot be received by any sentient beings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas; even bodhisattvas from the first stage up to the ninth stage cannot receive and uphold it. Only these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas dwelling on the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma are able to receive and uphold it entirely.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

It is like the great ocean, which can sustain the rain from a single dragon king when he raises great clouds; it can likewise sustain the rain when two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred dragon kings do so. Whether it be a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million, a billion, or a hundred thousand billion nayutas of dragon kings—even up to immeasurable and boundless great dragon kings—when they raise clouds and let their rain fall all at once, the ocean can receive and hold it all."
